foods.name: Almond butter

ageBands.servingNote: Smooth almond butter thinned until it pours off a spoon — never a spoonful, never a thick glob, never crunchy.
ageBands.prepMd:
Use **smooth** almond butter, never crunchy, and check the label for a plain
one: nut and maybe salt, and preferably not even the salt.

Put about a quarter teaspoon in a bowl and stir in warm water, breast milk,
formula, or a puree the baby already eats, a little at a time, until **it no
longer holds its shape and pours off the spoon.** That is the test, and it is
deliberately a test rather than a ratio.

**There is no issued dilution ratio, and the specific one you may have seen
quoted for nut butters is issued by nobody.** AAP's rule is qualitative — spread
thinly. CDC names the hazard and offers no fix at all. The one numeric
preparation anywhere in US guidance belongs to NIAID's peanut-allergy-prevention
protocol: it is **written for peanut**, it is an allergy-dosing instruction
rather than a choking rule, and it does not transfer to almond. A borrowed
number here would be the wrong ratio applied to the wrong food. Thin it until it
pours, and you have done what the guidance actually supports.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing. That is a
logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you are watching, and your clinic
is open. Watch for about two hours — IgE reactions happen within minutes to two
hours.

Same thinned form, or spread very thinly on something soft. **Thickness, not
quantity, is the hazard.** Nut butter stiff enough to hold its shape can
obstruct an airway, and a stiff quarter-teaspoon is more dangerous than a thin
tablespoon.

Thinned into [[oatmeal]] or [[yogurt]], or spread very thinly on a strip of
[[wheat-toast]]. Still never off a spoon, and still never a thick layer.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of smooth almond butter thinned with warm water, breast milk or formula until it pours off a spoon, stirred into a food your baby already eats. No body publishes a first-serving amount, a weekly target or an introduction order for tree nuts — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before the first exposure to tree nuts — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no tree-nut testing protocol, no tree-nut dose and no tree-nut weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Smooth only, never crunchy. Never a spoonful or a thick glob — AAP's hazard list names "thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters" and says to spread thinly instead. Thin it until it no longer holds its shape, or spread it very thinly on something soft.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention ("thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters — be sure to spread thinly instead")
CDC — choking hazards ("chunks or spoonful of nut and seed butters"; "whole or chopped nuts and seeds")

NIAID — Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy, Appendix D. Peanut-scoped. The "never off a spoon" mechanism is applied to almond butter here by analogy, not by issuance; NIAID's whole-nut floor of under 5 years is quoted as issued.
NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children (whole nuts; serve them finely ground)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
FDA — Food Allergies (tree nuts are a major food allergen)
USDA FoodData Central — whole almonds, fdcId 170567 (Fe 3.71, Zn 3.12, Na 1). A PROXY for the whole nut, not a value for the butter; no verified id for almond butter itself.

foods.backgroundMd:
Almond butter is one of three tree-nut records in this canon, alongside
[[cashew-butter]] and [[ground-walnut]]. They are three records rather than one
because **tree nut is not a single allergen.** Almond and cashew are separate
sensitizations, and tolerating one says nothing at all about the other. Reported
clustering runs cashew–pistachio and hazelnut–walnut; almond does not cluster
with cashew.

Which leaves an honest gap that this record will not paper over: **no US body
issues a multi-tree-nut introduction protocol.** How many tree nuts you need to
"cover" the tree-nut allergen, in what order, at what interval — none of that is
issued by anyone. The specialist guidance that exists describes the evidence base
as sparse and waits on trial results. So this record tells you how to serve
almond butter safely, and stops short of telling you how many nuts make a
programme, because nobody knows.

**On the numbers: this record deliberately publishes none.** There is a verified
USDA entry for *whole almonds* — 3.71 mg of iron per 100 g — and it is listed in
the sources as a proxy so you can see what the raw nut looks like. It is **not**
printed as almond butter's iron, and no USDA id is attached to this record.
Grinding a nut into butter changes its moisture and therefore its per-100 g
density, so carrying a whole-nut figure on a butter record would be a
fabrication with a citation stapled to it. **Almond butter's own composition is
unverified here.**
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**This food is on the hazard list by name.** AAP's entry reads "thick chunks of
peanut butter or **other nut butters**" — the words "other nut butters" are what
make it bind almond butter directly, not by analogy. CDC's parallel entry is
"chunks or spoonful of nut and seed butters."

**Never crunchy.** A crunchy butter is a nut butter with pieces of nut in it,
and pieces of nut are separately on the hazard list.

**Never off a spoon.** NIAID's instruction not to give nut butter directly from
a spoon or in lumps to a child under four is written for peanut; applying it to
almond butter is this record's judgement, not NIAID's ruling, and it is tiered
as expert opinion for that reason. The physical mechanism is identical, which is
why it is worth applying.

**Whole almonds are a different food and are not appropriate here.** NIAID:
whole nuts should not be given under **5 years**. AAP's general framing is "until
4 years of age or older." **The two bodies disagree, both positions are live, and
NIAID's five-year floor is the cautious default.** This record does not pick one
silently — it tells you they differ. Whichever you follow, almond butter thinned
is fine from six months; the age floor is about the nut, not the butter. See
[[ground-walnut]] for why "chopped fine" does not get you out of that rule.

foods.name: Apple

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked slices, or raw apple grated on the coarse side of a box grater. Both are guideline-issued forms; raw chunks are not.
ageBands.prepMd:
Two routes, pick either.

**Cooked.** Peel, core, and slice. Simmer with a splash of water, or roast
covered, until a slice collapses under a fork — five to fifteen minutes
depending on thickness. Serve as finger-length slices, which is also what NHS
suggests for apple: "slices instead of small chunks." At this age the whole-hand
grasp means the piece is held in a fist with an end sticking out, so the baby
sets the bite size.

**Grated raw.** Peel, then grate on the coarse side of a box grater. The shreds
are soft enough to gum and short enough that no single piece can lodge. Stir
into yogurt or porridge, or offer on a loaded spoon.

The pincer grasp arrives — AAP puts it at most often between 9 and 10 months —
so soft cooked cubes about the size of your thumbnail become pick-up-able. They
must still be cooked soft or grated. A pincer grip does not make a raw apple
cube safe; it just means the baby can now deliver one to their own airway.

Grated raw apple stays useful here and is the easier weekday version.

Still cooked soft or grated raw. Baked apple, apple stirred through oatmeal,
apple sauce, apple in a stew.

Raw apple chunks and raw apple slices thick enough to snap off are the one thing
that does not change at twelve months. AAP's line is four years, not one.

choking.note: AAP names "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" on its choking-hazard list and keeps them off the menu until 4 years of age or older. That restriction is about raw pieces, not about apple — cooked or grated apple is fine from six months.
choking.requiredModification: Never raw chunks. Either cook it until it mashes easily with a fork, or grate it raw. Peel it either way.

CDC — Choking Hazards
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods
NHS — Help your baby enjoy new foods
NHS — Foods to avoid giving babies and young children

foods.backgroundMd:
Apple is one of the few foods in this canon that three separate guideline
bodies name by name — and all three name it as a hazard in its raw form. AAP
lists "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" and says to keep them from
children "until 4 years of age or older." CDC's hazard list says "raw carrots or
apples." NHS covers it in its preparation guidance.

That is not a reason to skip apple. It is a reason to change its form, and
unusually there are **two fixes that guideline bodies actually issue** rather
than one someone extrapolated:

- **Cook it** until you can mash it easily with a fork (CDC and NHS both).
- **Grate it raw** (NHS).

Peel it either way. NHS notes that removing the skin makes food easier to
swallow, and apple skin does not break down under gums.

Nutritionally apple is close to filler: 0.12 mg of iron per 100 g raw, and
cooking destroys nearly all the vitamin C — USDA's cooked, peeled entry gives
0.2 mg per 100 g against 4.6 mg raw. So **cooked apple is not a useful vitamin-C
partner for an iron meal**; use [[mango]], [[green-peas]], or
[[butternut-squash]] for that. Apple's value here is that it is cheap,
year-round, familiar, and takes flavour well alongside things a baby is less
sure about.

No juice before 12 months. Applesauce is fine if it is unsweetened — added
sugars are off the menu under 24 months.

[[pear]] is handled differently because a ripe European pear goes soft;
[[korean-pear]] is handled like apple because it does not.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Raw apple is hard, smooth, and breaks into airway-sized wedges under a bite —
the exact combination that makes it one of the named entries on both the AAP and
CDC lists. A baby who can bite a piece off cannot reliably grind it, and the
piece that comes away is the wrong shape.

Cooking and grating are the two fixes, and they are guideline-issued rather than
inferred. Peeling is the third and applies to both.

Test cooked apple the way you would test any cooked fruit: press a piece between
your fingers. If it holds its shape, it needs longer.

foods.name: Atlantic mackerel

ageBands.servingNote: Flaked fine and searched by hand — mackerel is the boniest fish here — then moistened so the flakes hold together.
ageBands.prepMd:
Mackerel is the boniest fish in this set. Fillet it or buy it filleted, then take
the skin off and go over the raw flesh with your fingers along the whole length,
not just along the spine line — the fine bones run through the fillet. All of
this happens **before** cooking: that is CDC's order, NHS says to remove bones
from fish, and the Canadian Paediatric Society says plainly not to feed a baby
fish with bones. Raw flesh is also far easier to search than hot cooked flesh.

Bake, grill, or pan-cook until the flesh is opaque through and flakes apart.
USDA FSIS gives 145 °F for fish and shellfish.

Flake it fine, run the flakes through your fingers one more time, and moisten
with cooking liquid or a puree so they hold together. Mackerel is oilier than
cod, so it needs less added moisture — but it needs more searching.

Larger flakes, self-fed, still hand-searched every time. Mackerel's strong
flavour lands better mixed into rice or [[oatmeal]] than served plain, which
also makes it easier to gather.

However the family eats it, still deboned and still cooked through. Grilled
고등어구이 made without salt is fine; the salted version is not — see below.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned Atlantic mackerel, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish below twelve months, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway does not read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin and every bone before cooking, then flake and search the cooked fish by hand. Mackerel carries fine bones through the whole fillet, not just along the spine.

foods.backgroundMd:
This record is about one species: ***Scomber scombrus***, which FDA calls
**Atlantic mackerel**. Naming matters more here than for any other food in this
canon, so the species is on the page and stays on the page.

Nutritionally it is the best of the five fish here for iron — 1.57 mg per 100 g,
about three times [[cod]]'s and half again [[salmon]]'s — with 0.94 mg zinc and
83 mg sodium. On mercury, FDA and EPA place Atlantic mackerel in **Best
Choices**, and further, on the shorter sub-list of Best Choices that are *even
lower* in mercury. That is the safest classification FDA issues.

### 고등어 is usually a different mackerel, and you should know which

**Korean 고등어 is normally *Scomber japonicus*, which FDA calls Pacific chub
mackerel — not *Scomber scombrus*.** They are close relatives and they look
similar on ice, but they are not the same fish, and we are not going to pretend
otherwise on a page a parent uses.

What this changes and what it does not:

- **Safety tier: identical.** Pacific chub mackerel is also a **Best Choice**.
  If you buy 고등어 from a Korean grocer, you have bought a Best Choice fish.
- **Sub-list: different.** Only Atlantic mackerel is on FDA's "even lower in
  mercury" sub-list. Pacific chub mackerel is a Best Choice but is not on it.
- **Composition: we have no verified figures.** The numbers on this page come
  from USDA record 175120, which is *S. scombrus*. **No verified USDA record for
  cooked *S. japonicus* was located**, so if the fish in your pan is 고등어, treat
  the iron, zinc and sodium here as the closest available reference rather than a
  measurement of what you are cooking.

Everything else on this page — bones, cooking, salt-cured forms, raw forms —
applies to both fish equally.

### The label trap: three tiers collide on the word "Spanish"

FDA's Seafood List sets acceptable market names for seafood and marks other
names as prohibited vernaculars. Read together, they produce a genuine hazard:

- FDA's own acceptable market name for **King mackerel** — *Scomberomorus
  cavalla*, which is a **Choice to Avoid**, FDA's highest-mercury tier — is
  **"Mackerel, King or Spanish"**. A package lawfully labelled "Spanish
  mackerel" may therefore be King mackerel.
- "Spanish" is *also* a prohibited vernacular for **Pacific chub mackerel**, a
  Best Choice.
- And "Mackerel, Spanish" is the market name for *Scomberomorus maculatus*,
  Atlantic Spanish mackerel, which FDA tiers as a **Good Choice**.

So the words "Spanish mackerel" on a package can point at an Avoid fish, a Good
fish, or a Best fish. **The label is ambiguous and carries no reliable tier
information.** "Common mackerel" is no better — it maps to both Atlantic and
Pacific chub mackerel.

The practical instruction: buy mackerel where you can establish the species, and
do not treat "mackerel" as one food. If the only thing you know is the word on
the package, you do not know which tier you have.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones, more than any other fish here.** Deboned mackerel flesh is soft and
low-risk; the bones are the entire hazard, and mackerel has a lot of them
distributed through the fillet. Debone before cooking, then search the cooked
flakes by hand. The tweezers-and-fingertips technique is common practice, not a
rule anyone issued — the issued rule is simply that the bones come out, and that
they come out before cooking.

**No salt-cured mackerel.** 자반고등어 is salt-preserved, and salt is advised
against for babies by both NHS and CDC. We publish no sodium figure for it,
because none was verified against a primary source; the 83 mg per 100 g on this
page is plain cooked fish only.

**No raw mackerel.** FDA is explicit that children should not eat raw fish,
including sushi and sashimi. That rules out 고등어회.

**Mercury does not cook out.** FDA states directly that mercury is found
throughout the tissue of a fish, so cleaning or cooking will not reduce it. This
matters here because the species question above cannot be fixed in the kitchen —
if you bought the wrong mackerel, cooking it does not make it a Best Choice.

**How much per week — no infant answer, and two bodies disagree above twelve
months.** FDA and EPA's advice is titled for children **ages 1 to 11**, and its
smallest figure is one ounce at age one; **no US body publishes a per-week amount
for a six-to-eleven-month-old**, so this record does not invent one. Above the
first birthday the two frameworks diverge and it is worth knowing which you are
reading:

- **FDA/EPA** tier fish on **methylmercury** alone and issue no sex-specific cap
  for children — two servings a week from Best Choices.
- **NHS** caps oily fish for children **by sex** — boys up to 4 portions a week,
  girls no more than 2 — on **dioxins and PCBs**, a different contaminant
  entirely, because of pollutants that could accumulate before a future
  pregnancy. NHS names mackerel as an oily fish.

Neither framework reaches below twelve months. We are surfacing the disagreement
rather than picking a winner; the more cautious construction is NHS's, since it
adds a limit FDA does not.

**One wording point, because two rules look identical and are not.** FDA's fish
advice suggests watching your child for **several days before feeding fish a
second time**, while the same paragraph explicitly rejects delaying allergen
introduction. That sentence is about the gap between the **first and second
exposure to fish itself**. It is **not** the familiar "wait 3–5 days between new
foods" rule, which is about *unrelated* foods and is not evidence-based: IgE
reactions happen within minutes to two hours. Keep introducing other new foods
on your normal schedule. The tension between FDA's two sentences is real and we
are flagging it rather than resolving it.

foods.name: Avocado

ageBands.servingNote: Slippery is the whole difficulty. Expect it to squirt out of the fist before it gets anywhere near the mouth.
ageBands.prepMd:
Halve, remove the pit, and cut the flesh into long wedges — roughly the length
of an adult finger, thick enough not to collapse when squeezed. Leaving a
strip of skin along the back gives something dry to hold; the skin itself is
not eaten.

One honest caveat about that shape: AAP's published rule is to cut food for
infants into pieces no larger than one-half inch, and that is the only
dimensional instruction any US body issues. Longer soft-food spears are
widespread practice rather than a guideline instruction, and they rest on the
food yielding under light pressure. If a piece holds its shape when you press
it, it is the wrong piece regardless of its length.

Once your baby picks things up between thumb and forefinger instead of raking
at them, small cubes work and are less frustrating. Keep offering a wedge or
two alongside — biting off a piece is a separate skill from picking one up.

However the rest of the table is eating it: cubed, sliced, mashed on toast,
stirred through other foods. No caveat beyond ripeness.

choking.requiredModification: Use fruit ripe enough to yield to gentle thumb pressure. Underripe avocado is a firm food, not a soft one.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

foods.backgroundMd:
One of the few foods that needs no cooking and no softening — a ripe avocado
is already at the texture everything else has to be cooked down to. It appears
on no choking-hazard list, and no primary source restricts it.

Do not think of it as an iron food. At 0.55 mg per 100 g of non-heme iron it
contributes very little, so it belongs alongside the foods doing the real work —
[[beef]], fortified [[oatmeal]], [[lentils]] — rather than instead of them. It is
mostly fat and calories, which at this age is a point in its favour.

Related: [[banana]] is the other no-cook soft food and behaves much the same in
the hand.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Ripeness is the only real variable. A hard avocado is a firm raw food and
should be left to ripen rather than served, which is the same logic CDC
applies to hard raw fruit and vegetables generally.

Some people with latex allergy react to avocado, but no primary infant-feeding
source addresses that, so this record makes no claim about it either way.

foods.name: Banana

ageBands.servingNote: Peel back half the skin and leave the rest on — it is the only dry part of a banana.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel about half the skin down, cut the banana in half across the middle, and
hand over the piece with skin still on the bottom half. Bare banana is
notoriously slippery; the skin is the grip.

If you want it bare, one common trick is to score the peeled banana lengthwise
into thirds so it separates into long spears that hold together better than a
whole one. That is a kitchen technique, not an instruction from anybody.

On size: AAP's published rule is to cut food for infants into pieces no larger
than one-half inch, and that is the only dimensional instruction a US guideline
body issues. Longer soft-food spears are widespread practice rather than
guideline advice, and they depend entirely on the fruit yielding under light
pressure.

Once your baby picks things up between thumb and forefinger rather than raking
at them, small pieces stop being frustrating. Cut into short chunks, or leave
some longer pieces alongside so biting stays in practice.

However the rest of the table is eating it — in chunks, sliced onto oatmeal,
mashed into yoghurt. No caveat beyond ripeness.

choking.requiredModification: Use fruit ripe enough to bruise under light thumb pressure. A firm, underripe banana is a hard food.

American Academy of Pediatrics
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards

foods.backgroundMd:
One of the few foods named by a guideline body for this exact moment: NHS lists
bananas among the fruits to offer from around six months, and AAP names small
pieces of banana as a suitable finger food. No cooking, no softening, no
equipment.

It is not an iron food. At 0.26 mg of non-heme iron per 100 g it is close to
the bottom of anything in this canon, so serve it for what it is — an easy,
familiar carbohydrate that a baby can practise on — and keep the iron work with
meat, fortified cereal, beans, and lentils.

Related: [[avocado]] is the other no-cook soft food and behaves much the same in
the hand.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Ripeness is the whole story. A ripe banana compresses to nothing; a firm,
green-shouldered one behaves like a hard raw fruit and should be left a few days
instead.

You may have been told never to serve banana in rounds. Worth knowing where that
comes from: CDC's rule about round foods is written about grapes, cherries,
berries, tomatoes, hot dogs, and string cheese — **banana is not on that list**,
and no guideline body prohibits banana coins. Ripe banana does not hold a rigid
circular shape the way a grape or a hot-dog slice does, which is the property
the rule is actually about. Cut it however suits your baby's grip.

foods.name: Barley

ageBands.servingNote: Mix fortified barley cereal with breast milk, formula, or water — never cow's milk before 12 months.
ageBands.prepMd:
Fortified infant barley cereal: put a spoonful in a bowl and mix with breast
milk, formula, or water until it is smooth and thick enough to stay on a loaded
spoon. Start thinner and thicken it over the following weeks — that transition
is the point of the food as much as the iron is.

Whole barley is a different job. Pearled barley needs simmering for the better
part of an hour, well past the chewy texture an adult would want, and then
grinding or mashing. CDC's instruction for whole grains is to cook and finely
grind or mash the kernels; a whole cooked barley grain is on the hazard list as
written.

Barley cereal takes other foods well — mashed [[butternut-squash]], puréed
[[spinach]], mashed [[tofu]] — which is a good way to get the vitamin-C pairing
and the iron into the same bowl.

Thicker, lumpier cereal, and this is the age Health Canada flags for it: lumpy
textures should be offered no later than nine months. Cooked-and-mashed pearled
barley folded into the cereal is a natural step up from smooth.

Barley porridge with soft vegetables and a mashed protein is a full meal at this
age, and a spoon the baby holds themselves is worth the mess.

However the household eats it — boribap, barley in a soup or stew, barley
porridge. Keep grains soft and well cooked, and mash or chop through anything
that is still distinctly chewy.

Roasted barley tea (boricha) is a common household drink but it is a drink, and
before twelve months drinks other than breast milk or formula displace what a
baby actually needs. It also carries no nutrition worth counting.

choking.requiredModification: Cook whole barley well past the doneness you would eat yourself, then grind or mash it. CDC lists whole cooked grain kernels as a hazard and says to cook and finely grind or mash them.

foods.backgroundMd:
FDA names barley explicitly as an alternative to rice cereal in its
inorganic-arsenic guidance, and CDC recommends offering a variety of fortified
infant cereals — oat, barley, multi-grain — rather than only rice. That is why
barley is here.

**The wheat and gluten question, stated exactly, because it is routinely
muddled.**

Barley is **not wheat** and is **not one of the nine US major allergens**. It
carries no US allergen labelling requirement, and a child with an IgE wheat
allergy is not, by that fact, allergic to barley.

Barley **is** a gluten-containing grain. FDA's gluten-free rule defines those as
"wheat, rye, barley, and other grains produced by breeding" them, so a food
containing barley cannot be labelled gluten-free.

Put together: **barley is a celiac question, not a wheat-allergy question.** A
child with celiac disease must avoid it. But do not read "not wheat" as "safe
for a wheat-allergic child" and serve it on that basis — if there is a diagnosed
wheat allergy in the picture, that decision belongs with the clinician managing
it, not with a labelling technicality.

**On timing, there is nothing to wait for.** ESPGHAN's position is that gluten
may be introduced at any point between 4 and 12 completed months, and that
timing does not affect the cumulative incidence of celiac disease — a position
its 2024 update maintains. No delay is warranted, and delaying does not prevent
anything.

**Fortification is the entire nutritional story, and the gap is about 36-fold.**
Dry fortified barley infant cereal carries **48.2 mg of iron per 100 g**. Cooked
pearled barley carries 1.33 mg. Hulled barley is 3.6 mg raw and pearled 2.5 mg
raw, both before the dilution of cooking. Against an iron requirement of 11 mg a
day at 7 to 12 months, fortified infant cereal is the single realistic vehicle
short of meat — the 48.2 mg figure is for the dry powder, so what actually
reaches the bowl depends on how thickly you mix it, but the ratio holds.

Added iron absorbs inefficiently, so pair it with a vitamin-C food in the same
meal: [[mango]], [[green-peas]], [[butternut-squash]]. Do not pair it with
[[yogurt]] — dairy calcium inhibits non-heme absorption.

**Prepare it with breast milk, formula, or water. Not cow's milk before 12
months.** USDA's "prepared" barley cereal entry is made up with whole milk,
which is not the preparation to copy at this age.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Whole cooked grain kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list.** Barley grains
are small but firm and slippery, and pearled barley cooked to an adult's
"al dente" is exactly the texture the list is about. Cook it soft, then grind or
mash.

**Gluten, not wheat allergy.** Barley belongs in a conversation about celiac
disease. It does not belong in a wheat-free diet, and it should not be presented
as a safe substitute for a wheat-allergic child without a clinician's say-so.

**Never cow's milk to mix it before 12 months.** Breast milk, formula or water
only. This is about volume of unmodified cow's milk, not about dairy in general
— see [[yogurt]], which is fine from around six months.

foods.name: Beef

ageBands.servingNote: Ground and loosened with its own juices, broth, or a puree — dry mince scatters and is hard to gather.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy ground, or grind it yourself. Brown it through, breaking it up finer than
you would for yourself, then stir in enough of its own juices, unsalted broth,
or a familiar puree that it clumps instead of scattering. Loose dry mince is
genuinely hard for a six-month-old to collect — it goes everywhere and nothing
gets eaten.

Cook ground beef to 160 °F (USDA FSIS). Remove any fat or gristle **before**
cooking rather than picking it out afterwards; that is CDC's instruction and it
is easier that way.

A common alternative at this age is a large, palm-sized patty or a strip of
slow-cooked beef the baby gnaws on without detaching pieces. That is widespread
practice, not a guideline instruction, and it depends on the meat being soft
enough to shred under pressure. If it holds together when you pull at it, it is
the wrong piece.

Same ground form, and now easier — a pincer grasp picks up mince that a whole
hand could only push around. Mixed into [[oatmeal]] or mashed vegetables it goes
down faster than on its own.

Whatever the table is eating, subject to two things. Meat still needs to be soft
and cut small: "tough or large chunks of meat" stays on CDC's hazard list past
the first birthday. And processed beef stays out — hot dogs, sausages, and lunch
meat are excluded twice over, once for sodium and once because CDC's rule for
cylindrical foods is to cut them into short thin strips rather than rounds.

choking.requiredModification: Ground or finely minced, never chunks. Remove fat, skin, and bones before cooking, and cook until it mashes with light pressure.

foods.backgroundMd:
Beef is the clearest example of why the old "food before one is just for fun"
line does not hold. WHO's 2023 complementary feeding guideline recommends
animal-source foods — meat, fish, or eggs — **daily** from six months as a
strong recommendation, and Health Canada and the Canadian Paediatric Society ask
for iron-rich foods from about six months, at least twice a day.

What makes beef different from the plant sources is the *form* of the iron. CDC
classifies the iron in meat, poultry, and fish as heme iron and says plainly
that it is more easily absorbed than the non-heme iron in plants and fortified
cereals. Pan-browned ground beef carries 2.93 mg per 100 g, plus zinc, and
unlike [[lentils]] or [[black-beans]] it does not need a vitamin-C food beside
it — heme absorption is not vitamin-C dependent. Pair it with [[broccoli]] if
you like, but for taste, not chemistry.

CPS names "minced" among suitable forms, which lines up with the hazard list:
ground beef is the guideline-friendliest way to serve it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Two separate things, both real.

**Choking.** Chunks of meat are a named hazard-list entry. Ground, finely
minced, or shredded-to-collapse is the safe form; a cube of steak is not, at any
age in this range.

**Cooking.** Ground beef to 160 °F, whole cuts to 145 °F with a three-minute
rest. Ground meat mixes surface bacteria all the way through, which is why its
target is higher than a steak's — for a baby that margin is not worth trimming.

foods.name: Beef liver

ageBands.servingNote: A very small amount, cooked through and blended into a food the baby already eats — not a portion of its own.
ageBands.prepMd:
Rinse the liver, pull off the thin outer membrane, and cut out the pale tubes —
all before cooking. Braise or gently pan-cook it until it is firm and uniformly
brown through the middle, with no red or bloody centre.

**There is no cooking temperature on this page, and that is deliberate.** USDA
FSIS issues no safe internal temperature for beef liver: it is not on the safe
temperature chart, whose beef row covers steaks, chops and roasts, and it is not
in FSIS's beef handling guidance. Rather than borrow a number from a different
cut, we describe the doneness test instead — cooked through, firm, no red in the
centre. FDA is explicit that children should only eat meat cooked to a safe
internal temperature, so undercooked liver is out even though the number is
missing. (Chicken liver *does* have an issued temperature, because FSIS covers
it as a giblet. Beef liver does not.)

Then puree or mince it very fine and stir a **small** amount into a food your
baby already eats — a mashed vegetable, [[oatmeal]], or a mince the baby is used
to. Liver on its own is dry, grainy and strong-tasting, and a baby will usually
refuse it; blended in, it disappears.

The same form and the same small amount. Nothing about the pincer grasp changes
the vitamin A arithmetic, so this does not become a finger food or a portion in
its own right — it stays an ingredient stirred through something else.

Still blended in, still bounded by the frequency note. One caution about the
numbers as your baby gets older: the 600 µg/day UL we cite is the figure for
**birth to 12 months**. We have not verified a figure for the year after that,
so this record does not print one, and the honest thing is to keep the same
caution rather than assume the ceiling rises.

Liver pâté, parfait, and 간 요리 built on cured or heavily salted bases stay out —
those are salt products as much as liver products.

choking.requiredModification: Trim membrane and any tubes before cooking, cook through, then puree or mince very fine and stir into another food. Cooked liver goes grainy and dry, which is hard to swallow on its own.

frequencyLimit.reason: Preformed vitamin A accumulates in the body, and beef liver is the densest source in ordinary food — 9,440 µg RAE per 100 g braised (USDA). Be clear about what this once-a-week ceiling is: NO health body issues an infant frequency cap for liver. It is absent from AAP, CDC, FDA, the Canadian Paediatric Society, WHO, and every NHS baby page. This limit is common practice, borrowed from NHS's "do not eat liver or liver products more than once a week" — advice written for the general adult population, on a page that never mentions children or babies. The only infant-applicable figure anyone has issued is NIH ODS's Tolerable Upper Intake Level for preformed vitamin A: 600 µg per day, birth to 12 months. That UL is the guideline; the weekly cap is a convention laid on top of it.

foods.backgroundMd:
Beef liver is the densest iron and zinc in ordinary food: 6.54 mg of iron and
5.30 mg of zinc per 100 g braised, which is more than twice [[beef]] mince on
iron. It is heme iron, the readily absorbed form.

**And iron is not the constraint on this food. Vitamin A is.**

Braised beef liver carries 9,440 µg RAE of preformed vitamin A per 100 g. NIH
ODS sets the Tolerable Upper Intake Level for preformed vitamin A at **600 µg
per day from birth to 12 months**, and says chronic intake above the UL can
cause congenital birth defects. Those two numbers are both issued, both
verified, and they are three orders of magnitude apart per unit weight. That
gap, not the iron, is what governs how this food is served.

If you want the arithmetic: dividing the UL by the density puts 600 µg at
roughly **6 g of braised liver**, or about 8 g pan-fried. **That is arithmetic
we did, not guidance anyone issued** — no body has published a gram figure for
infant liver, and you should treat ours as an illustration of the scale rather
than a portion to measure out. What it illustrates is that a normal-looking
spoonful of liver is already past the daily ceiling.

**Where the guidance actually stands.** No health body names liver as an infant
food, and none prohibits it either. That is an absence of guidance, not
permission and not a warning — we are reporting it rather than filling it in.
The one number that is issued and applies to a baby is the 600 µg/day UL. The
once-a-week limit on this page is convention, and the frequency note explains
exactly whose convention it is.

[[chicken-liver]] carries roughly half the vitamin A density and about twice the
iron, which makes it the better-value liver on both axes if you are choosing
one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Vitamin A is the hazard, and it is cumulative.** Preformed vitamin A — the
animal form, which is what liver contains — is stored rather than excreted, so
the risk is not from one meal but from repetition. That is why this record
carries a frequency limit at all, and why it is the only food in the canon that
needs one.

Read the frequency limit for exactly what it says: the 600 µg/day UL is issued
by NIH ODS and applies to your baby. The once-a-week ceiling is not issued by
anyone for a baby. It comes from an NHS page written for adults that does not
mention children, and applying an adult rule to a body a fraction of the weight
is an extrapolation. We have made that extrapolation in the cautious direction
and labelled it, because the alternative was to publish no limit at all beside a
food carrying 15 times the daily UL in a 100 g portion. If you want a number for
your own baby, this is a good question for your pediatrician — and one they can
actually answer, because it depends on what else your baby eats.

**No cooking temperature exists.** See the prep note. Cook it through and judge
by colour and firmness, and do not let anyone tell you liver is best served
pink — for a baby it is not.

**Texture.** Cooked liver goes grainy and can pack at the back of the mouth. It
needs to be pureed or minced very fine and carried in something moist, which is
also how it becomes edible.

**Supplements.** If your baby is on a vitamin A-containing supplement or a
multivitamin, that counts toward the same 600 µg ceiling. Check the label before
adding liver to the week.

foods.name: Black beans

ageBands.servingNote: Every bean flattened — a whole cooked bean is a named choking hazard, however soft it feels.
ageBands.prepMd:
Cook from dry until the beans collapse, or use canned. Then flatten every single
bean — press each one between thumb and forefinger, or run a fork or potato
masher through the lot until nothing round is left. Loosen with cooking liquid,
unsalted broth, or a puree so the mash gathers on a spoon.

Bean skins sometimes separate and float free of the mash. No guideline body
instructs removing them; parents who do it are following common practice, not a
rule.

Same mash, now self-fed, and it works well spread on a strip of toast or stirred
into [[oatmeal]]. A pincer grasp can pick up an individual bean, which is exactly
the reason to keep flattening them.

Still flattened. This is the part parents are surprised by: "whole beans" is on
CDC's hazard list without an age qualifier, and a toddler who bolts food is not
obviously safer with a round bean than a nine-month-old. Refried, mashed into
rice, or squashed into a burrito filling all work.

choking.requiredModification: Mash, puree, or flatten every bean between two fingers. Whole beans are a named entry on the CDC/WIC choking-hazard list.

foods.backgroundMd:
A cheap, storable, iron-carrying protein that both NHS and the Canadian
Paediatric Society name for this age — CPS's phrase is "mashed beans, peas or
lentils," and the mashing is not decoration.

The iron is non-heme, 2.10 mg per 100 g cooked, which means absorption depends
on what is on the plate beside it. Black beans contain **zero vitamin C**, so
they are the clearest case in this canon for deliberate pairing: CDC advises
serving non-heme iron with a vitamin-C food and names broccoli among its
vitamin-C foods. **[[broccoli]] with black beans is a pairing CDC's own advice
supports**, not a folk tip. [[lentils]] carry more iron per 100 g if you are
choosing between pulses.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Whole beans are a direct entry on the CDC/WIC choking-hazard list**, alongside
whole grapes and chunks of meat. They are small, round, smooth, and about the
size of an infant airway, and being soft does not change the geometry. Mashing
or flattening is the required modification, not a texture preference.

**Sodium, if you use canned.** Beans cooked from dry are about 1 mg of sodium per
100 g. Canned beans are substantially higher — this record does not publish a
figure because we could not verify one, so read the can. Rinsing canned beans
under running water is common practice for cutting the sodium; it is not
guideline-issued, and a no-salt-added can is the more reliable route.

foods.name: Braised short rib (갈비찜)

ageBands.servingNote: The meat only, lifted out of the pot BEFORE 간장 goes in, shredded along the grain and moistened with unsalted braising liquid.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Braise the meat, then pull the baby's portion before you season.**

Practically, that means one of two things. Either braise a piece separately in
unsalted stock or plain water with the aromatics you like — garlic, onion, pear,
radish, all fine — or, if you are making one pot, take the baby's rib out early,
before the 간장 mixture is added, and finish it in a small pan with a little
unsalted liquid.

**Sodium is why, and it cannot be diluted away.** Sodium adequate intake is
110 mg a day from birth to six months and 370 mg from seven to twelve months
(NASEM 2019). There is **no upper limit and no EAR for sodium at any age** — so
370 mg is an adequacy target rather than a ceiling anyone issued. It is still
small enough that a single seasoned adult portion of 갈비찜 overwhelms it. Once
the sauce is in the braise it is in the meat, and adding water or rice does not
take it back out. Pulling the portion before seasoning is widely advised and
sound, but it traces to no numbered rule — treat it as practice.

**Then take it apart, in this order:**

1. **Meat off the bone**, after braising. 🚩 Note the conflict this creates and
   we are not going to hide it: **CDC says remove bones *before* cooking**, and
   갈비찜 by definition does not — the bone is what makes the dish. Taking the
   meat off afterwards is the closest available compliance, and it is our
   accommodation, not CDC's instruction. "Bones in meat or fish" is a named
   entry on CDC's choking-hazard list.
2. **Remove the fat and the cartilage.** Short rib has a lot of both, and
   cartilage stays rubbery no matter how long it braises.
3. **Shred along the grain**, not across it. Shredding along the grain gives
   soft separable strands; cutting across leaves short dense blocks that behave
   like the "tough or large chunks of meat" CDC lists as a hazard.
4. **Nothing over half an inch** — AAP's rule, and the only dimensional rule any
   US guideline body issues.
5. **Moisten** with a spoonful of the unsalted braising liquid so the shreds
   hold together instead of scattering.

🚨 **Never hand a baby the rib bone.** Not to gnaw on, not to hold, not to
"keep them busy while you eat." It is a hard bone with meat and cartilage
attached, and it is on the hazard list in its own right.

No change in principle: still the unseasoned meat, still off the bone, still
shredded along the grain. A pincer grasp makes shreds much easier to pick up
than they were at seven months, so this is often when braised beef finally gets
eaten in quantity rather than pushed around.

You can serve slightly longer strands now — a two-inch shred that the baby bites
from is fine as long as it pulls apart easily under light pressure. If it holds
together when you tug at it, it needs more braising or a different piece.

ageBands.servingNote: The seasoned dish as the family eats it — this is the point at which 갈비찜 itself, rather than just the beef, becomes reasonable.
ageBands.prepMd:
**This is where 갈비찜 itself becomes reasonable**, seasoned, as the family eats
it — and the reason is that the sodium context changes: adequate intake rises to
800 mg a day for a one-to-three-year-old.

Even so, it is a salty dish. Serve it as part of a meal with plenty of unsalted
rice and vegetables rather than as the whole plate, and do not make it the
everyday dinner. If you are cooking a pot for the week, seasoning it a little
lighter than usual costs the adults very little.

The physical rules do not relax: **meat off the bone, fat and cartilage
removed, shredded or cut small, no rib bone handed over.** "Tough or large
chunks of meat" stays on CDC's hazard list past the first birthday.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of meat that has been braised in the seasoned sauce, shredded fine. If you want to introduce soy earlier and more cleanly than a soy-sauce dish allows, plain tofu is the better vehicle — it carries soy without the sodium and without the wheat that comes with 간장.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an existing food allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first exposure to soy — and note that this dish carries TWO of the nine major allergens, because most brewed Korean and Japanese soy sauces contain wheat as well as soybean. That group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of foods the child could have eaten safely.

choking.requiredModification: Take the meat off the bone after braising, remove fat and cartilage, shred along the grain, and cut to no larger than half an inch. Never hand a baby the rib bone.

foods.backgroundMd:
**The most useful thing to understand about 갈비찜 is that the beef and the dish
have different answers.**

The beef is a six-month food, and a good one. WHO's 2023 complementary feeding
guideline asks for animal-source foods daily from six months as a strong
recommendation, and beef carries **heme** iron — the form CDC says is absorbed
more readily than the non-heme iron in plants — plus zinc. Slow-braised short
rib is about as soft as beef gets. On its own merits it is close to an ideal
first protein.

**갈비찜 is a twelve-month dish, and the reason is 간장, not the beef.** The
sodium in the sauce is the constraint, and it is the only thing standing between
this dish and a much earlier start. Which means the practical move is available
to any family: **lift the baby's piece of meat out of the pot before the
seasoning goes in.** At that point it is braised beef, and braised beef is a
six-month food. The three prep sections below are built around that split.

🚩 **Two of the nine major US allergens arrive through the sauce, and the second
one surprises people.** Soy is obvious. **Wheat is not** — most brewed Korean and
Japanese soy sauces are made from soybeans *and* wheat, so 간장 typically carries
both. Families avoiding wheat routinely miss this. Read the bottle: some soy
sauces are wheat-free and say so, and the two are not interchangeable for a
child with a wheat allergy. We could not verify any figure for how much wheat or
residual gluten a given 간장 contains, so this record gives no threshold — only
the instruction to read the label.

If your reason for serving this dish is to get soy into the rotation, [[tofu]]
does that job better: it carries soy without the sodium and without the wheat
that rides along with 간장.

**Composition figures are not published here.** The USDA database was
unavailable when this record was researched, so there is no verified per-100-g
iron figure for short rib. We have deliberately **not** borrowed the ground-beef
number from [[beef]] — a different cut, a different fat content, a different
value. The iron *type* is heme; the amount is pending verification.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Two entries from CDC's choking-hazard list apply to this one dish** — "tough or
large chunks of meat" and "bones in meat or fish." That is unusual and it is why
this record is as specific as it is.

**The bone.** CDC's rule is to remove bones before cooking. 갈비찜 cannot comply,
because the bone is the dish. Take the meat off after braising, and never hand
the bone to the baby. That accommodation is ours.

**The meat.** Shred along the grain, remove fat and cartilage, keep pieces under
half an inch. Braised short rib is soft when it is properly done — if it does
not pull apart under light pressure, it is not ready, and cutting it smaller is
not a substitute for cooking it longer.

**Sodium is the reason this is a twelve-month dish, and it is not adjustable by
dilution.** Braise the baby's portion separately or in unsalted stock. This is
the single most important thing on this page for a family that wants to serve
갈비찜 early: the beef was never the problem.

**Two allergens, one of them hidden.** Soy and — through 간장 — wheat. See the
medical gate above. Read the soy sauce label; wheat-free 간장 exists but is not
the default.

**No guideline body addresses 갈비찜 as an infant food.** What is issued: WHO on
animal-source foods, CDC on bones and chunks of meat and on removing bones
before cooking, AAP's half-inch limit, FDA on soy and wheat as major allergens,
NASEM's sodium intakes. Everything specific to this dish — the pull-before-
seasoning move, shredding along the grain, taking the meat off the bone after
braising — is inherited category rule plus our inference.

foods.name: Broccoli

ageBands.servingNote: A cooked floret with a length of stalk left on — the stalk is the handle, the head is the part that gets eaten.
ageBands.prepMd:
Steam or boil florets until the thickest part of the stalk takes a knife with no
resistance — softer than you would serve yourself, softer than "tender-crisp".
Leave each floret attached to two or three centimetres of stalk so there is
something narrow to hold while the bushy head goes in the mouth.

The tree shape is why broccoli works early: the head is easy to gum and the stalk
is a built-in handle. Pieces cut small are harder at this age, not safer — a
baby who cannot pick them up ends up raking a handful in at once.

The length of that stalk is common practice, not a rule from anybody. AAP's
published dimensional guidance is the single instruction to cut food for infants
into pieces no larger than half an inch, and no body issues per-food shapes. What
carries the safety here is the cooking: if the stalk resists, it is not ready,
whatever length it is.

Small soft pieces of head and stalk, picked up between finger and thumb. Keep a
whole floret on the tray too — biting a piece off is a separate skill from
picking one up, and it is worth practising.

However the rest of the table is eating it, as long as it is cooked soft. Raw
broccoli and thick raw stalks stay out.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until the stalk gives with no resistance and the head mashes between two fingers. Raw broccoli is a hard raw vegetable.

foods.backgroundMd:
**Broccoli's job in a baby's diet is not its own iron — it is everybody else's.**
At 64.9 mg of vitamin C per 100 g it is one of the foods CDC names when it
advises pairing non-heme iron sources with vitamin C so more of the iron is
absorbed. Its own 0.67 mg of iron is a rounding error next to that.

So serve it *with* something: [[black-beans]], which contain no vitamin C at all,
or [[lentils]], which carry the most non-heme iron in this batch and only 1.5 mg
of C. Fortified [[oatmeal]] is the same case. Broccoli beside any of those is a
CDC-supported combination rather than a nice idea.

It is also the food NHS puts first by name. NHS recommends starting with the
less-sweet vegetables — "broccoli, cauliflower and spinach" — so that a baby
gets used to a range of flavours before the sweeter foods arrive.

Frozen broccoli is a legitimate substitute with one caveat worth knowing: USDA's
figures put frozen at 40.1 mg of vitamin C against fresh broccoli's 64.9 — about
a 38% drop. Iron is essentially unchanged at 0.61 mg. Frozen is still a good
vitamin-C food; fresh is a better one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Raw broccoli is a hard raw vegetable, the category CDC says usually needs cooking
so it mashes easily. Raw florets, crudités, and slaw are not a form to serve in
this age range.

The stalk is firmer than the head and is what to test — a head that mashes on a
stem that does not is the piece most likely to be swallowed in a lump. Press the
stalk, not the florets.

foods.name: Buckwheat

ageBands.servingNote: Groats cooked soft and then mashed or ground — a cooked groat is a whole grain kernel.
ageBands.prepMd:
Simmer groats until they are soft all the way through, well past the point where
they still have a bite, then mash or grind them. **A cooked buckwheat groat is a
cooked whole grain kernel**, and CDC's instruction for those is to cook and then
finely grind or mash — buckwheat is not named, but "and other grains" is, and
this is one.

Mashed groats fold into puréed [[butternut-squash]] or [[apple]] easily. Buckwheat
carries no vitamin C, so if you want the iron to count, put a vitamin-C food in
the same bowl.

Soba is not a 6–8 month food in any useful form, and most of it contains wheat
in any case.

Softly cooked groats, mashed rather than ground, mixed through other foods.
Buckwheat porridge takes strong flavours well, which is useful at the age when
plain food starts getting refused.

If you introduce soba here, cut it into short lengths a baby can bite through
rather than serving long strands. No guideline body addresses noodle length, so
that is judgement rather than instruction.

However the table eats it, kept soft. Memil-guksu and soba are normal family
food at this age; cut noodles short, skip the dipping sauce, and check the
package for wheat if that matters to you. Cold noodle broths are usually heavily
salted, which is a separate reason to serve the noodles plain.

choking.requiredModification: Cook groats until soft, then finely grind or mash them, per CDC's rule for whole-grain kernels. Soba noodles should be cut short — long noodles are not addressed by any guideline body, but a length a child can bite through is the sensible reading of the rules that do exist.

CDC — Choking Hazards
FDA — Food Allergies (the nine major food allergens under US law; buckwheat is not among them)
