foods.backgroundMd:
Buckwheat is not wheat and not a cereal grain at all — it is a seed, botanically
closer to rhubarb. Cooked groats carry 0.80 mg of iron per 100 g, which is
modest; the dry roasted groats measure 2.47 mg per 100 g, but that is before the
water goes in. It earns its place here on flavour and texture and on being a
familiar Korean and Japanese food, not on iron.

**The allergen situation is genuinely asymmetric between the countries in this
family's life, and both directions of confusion are common.**

- **In the United States, buckwheat is not one of the nine major food
  allergens.** No US label has to declare it, and none of the FDA labelling
  rules apply to it.
- **Japan and Korea both require buckwheat to be declared on food labels.**
  Korea's list goes beyond the common eight to include buckwheat, beef, chicken,
  peach, pork, tomato and pine nut, reflecting what actually triggers
  immediate-type reactions in Korean children. Korea is also the only country
  where precautionary "may contain" labelling is mandated by law.

So the same product, sold in Seoul and in Los Angeles, carries a buckwheat
declaration in one place and legally need not in the other. **A parent who
learns "buckwheat isn't an allergen" from a US source will misread a Korean
label as alarming; a parent who learns it from Korean relatives will hunt for a
US warning that does not have to exist.** Neither country is wrong. The
asymmetry is the fact, and knowing it is what keeps a label from being
misread in either direction.

(Allergen lists are revised periodically — Japan's has changed more than once in
the last few years — so treat any count you read, including in older reviews, as
a snapshot rather than a constant.)

**"Buckwheat is gluten-free" is true of the seed and false of most soba.**
Buckwheat itself contains no gluten. Commercial soba noodles are commonly
blended with wheat flour, sometimes mostly wheat flour, and wheat *is* one of
the US nine. If wheat matters in your household, the label is the only thing
that settles it — the word "soba" does not.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cooked groats are whole grain kernels** and sit inside CDC's grinding rule.
Cook them soft and mash or grind them; the degree is not specified by anyone, so
judge it by whether a kernel still has structure between two fingers.

**On allergy, hold both facts at once.** Buckwheat is not a US major allergen
and carries no US labelling requirement. It is a recognised, labelled allergen
in Japan and Korea, which is a real signal about how often it causes reactions
in children there — not a labelling quirk. Introduce it the way you would any
new food, watch the first exposure as you would any first exposure, and read
Korean and Japanese labels knowing what they are telling you.

**Soba is a wheat question until the label says otherwise.**

foods.name: Butternut squash

ageBands.servingNote: Roast rather than boil if you can — it keeps its shape better in a fist.
ageBands.prepMd:
Halve it, scoop the seeds, and roast cut-side down at around 200 °C / 400 °F
until a fork slides in with no resistance — usually 35 to 45 minutes. Steaming
works too but leaves it wetter and harder to hold.

Cut finger-length wedges about as thick as two of your fingers. At this age the
whole-hand grasp means the piece is held in a fist with an end sticking out, so
the baby controls the bite. Small pieces are harder now, not safer — they can't
be picked up and end up scooped by the handful.

Skin on or off is your call. Roasted butternut skin is edible and gives
something to grip; peeled is tidier and NHS notes that removing skin makes food
easier to swallow.

Once the pincer grasp appears — AAP puts that at most often between 9 and 10
months — switch to soft cubes about the size of your thumbnail, keeping a few
larger wedges alongside so biting and tearing stay in practice.

Mashed butternut is also a good carrier for something the baby is less sure
about: iron-rich purées, a spoonful of yogurt, ground meat.

However the rest of the table is eating it — cubed, mashed, in soup, roasted in
wedges. Keep some pieces big enough to bite from rather than only pincer-sized
ones.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a piece smashes with light pressure between thumb and forefinger. Raw squash is a hard vegetable and is not appropriate at any age in this range.

sources.body: NHS — Your baby's first solid foods
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
AAP — Infant Methemoglobinemia (Pediatrics 2005;116:784) — RETIRED by AAP June 2025
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 169296, cooked; 2685570, Foundation)

foods.backgroundMd:
A sweet winter squash that roasts to a texture a six-month-old can manage
without any special technique. NHS names squash among the vegetables to start
weaning with, and CDC names squash at the category level.

Treat it as a negligible iron source. USDA's two datasets disagree by roughly
threefold — the legacy cooked entry gives 0.6 mg of iron and 15.1 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g, while the newer Foundation sample gives 0.213 mg and 7.6 mg. The
figure in this record is the higher of the two, and even that is small next to
the 11 mg a day a 7–12 month old needs. Its real job at the table is as a
vitamin-C partner: serve it alongside an iron food such as [[tofu]],
[[green-peas]], or [[barley]] cereal, since vitamin C improves absorption of
plant (non-heme) iron eaten in the same meal.

[[kabocha]] behaves almost identically once cooked, and the prep below applies
to both.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Undercooked squash is firm enough to be a hazard. Test a piece between your own
fingers rather than trusting the timer; if it holds its shape under pressure, it
needs longer.

Home-made vegetable purées, squash included, should be cooled quickly,
refrigerated promptly, and not kept for days.

That advice used to have a formal citation behind it: AAP's 2005 clinical report
on infant methemoglobinemia named well water as the main risk vector, found
little or no risk from commercially prepared US infant food, and noted that
cases from home-prepared vegetable foods kept too long continued to occur.
**AAP retired that report in June 2025**, so it is no longer current guidance
and nothing has replaced it. The storage habit stands on its own merits — cool
it fast, refrigerate it, don't keep it for days — but it is now ordinary food
hygiene rather than a cited recommendation. [[spinach]] covers the whole
argument, including where US and EU advice still differ.

foods.name: Canned light tuna

ageBands.servingNote: No-salt-added only, drained and then deliberately re-moistened — dry tuna packs at the back of the mouth.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy **no-salt-added** light tuna canned in water. Drain it, then flake it fine
and stir it into a food your baby already eats — a mashed vegetable, plain
[[yogurt]], [[oatmeal]], or a puree — until it is properly wet rather than merely
damp.

There is no cooking temperature on this page and none is missing: canned tuna is
retort-sterilised in the tin, so it arrives cooked. Nothing needs to reach a
target temperature. If you warm it, you are doing that for palatability.

Unlike the other four fish here, there is no bone step. Canned light tuna is
already flaked and boneless.

Same form. A pincer grasp still cannot pick up dry flakes usefully, so the
moistening does not stop being necessary — bound into a puree or mashed
[[avocado]] it becomes something a baby can actually get to their mouth.

Mixed into a soft salad, a rice bowl, or a spread, still no-salt-added and still
moist. Regular canned tuna, tuna in brine, and seasoned 참치캔 do not become
appropriate at twelve months; the sodium guidance runs to twenty-four.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of no-salt-added canned light tuna, flaked and moistened into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish below twelve months, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway does not read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Moisten the drained flakes with a puree, unsalted broth, or yoghurt until they hold together. Dry canned tuna is powdery and packs at the back of the mouth.

sources.body: FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (revised Oct 2021; scoped to children ages 1–11). Q&A I.3 tiers canned light tuna as a Best Choice, albacore/white and yellowfin as Good Choices, bigeye as a Choice to Avoid. Q&A VI.1 — canned light tuna is a mix of generally smaller species, most often skipjack. Q&A VI.3 — albacore typically contains three times more mercury than canned light tuna.

FDA Seafood List — acceptable market names and prohibited vernacular names (updated 2026-01-29). "Ahi" is a prohibited vernacular for both bigeye and yellowfin tuna; both bear the single market name "Tuna".
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — foods and drinks to avoid or limit (sodium under 24 months)
NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children (salt under 12 months)
NHS — fish and shellfish ("Fresh and canned tuna do not count as oily fish")
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 171986, light tuna canned in water, no salt added, drained — Fe 1.53 mg, Na 50 mg per 100 g; 334194, canned in water drained — Fe 1.67 mg, Zn 0.66 mg, Na 219 mg)

foods.backgroundMd:
Canned light tuna is the most convenient iron in this set — 1.53 mg per 100 g in
the no-salt-added version, no cooking, no bones — and it is also the food on this
list where the wrong tin is genuinely a different safety decision. Read the
species notes below before you buy.

**"Light" is a mercury tier, not a species.** FDA says canned light tuna can be a
mix of generally smaller tuna species, most often skipjack. That is why FDA
places **canned light tuna in Best Choices** — its safest tier. Note the
precision, though: canned light tuna is a Best Choice but is **not** on FDA's
shorter sub-list of Best Choices that are *even lower* in mercury.
[[rainbow-trout]] and [[pollock]] are on that sub-list; this is not.

**The other tunas are not interchangeable with it.**

| What the tin or menu says | FDA tier | What that means |
|---|---|---|
| Light / skipjack | **Best Choice** | The subject of this record |
| Albacore, or "white" tuna | **Good Choice** | Typically three times more mercury than canned light |
| Yellowfin | **Good Choice** | |
| Bigeye | **Choice to Avoid** | FDA's highest-mercury tier |

For a Good Choice, FDA's instruction is one serving that week **and no other
fish at all that week** — a much tighter rule than it looks, because it removes
every other fish from the week, not just other tuna. That advice is written for
children ages 1 to 11.

**"Ahi" tells you nothing.** FDA's Seafood List records "Ahi" as a *prohibited*
vernacular name for **both** bigeye tuna (a Choice to Avoid) and yellowfin tuna
(a Good Choice), and both species lawfully carry the single market name "Tuna".
So "ahi" on a menu or at a counter carries no tier information at all — it could
be either. This is a naming fact, not an inference from one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Buy no-salt-added, and understand that draining does not fix it.** This is the
most actionable purchasing instruction in this set of records. USDA's figures:
regular light tuna canned in water and drained carries **219 mg of sodium per
100 g**; the no-salt-added version carries **50 mg**. That is a **4.4× gap, and
it is measured after draining** — the salt is in the fish, not floating in the
water you pour off. CDC advises against high-sodium foods for children under two,
and NHS says babies should not eat salty foods. One label choice at the shop
closes the gap entirely; nothing you do in the kitchen does.

**Never substitute albacore.** Albacore is sold as "white" tuna, sits beside
light tuna on the shelf at a similar price, and looks like an upgrade. FDA states
that it typically contains **three times more mercury** than canned light tuna,
and tiers it as a Good Choice rather than a Best Choice, with the "no other fish
that week" restriction attached. It is not a swap for this food. Neither is
yellowfin, and bigeye is on FDA's Avoid list outright.

**Texture is the choking consideration, not bones.** Canned tuna is boneless, so
the bone rule that governs the other four fish does not apply. Its risk is
different: drained tuna is dry and powdery and can pack at the back of the mouth.
Moistening it is the modification, and that instruction is common practice rather
than a rule any guideline body issued — but it is the difference between a food a
baby eats and one they gag on.

**Mercury does not cook out.** FDA states that mercury is found throughout the
tissue of a fish, so cleaning or cooking will not reduce it. The species decision
is made at the shop and cannot be undone at the stove.

**How much per week — there is no infant answer.** FDA and EPA's advice is titled
for children **ages 1 to 11**, and its smallest figure is one ounce at age one.
**No US body publishes a per-week amount for a six-to-eleven-month-old**, so this
record does not invent one. Ask your pediatrician if you want a number for your
own baby.

One divergence worth knowing above twelve months: **NHS states that fresh and
canned tuna do not count as oily fish**, so its sex-based oily-fish caps for
children — boys up to 4 portions a week, girls no more than 2, set on dioxins and
PCBs — do not apply to canned tuna. FDA does not address that classification at
all. Neither framework reaches below twelve months.

**One wording point, because two rules look identical and are not.** FDA's fish
advice suggests watching your child for **several days before feeding fish a
second time**, while the same paragraph explicitly rejects delaying allergen
introduction. That sentence is about the gap between the **first and second
exposure to fish itself**. It is **not** the familiar "wait 3–5 days between new
foods" rule, which is about *unrelated* foods and is not evidence-based: IgE
reactions happen within minutes to two hours. Keep introducing other new foods on
your normal schedule. The tension between FDA's two sentences is real and we are
flagging it rather than resolving it.

foods.name: Carrot

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked to fork-mashable first. Raw carrot is on two separate choking-hazard lists.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel, cut into batons roughly the length of an adult finger, and steam, boil, or
roast until a fork goes through with no resistance and the piece mashes when you
press it. Undercooked carrot is the failure mode — it looks done, softens on the
outside, and stays firm in the middle. Test the thickest piece, not the thinnest.

That baton length is common practice, not a rule any body issues. AAP's one
published dimension is to cut food for infants into pieces no larger than half an
inch, and everything else about shape and length in circulation — here and
everywhere — is convention. What actually carries the safety is the mash test.

Soft cubes, picked up between finger and thumb. Keep a few longer soft batons on
the tray as well, since biting a piece off is its own skill.

However the family eats cooked carrot — in soups, roasted, mashed, stirred
through rice. Raw carrot is still out; see below.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a fork mashes it with light pressure. Raw carrot — sticks, batons, coins, or shreds — is named by both CDC and AAP and is not appropriate in this age range.

sources.body: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
NHS Start for Life — what to feed your baby around 6 months

foods.backgroundMd:
Carrot is the most heavily flagged food in this batch, and the reason is narrow:
**raw** carrot is named by name on both US hazard lists — CDC's, which lists
"raw carrots" among hard raw vegetables, and AAP's, which names "raw vegetables
like carrot sticks" among foods to avoid until age four or older. Two bodies
naming the same food is rare.

Cooked carrot is a different food mechanically and is fine. CDC's instruction is
explicit: "Cook hard vegetables and fruits, such as carrots and apples, so you
can easily mash or puree them." That single sentence is the whole record.

Nutritionally it is unremarkable here — 0.34 mg of non-heme iron per 100 g, and
3.6 mg of vitamin C, which is too little to count as the vitamin-C partner for
an iron food. CDC does not list carrots among its vitamin-C foods; use
[[broccoli]] for that job. Serve carrot because it is sweet, cheap, holds its
shape when cooked, and babies like it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Raw carrot is the hazard, and it does not stop being one at twelve months.**
AAP's list of foods to avoid — raw carrot sticks among them — runs to "4 years of
age or older." The concern is a hard food that does not compress meeting an
airway that is still small.

This record allows carrot with a required modification rather than banning it,
because the cooking *is* the modification. If it does not mash under a fork, it
has not been modified yet, and it is still the raw-carrot problem in a warm
disguise.

One place the bodies differ: the Canadian Paediatric Society offers **grating**
as a way to serve raw vegetables, where AAP's list simply keeps raw carrot out
until four. Grated raw carrot is not the same object as a stick — but it is
still hard, and AAP names no exception for it. This app follows the more
cautious of the two and treats cooking as the modification for carrot in this
age range.

**On carrot coins, an honest note.** You will be told never to serve cooked
carrot in rounds. The reasoning is sound — CDC's rule for round foods is to cut
them into small pieces or short thin strips rather than discs, because a disc
can seal an airway. But that rule is written about grapes, cherries, berries,
tomatoes, hot dogs, and string cheese. **Carrot is not named in it.** Cutting
cooked carrot into sticks or half-moons rather than coins is a sensible
extrapolation from a guideline, not an instruction from one — and if the carrot
is cooked soft enough to mash, the shape is much less of the story than the
texture is.

foods.name: Cashew butter

ageBands.servingNote: Smooth cashew butter thinned until it pours off a spoon — never a spoonful, never a thick glob, never crunchy.
ageBands.prepMd:
Use **smooth** cashew butter, never crunchy, with as short an ingredient list as
you can find — ideally just cashews.

Put about a quarter teaspoon in a bowl and stir in warm water, breast milk,
formula, or a familiar puree, a little at a time, until **it no longer holds its
shape and pours off the spoon.**

**There is no issued dilution ratio.** The specific one in circulation for nut
butters is issued by nobody. AAP's rule is qualitative — spread thinly. CDC names
the hazard and offers no fix. The one numeric preparation anywhere in US guidance
belongs to NIAID's peanut-allergy-prevention protocol: **written for peanut**, a
dosing instruction rather than a choking rule, and it does not transfer to
cashew. A borrowed number would be the wrong ratio applied to the wrong food.
Thin until it pours.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on an unhurried day, and watch for about two
hours — IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours.

Same thinned form, or spread very thinly on something soft. **Thickness, not
quantity, is the hazard**: butter stiff enough to keep its shape can obstruct an
airway, so a stiff quarter-teaspoon is worse than a thin tablespoon.

Thinned into [[oatmeal]] or [[yogurt]], stirred through a curry or a dal, spread
very thinly on [[wheat-toast]]. Never off a spoon, never a thick layer.

Cashew appears in a lot of South Asian cooking as **whole or halved nuts** — in
pilaf, in [[semolina-upma]]'s tempering, on top of sweets. Those are pieces of
nut, they are on the hazard list, and they are a different question from the
butter. Grind them in or leave them out.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of smooth cashew butter thinned with warm water, breast milk or formula until it pours off a spoon, stirred into a food your baby already eats. No body publishes a first-serving amount, a weekly target or an introduction order for tree nuts — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before the first exposure to tree nuts — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no tree-nut testing protocol, no tree-nut dose and no tree-nut weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food. Tolerating almond does not predict tolerating cashew.

choking.requiredModification: Smooth only, never crunchy. Never a spoonful or a thick glob — AAP's hazard list names "thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters" and says to spread thinly instead. Thin it until it no longer holds its shape, or spread it very thinly on something soft.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention ("thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters — be sure to spread thinly instead")
CDC — choking hazards ("chunks or spoonful of nut and seed butters"; "whole or chopped nuts and seeds")

NIAID — Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy, Appendix D. Peanut-scoped. The "never off a spoon" mechanism is applied to cashew butter here by analogy, not by issuance; NIAID's whole-nut floor of under 5 years is quoted as issued.
NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children (whole nuts; serve them finely ground)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
FDA — Food Allergies (tree nuts are a major food allergen)
USDA FoodData Central — dry-roasted cashews, fdcId 170571 (Fe 6.00, Zn 5.60). A PROXY for the whole nut, not a value for the butter; no verified id for cashew butter itself.

foods.backgroundMd:
Cashew is a **distinct tree-nut sensitization from almond**, which is why it has
its own record rather than sharing one with [[almond-butter]]. A baby who eats
almond butter without trouble has told you nothing about cashew. The clustering
that is reported runs **cashew with pistachio**, and hazelnut with walnut —
almond sits outside both groups.

That distinctness cuts the other way too, and it is the reason a cashew reaction
is worth taking seriously on its own terms rather than assuming the tree-nut
question was settled by an earlier nut.

**No US body issues a multi-tree-nut introduction protocol.** The number of nuts
that "covers" the tree-nut allergen, the order, and the interval between them
are all unissued. The specialist guidance that exists is explicitly provisional
and waits on trial results. This record covers how to serve cashew butter
safely; it does not tell you how many nuts make a programme, because nobody has
said.

**This record publishes no iron figure and no USDA id.** There is a verified
entry for *dry-roasted cashews* — 6.00 mg of iron and 5.60 mg of zinc per 100 g
— and it appears in the sources as a labelled proxy. It is not printed as cashew
butter's iron. Grinding a nut into butter changes moisture and therefore
per-100 g density, so a whole-nut number carried on a butter record would be
invented. **Cashew butter's own composition is unverified here.**

One question this pre-empts, since the jars invite it: **cashews are never truly
raw.** Retail "raw" cashews have been steamed, because the shell oil is caustic
and has to be driven off. That is not a safety problem for your baby — it is
simply what the word means on that label.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**On the hazard list by name.** AAP: "thick chunks of peanut butter or **other
nut butters**." CDC: "chunks or spoonful of nut and seed butters." Cashew butter
is inside both entries directly.

**Never crunchy**, because a crunchy butter contains nut pieces, which are
separately a hazard.

**Never off a spoon.** NIAID's instruction against nut butter from a spoon or in
lumps under four years is written for peanut; applying it here is this record's
judgement and is tiered as expert opinion. The mechanism is identical.

**Whole cashews are not appropriate at any age in this app's range.** NIAID
puts whole nuts at **under 5 years**; AAP's framing is "until 4 years of age or
older." **The two disagree, both are live, and NIAID's five-year floor is the
cautious default.** This is stated rather than quietly resolved. The butter,
thinned, is fine from six months — the age floor is about the nut.

**Watch for cashew hidden in adult food.** Cashew is a common thickener in
restaurant curries and sauces, where it is blended in and invisible. That is
worth knowing after a reaction, not before one: if something happened and you
are trying to work out what was in the dish, cashew paste is a frequent unlisted
answer.

foods.name: Cassava

ageBands.servingNote: Peeled completely, boiled through from cold water, mashed. Never raw, never lightly cooked, never grated raw.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Peel it completely.** FAO is direct that "the cyanide content is substantially
higher in the cassava peel," so the peel is not a marginal loss — it is the part
you are removing on purpose. Take the woody core out too.

**Cut it up, put it in cold water, and bring it to the boil from cold.** This is
the one preparation detail that changes the outcome measurably: after thirty
minutes of cooking, residual cyanide is **about 8 percent of the starting level
when the cassava went in cold**, against **about 30 percent when it was dropped
into already-boiling water** — roughly a fourfold difference for a step that
takes no extra effort. Soaking the peeled pieces for 18 to 24 hours beforehand
cuts levels by around half again, and is worth doing if you have the time.

Boil until a piece falls apart under a fork with no resistance anywhere, then
mash and thin with the cooking liquid, breast milk or formula.

Same preparation, mashed rather than puréed, mixed with something carrying iron
and something carrying vitamin C. Cassava is bland and heavy, so it works best
as a base under a bean or meat mash rather than as a bowl of its own.

However the household eats boiled or stewed cassava, as long as it has been
peeled and cooked right through. Take the baby's portion out before salt.

Fried yuca is hard-edged and salted, which is the wrong direction on both
counts.

choking.requiredModification: Peel completely, remove the fibrous core, and boil from cold water until it mashes with no resistance. The long cook is a toxicology requirement here, not only a texture one.

sources.body: FAO — Roots, tubers, plantains and bananas in human nutrition (Food and Nutrition Series 24, 1990), toxic substances: cyanide content substantially higher in the peel; after 30 minutes' cooking the remaining cyanide is about 8 percent of initial when started in cold water versus about 30 percent when dropped into boiling water; soaking reduces levels; symptoms of raw or insufficiently processed cassava include vertigo, vomiting, collapse and in some cases death
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (cook hard vegetables and fruits until they mash easily)
CDC — Iron
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 169985 cassava, raw — iron 0.27 mg/100 g)

foods.backgroundMd:
Cassava — yuca, manioc — is a staple starch across West Africa, Latin America
and Southeast Asia, and a properly prepared one is a perfectly reasonable food
for a baby. It comes with a preparation rule that is not optional, and one
number worth knowing before you build meals around it.

**It carries the lowest iron of any food in this part of the canon: 0.27 mg per
100 g.** That is a starch, not a nutritional contribution. Cassava fills a baby
up, which is its own risk at an age when appetite is limited and iron
requirements are at their lifetime peak. Serve it alongside iron — [[beef]],
[[lentils]], [[black-beans]], [[fortified-infant-cereal]] — rather than as the
centre of a meal.

**Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides** — linamarin and lotaustralin —
which release cyanide when the plant tissue is damaged. Concentration "varies
greatly between varieties," so you cannot tell by looking, and the preparation
below assumes you are working with a root that has some. That is the safe
assumption and it costs you nothing but time.

This record publishes **no cyanogen concentration for retail cassava**, because
no verified figure for what is on a US or Korean shelf exists in the sources
behind this canon. Numbers circulate; none of them survived checking.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Never raw. Never lightly cooked. Never grated raw into anything, and never in
a smoothie.** FAO records the symptoms of eating raw or insufficiently processed
cassava as "vertigo, vomiting, collapse and in some cases death." That is the
reason the prep instructions above have no shortcuts in them, and it is the
whole of why this food is rated modify-required rather than low.

**Peel completely and boil through from cold water.** Both halves matter: the
peel is where the cyanogens concentrate, and starting cold gives roughly four
times the reduction of dropping the pieces into boiling water.

**Cassava flour, tapioca, tapioca pearls and garri are separately processed
foods, and none of this transfers to them in either direction.** They are made
by grating, pressing, fermenting, drying or roasting, and each process handles
the cyanogens differently. Do not read this record as clearing them, and do not
read a packet of tapioca starch as evidence that the root is easy. Tapioca
pearls in particular are a distinct choking hazard and are not addressed here.

**Vitamin C:** raw cassava measures 20.6 mg per 100 g, but the long boil this
food requires destroys much of it, and no verified figure exists for the cooked
root. So this record does not present cassava as a vitamin-C partner for an iron
meal. Use [[potato]], [[broccoli]] or [[mango]] for that.

foods.name: Chicken liver

ageBands.servingNote: A very small amount, simmered through and blended into a food the baby already eats — not a portion of its own.
ageBands.prepMd:
Trim the connective tissue where the two lobes join, and cut away any
green-stained patch — that is bile, and it is bitter enough to ruin the dish.
Do this before cooking.

Simmer the livers gently in water or unsalted stock until they are firm and
uniformly brown through the middle with no red centre. **Cook to 165 °F (USDA
FSIS)** — poultry giblets are explicitly covered by the all-poultry row on the
safe temperature chart, so unlike beef liver this food does have an issued
temperature, and you should use it. Pan-frying works too; simmering just makes
the result easier to blend.

Then puree or mince very fine and stir a **small** amount into a food your baby
already eats — a mashed vegetable, [[oatmeal]], or a mince they are used to.
Chicken liver is milder than beef liver but still strong on its own, and blended
in it is barely detectable.

Same form, same small amount. The pincer grasp does not change the vitamin A
arithmetic, so liver does not graduate to a finger food or to a portion of its
own — it stays an ingredient stirred through something else.

Still blended in, still bounded by the frequency note. One caution as your baby
gets older: the 600 µg/day UL we cite is the figure for **birth to 12 months**.
We have not verified a figure for the year after, so this record does not print
one, and the honest move is to keep the same caution rather than assume the
ceiling rises.

choking.requiredModification: Trim connective tissue and any green-stained spots before cooking, cook to 165 °F, then puree or mince very fine and stir into another food.

frequencyLimit.reason: Preformed vitamin A accumulates in the body, and chicken liver carries 3,980–4,300 µg RAE per 100 g (USDA) — roughly 6.6 times the infant daily upper limit in a 100 g portion. Be clear about what this once-a-week ceiling is: NO health body issues an infant frequency cap for liver. It is absent from AAP, CDC, FDA, the Canadian Paediatric Society, WHO, and every NHS baby page. This limit is common practice, borrowed from NHS's "do not eat liver or liver products more than once a week" — advice written for the general adult population, on a page that never mentions children or babies. The only infant-applicable figure anyone has issued is NIH ODS's Tolerable Upper Intake Level for preformed vitamin A: 600 µg per day, birth to 12 months. That UL is the guideline; the weekly cap is a convention laid on top of it.

foods.backgroundMd:
Chicken liver has the highest iron of any food in this entire canon: **11.6 mg
per 100 g simmered, 12.9 mg pan-fried**. That is about twice [[beef-liver]] and
roughly five times [[beef]] mince, in heme form — the readily absorbed kind CDC
contrasts with the non-heme iron in plants and fortified cereals. Nothing else
here is close.

**And as with any liver, iron is not the constraint. Vitamin A is.**

Chicken liver carries 3,980 µg RAE of preformed vitamin A per 100 g simmered and
4,300 µg pan-fried. NIH ODS sets the Tolerable Upper Intake Level for preformed
vitamin A at **600 µg per day from birth to 12 months**, and says chronic intake
above the UL can cause congenital birth defects. A 100 g portion is therefore
about **6.6 times the daily ceiling** — that ratio is our arithmetic on two
issued numbers, not a figure anyone published.

Compared with beef liver, chicken liver is roughly half the vitamin A density
and about twice the iron. On both axes that makes it the better-value liver, and
if you are going to serve one liver a week this is the one to choose. It is
still a food where a small amount does the whole job.

Dividing the UL by the density puts 600 µg at roughly **15 g of simmered chicken
liver**. Again: **arithmetic, not guidance.** No body has issued a gram figure
for infant liver. Treat it as a sense of scale.

**Where the guidance actually stands.** No health body names liver as an infant
food, and none prohibits it. That is an absence of guidance rather than a verdict
either way, and we would rather report the gap than manufacture a bridge across
it. The one issued number that applies to a baby is the 600 µg/day UL; the
once-a-week limit on this page is convention, and the frequency note says whose.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Vitamin A is the hazard, and it is cumulative.** Preformed vitamin A is stored
rather than excreted, so the risk comes from repetition, not from one meal. That
is why this record carries a frequency limit — the only kind of limit in this
canon that says "yes, but not this often."

Read that limit for exactly what it says. The 600 µg/day UL is issued by NIH ODS
and applies to your baby. The once-a-week ceiling is issued by nobody for a baby:
it comes from an NHS page written for the general adult population that does not
mention children, and stretching an adult rule onto a body a fraction of the
weight is an extrapolation. We made it in the cautious direction and labelled it,
because publishing no limit beside a food this dense would have been worse. For a
number fitted to your own baby, ask your pediatrician — it depends on what else
they eat that week.

**Pâté and parfait are excluded**, and for two reasons rather than one. Both are
salt-heavy, and CDC advises against high-sodium foods for children under two;
commercial parfaits and some pâtés are also mould-ripened or set with cultures.
No sodium figure is published here for either, because none was verified against
a primary source while this record was written. Making liver pâté at home does
not solve the salt: the salt is structural to the recipe.

**Cook it through.** 165 °F, measured. Poultry liver is not a food to serve pink,
and undercooked poultry offal is a food-safety problem rather than a texture
preference.

**Texture.** Cooked liver goes grainy and can pack at the back of the mouth.
Pureed or minced very fine, carried in something moist, is both the safe form and
the palatable one.

**Supplements.** A vitamin A-containing supplement or multivitamin counts toward
the same 600 µg ceiling. Check the label before you add liver to the week.

foods.name: Chicken thigh

ageBands.servingNote: Finely chopped and moistened with unsalted broth or the pan juices — chicken dries out faster than beef.
ageBands.prepMd:
Take the skin, fat, and bones off **before** cooking, not after — CDC is
explicit about the order, and it means no bone fragments end up in the finished
meat. Braise, poach, or roast the thigh until it pulls apart with a fork, cook
all poultry to 165 °F (USDA FSIS), then chop it finely and stir in enough
unsalted broth or pan juices that it holds together on a spoon.

Run the chopped meat between your fingers before serving. Thigh meat carries
small tendons and the occasional splinter of bone, and that check takes ten
seconds.

Shredded rather than chopped — long soft strands are easy to pick up with a
pincer grasp and easy to gum apart. Chicken mixed into [[oatmeal]] or mashed
vegetables still travels better than chicken alone.

However the family eats it, still soft and still cut small. "Tough or large
chunks of meat" does not drop off CDC's hazard list at twelve months, and neither
do bones.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin, fat, and bones before cooking, then finely chop or shred. Never chunks, and never a piece with a bone in it.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics
Canadian Paediatric Society
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — iron
USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service — safe minimum internal temperatures

foods.backgroundMd:
AAP names "well-cooked, finely chopped chicken" as a finger food, and the
Canadian Paediatric Society lists cooked chicken among iron-rich first foods.
That is unusually specific for a guideline body — most of them describe
textures, not dishes — so the form to serve is not a matter of interpretation
here.

The iron is heme iron, the readily absorbed kind, at 1.13 mg per 100 g roasted.
That is well below [[beef]]'s, so if the week's iron is coming from one animal
food, beef does more of the work. Chicken's advantage is that it is cheap,
mild, and goes with everything.

Thigh rather than breast is a texture preference, not a guideline position: dark
meat stays moist through longer cooking, and dry chicken breast is the most
common way a promising meat meal ends up on the floor. Breast is not unsafe —
it just needs more help staying wet.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Bones and chunks are the hazard, and CDC handles both with one instruction:
remove all fat, skin, and bones from poultry before cooking, then cook until it
mashes easily with a fork.

Cook all poultry to 165 °F. Undercooked chicken is a food-safety problem, not
just an unpleasant texture, and an infant is the worst person to test it on — no
pink at the bone, and a thermometer rather than "it looked done".

foods.name: Cod

ageBands.servingNote: Flaked fine, checked by hand for bones, and moistened so the flakes hold together instead of powdering.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy it boneless if you can, then go over the raw fillet with your fingers
anyway. Skin and bones come off **before** cooking — that is CDC's order, NHS
says to remove bones from fish, and the Canadian Paediatric Society says plainly
not to feed a baby fish with bones. A raw fillet is also simply easier to search
than a hot cooked one.

Bake, poach, or steam until the flesh is opaque all the way through and separates
into flakes under light pressure. USDA FSIS gives 145 °F for fish and shellfish;
cod hits that about when it stops being translucent.

Flake it fine, run the flakes through your fingers once more, and moisten with a
spoonful of the cooking liquid or a puree so they hold together. Dry cod flakes
powder on the tray and are hard for a six-month-old to gather.

Larger flakes, self-fed. Cod's flake structure suits a pincer grasp well — the
pieces come apart into roughly finger-sized soft chunks that collapse when
squeezed. Still checked by hand for bones every time.

However the family eats it, still deboned and still cooked through. Battered and
deep-fried cod is a different question — the batter carries the salt, not the
fish.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned cod, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish below twelve months, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway does not read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove all bones and the skin before cooking, then flake the cooked fish and run it through your fingers to find any bone you missed.

sources.body: FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (revised Oct 2021; scoped to those who might become or are pregnant or breastfeeding and children ages 1–11). Cod is a Best Choice but is not on the "even lower in mercury" sub-list. Q&A III.2 gives about 6 months as the age fish can be introduced.
FDA — food allergies and major food allergen labeling; fish is a major allergen, illustrated statutorily as "bass, flounder, cod"
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
Canadian Paediatric Society — feeding your baby in the first year ("Don't feed your baby… fish with bones")
NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children (remove bones from meat or fish; salt under 12 months)
USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service — safe minimum internal temperatures, fish and shellfish 145 °F (updated 2025-04-14)
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 171956, cooked cod — Fe 0.49 mg, Zn 0.58 mg, Na 78 mg per 100 g)

foods.backgroundMd:
**Cod is not on this list for iron.** At 0.49 mg per 100 g it is the lowest-iron
fish in this set — a third of [[salmon]]'s and a seventh of a serving of red
meat. Its zinc, 0.58 mg, is similarly modest. If you are here to solve iron, cod
is not the tool; [[beef]] or liver is.

What cod is genuinely good for is two things.

**Allergen introduction.** Fish is one of the nine major US allergens, and cod
is the one US labelling law itself reaches for as an example — the statute
illustrates the fish category as "bass, flounder, cod". That makes cod about as
canonical a fish for this purpose as exists. AAP's position is that there is no
evidence delaying fish past four to six months prevents allergy, and FDA states
directly that you can introduce fish at about six months of age. Fish is
introduced like any other food, with the medical gate above for the babies who
need it.

**Texture.** Cooked cod breaks into large, soft, clean flakes that dissolve
under gum pressure. Among first fish that is close to ideal, and it is why cod
is often the easiest fish for a baby who has refused others.

On mercury: FDA and EPA place cod in **Best Choices**, their safest tier. Worth
knowing precisely, though — cod is a Best Choice but is **not** on FDA's shorter
sub-list of Best Choices that are *even lower* in mercury. [[pollock]] and
[[rainbow-trout]] are on that sub-list; cod is not. It is a real distinction and
we would rather show it than flatten it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones are the whole hazard.** Deboned cod flesh is soft and low-risk. Cod
carries fine bones through the fillet, and both CPS and NHS put fish bones on
the do-not-feed list. Debone before cooking, then check the cooked flakes by
hand. Whole small fish and bone-in steaks are not a form to serve here.

**No salt cod.** 자반대구, bacalao, and any dried or salt-preserved cod are
excluded: they are salt-preservation products, and NHS and CDC both advise
against salt for babies. We publish no sodium figure for salt cod because none
was verified against a primary source — the figure on this page, 78 mg per 100 g,
is for plain cooked cod only.

**No raw fish.** FDA is explicit that children should not eat raw fish,
including the kind found in sushi and sashimi. That covers 대구회 and any raw
preparation.

**How much per week — there is no infant answer.** FDA and EPA's fish advice is
titled for children **ages 1 to 11**. Its smallest serving figure is one ounce at
age one. **No US body publishes a per-week amount for a six-to-eleven-month-old**,
so this record does not invent one. Serve cod as one of several protein foods
across the week, and ask your pediatrician if you want a number for your own
baby.

**One wording point, because two rules look identical and are not.** FDA's fish
advice suggests watching your child for **several days before feeding fish a
second time** — while the same paragraph explicitly rejects delaying allergen
introduction. That sentence is about the gap between the **first and second
exposure to fish itself**, so a delayed reaction to *this* food has time to show.
It is **not** the familiar "wait 3–5 days between new foods" rule, which is a
different claim about *unrelated* foods and is not evidence-based: IgE reactions
happen within minutes to two hours, so spacing out unrelated foods buys nothing
diagnostically and just slows down variety. Keep introducing other new foods on
your normal schedule. We are flagging the tension between FDA's two sentences
rather than resolving it, because FDA has not.

foods.name: Corn tortilla (masa)

ageBands.servingNote: Warm and soft, torn into strips the baby can hold — never crisp, toasted hard, or fried.
ageBands.prepMd:
Warm a plain tortilla on a dry pan just until it is pliable and steamy — **not
until it browns, crisps or blisters hard.** Tear it into strips a couple of
fingers wide that the baby can hold with the whole hand, and serve it with
something wet: mashed [[avocado]], puréed [[black-beans]], a spoonful of
[[plantain]].

A dry tortilla left in the mouth can gum together into a wad, which is the
realistic hazard at this age rather than a hard chunk. Keeping it damp and
served alongside something soft solves it.

**Buy the no-added-salt version if you can find it.** USDA's unsalted tortilla is
11 mg of sodium per 100 g against 45 mg for the salted one — small numbers on
their own, but babies do not need added salt and it accumulates across a day.

Same tortilla, smaller pieces once the pincer grasp arrives, and it becomes a
useful wrapper: a soft tortilla folded around mashed beans and soft vegetables
is a whole meal that a baby can hold.

Keep offering some larger strips alongside the small pieces — biting and tearing
are skills that need practising.

However the table eats them, kept soft. Fillings become the thing to watch more
than the tortilla: salt, chilli and cheese add up quickly.

choking.requiredModification: Serve soft and warm, not crisp or fried, and never with whole corn kernels in or on it. A dry tortilla can also ball up in the mouth, so dampening it or serving it with something wet helps.

sources.body: CDC — Choking Hazards ("cooked or raw whole corn kernels" is its own listed hazard)
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (cook hard foods until soft; grind or mash whole-grain kernels)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (sodium)
FAO — Maize in human nutrition (Food and Nutrition Series 25, 1992): lime-cooking raises calcium and makes niacin more available, while total niacin falls during processing
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 173241 corn tortilla, no added salt; 175036 salted; 170288 corn grain)

foods.backgroundMd:
A plain masa tortilla, warmed until it is soft and floppy, is one of the easier
things to hand a baby: it tears rather than snaps, it holds other food, and it
carries 1.40 mg of iron per 100 g.

**Nixtamalization — what it actually does, because the usual version of this
story is wrong.** Cooking corn in lime before grinding it into masa raises the
calcium enormously: whole corn grain measures **7 mg of calcium per 100 g**, a
corn tortilla **175 mg** — roughly **twenty-five times**, and that calcium comes
from the lime itself. That part is a straightforward measurement.

The niacin claim, as it is usually told, does not survive the data. **Total
niacin falls**: corn grain 3.63 mg per 100 g, tortilla 1.5 mg. What
nixtamalization changes is **bioavailability** — maize niacin is bound up as
niacytin and largely unavailable, and alkaline processing releases it into a
form the body can absorb. FAO's own maize monograph says both things: niacin is
"slightly more available from lime-treated maize than from raw maize," and
processing losses of niacin are real.

So the accurate sentence is: **nixtamalization sharply raises calcium and
releases bound niacin into an absorbable form; it does not raise total niacin.**
**How much more absorbable is not quantified in anything verifiable**, so this
record publishes no figure for it.

None of this makes a tortilla an iron food on the scale of
[[fortified-infant-cereal]]. It is a useful, calcium-bearing carbohydrate and a
good vehicle for mashed [[black-beans]] or [[avocado]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Whole corn kernels are their own entry on CDC's choking-hazard list — "cooked
or raw whole corn kernels" — and cooking does not clear it.** This is worth
saying precisely because most hazard rules on this app are discharged by cooking
something soft. This one is not. A kernel is a hazard cooked or raw.

**Only ground masa escapes that.** A tortilla, masa porridge, or anything where
the corn has been ground is a different food from a kernel. Corn on the cob,
canned corn, corn kernels stirred through rice or a stew, and corn kernels in a
tortilla filling are all the hazard as listed.

**Not crisp, not fried.** Tortilla chips, tostadas and hard taco shells are hard
food; CDC's principle is to cook hard foods until they are soft enough to mash
easily, and a chip is the opposite of that. That is a derived reading of a
general rule rather than a rule about chips, but it is not a close call.

foods.name: Cucumber

ageBands.servingNote: Peeled, and cut as a narrow baton — never a coin. Grating is the easier alternative and needs no judgement about thickness.
ageBands.prepMd:
Peel it. Then cut lengthways into narrow batons — long enough that an end sticks
out of a closed fist, and narrow rather than thick, so that if a piece does come
away it is a sliver and not a chunk. Cutting out the seedy core makes the batons
softer.

If judging thickness feels like guesswork, grate it instead. Grated peeled
cucumber is soft, wet, and short, and it stirs into [[yogurt]] or mixes with
other vegetables without any decision to make.

At this age most of what happens is mouthing and gumming rather than eating, and
that is fine — a cold cucumber baton is a pleasant thing to chew on.

Same form: peeled, narrow batons, or grated. The pincer grasp arriving does not
change the geometry rule, and this is the age at which coins become tempting
because they are easy to pick up. They are the one shape to avoid.

Still peeled and still batons rather than rounds. AAP's round-and-firm line runs
to four years, and cucumber is a firm raw vegetable for the whole of that
period.

Grated cucumber folded through plain yogurt is the easy household version and
works as a side for the whole table.

choking.requiredModification: Never raw coins or rounds. Peel it and cut narrow batons, or grate it. The skin is the specific hazard — it does not break down under gums.

sources.body: NHS — Help your baby enjoy new foods (narrow batons; removing skin)
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
CDC — Choking Hazards
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods

foods.backgroundMd:
**No AAP or CDC infant food list names cucumber.** NHS covers it, but only
inside its general preparation guidance, in a list of vegetables to cut into
narrow batons. So everything in this record is a category rule applied to
cucumber, not a food-specific ruling anyone issued. That is worth saying out
loud, because the category rule it lands in is strict and the food looks
harmless.

Two category rules apply. AAP's is about geometry: "do not feed children younger
than 4 round, firm food unless it is chopped completely." A raw cucumber round
is exactly that shape — a firm disc, roughly airway-sized, with a smooth rim.
CDC's is about hard raw vegetables generally, the same line that puts raw
carrots on the list.

**The skin is the specific hazard**, and it is what makes cucumber different
from a soft raw fruit. Cucumber flesh is watery and yields; the skin is tough,
does not break down under gums, and holds a bitten piece together as an intact
ring rather than letting it collapse. Peeling removes that.

NHS gives the fixes directly: cut vegetables like carrots, peppers, cucumber and
celery into **narrow batons**; remove the skin, which "makes it easier to
swallow"; or grate it for very young children.

**Nutritionally it contributes nothing to speak of.** A USDA entry for cucumber
could not be verified at the time of writing, so this record publishes no iron
or vitamin C figure at all rather than a plausible-looking guess. Treat it as a
hydration and texture food. If you want iron, that is [[tofu]] or [[barley]]
cereal; if you want a vitamin-C partner, [[mango]] or [[green-peas]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Never coins.** This is the single thing to take from this record. A raw
cucumber round is the geometry AAP explicitly warns about, and it is also the
way almost everyone cuts a cucumber.

**Peel it.** The skin does not break down under gums and holds a bitten piece
together. Peeling is a guideline-issued fix, not a nicety.

**Chilled cucumber for teething is common practice, not guidance.** Nobody
issues it. If you do it, the guideline-issued part is unchanged — peel it, cut a
baton — and the chilling is just comfort. A whole unpeeled chilled cucumber, or
a thick unpeeled spear, is not made safe by being cold.

Pickled cucumber is a different food: high sodium, and not appropriate before 24
months.

foods.name: Dried anchovy

ageBands.servingNote: Heads and viscera removed, ground to a powder, used as a seasoning stirred into food — not offered as a piece.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Buy unsalted, and read the label to confirm it.** This is the single most
important purchasing decision for this food, and it is easy to get wrong:
commercial dried anchovies are very often salted, and there is no way to tell by
looking. Products vary enormously and **we could not obtain a sodium figure for
any of them**, so this record gives none.

What it can give you is the scale of a baby's whole day. Sodium adequate intake
is **110 mg a day from birth to six months** and **370 mg a day from seven to
twelve months** (NASEM 2019). Note carefully what that is and is not: there is
**no upper limit and no EAR for sodium at any age**, so 370 mg is an adequacy
target, not a ceiling anyone issued. It is nonetheless small enough that a
salted adult ingredient can overwhelm it in one go.

Then:

1. **Pull the heads off** and pinch out the dark viscera along the belly. On the
   small stock anchovies this takes seconds each.
2. **Toast them briefly** in a dry pan to drive off moisture — this makes them
   grind properly instead of turning gummy.
3. **Grind to a fine powder** in a spice grinder or mortar. Fine means fine: no
   fragments you can feel between your fingers.
4. **Stir a small amount into food the baby already eats** — [[oatmeal]], soft
   rice, mashed [[sweet-potato]], a vegetable puree.

Store the powder airtight in the fridge and make small batches; it goes stale
quickly.

No change. The powder is still the form, for the same reason: a pincer grasp
makes it *easier* for a baby to pick up a whole dried anchovy, which is exactly
what we do not want. Better hand skills do not make a skeleton chewable.

You can be more generous with where the powder goes — through vegetables,
stirred into rice porridge, mixed into a patty — but it stays a seasoning.

Still ground. A toddler can chew far more than an infant, but "bones in meat or
fish" remains a named entry on CDC's choking-hazard list past the first
birthday, and a whole dried anchovy is nothing but bones.

The other thing that arrives at this age is the family version of the dish —
멸치볶음, stir-fried with 간장 and syrup. That is a sodium-and-sugar dish rather
than a fish dish; if you want the child to eat 멸치, the powder is still the way,
and the stir-fry can wait.

**Stock is a partial exception worth understanding.** Anchovies simmered and
then *strained out* leave a broth rather than a food — the fish never reaches
the baby. That is fine as a cooking base as long as the broth is not salted. It
is the anchovies themselves, left in and eaten, that this record is about.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a quarter teaspoon of unsalted dried anchovy ground to a fine powder, stirred into a food the baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish, so treat this as a practical starting point rather than a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the child could have eaten safely. Note also that NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only — there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway should not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Heads and viscera removed and the fish ground to a fine powder used as seasoning. A whole dried anchovy is a whole skeleton and is not a finger food at any age in this range.

sources.body: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards (remove all fat, skin and bones from poultry, meat and fish before cooking)
FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (anchovy is a Best Choice, on the "even lower" mercury sub-list)
FDA — Food Allergies (fish is a major allergen; the species must be declared)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
NASEM (2019) — Dietary Reference Intakes for Sodium and Potassium
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — foods and drinks to avoid or limit
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention

foods.backgroundMd:
멸치 is the backbone of Korean home cooking — the stock under most soups, the
side dish stir-fried with soy and syrup, the handful eaten straight from the
bag. It is also the food in this batch that sits in the most direct conflict
with a rule an American guideline body actually issues, and we would rather show
you the conflict than quietly resolve it.

🚩 **CDC's instruction is to "remove all fat, skin and bones from poultry, meat
and fish before cooking." A dried anchovy *is* the bones.** There is no version
of a whole 멸치 that satisfies that sentence. The whole skeleton, the head, the
spine — that is the food.

**The only preparation that reconciles the two is this: heads and viscera off,
the fish ground to a fine powder, and the powder used as a seasoning stirred
into food rather than eaten as a piece.** Ground finely enough, there is no bone
left to remove because there is no intact bone left at all. **Whole 멸치 as a
finger food is not defensible under CDC's own text**, and this record does not
recommend it at any age in its range — which is why all three age bands below
say the same thing.

That reconciliation is **ours, not CDC's.** CDC names the rule; it does not
offer this fix, or any fix, for small whole fish. You are entitled to know which
part came from the guideline and which part came from us.

**Mercury is the good news, and it is worth saying out loud because small oily
fish make parents nervous.** FDA and EPA place anchovy in **Best Choices**, and
within that on the sub-list of fish that are *even lower* in mercury. It is one
of the safest fish on the entire chart — the opposite of the tuna-and-swordfish
worry that the word "fish" tends to trigger. Small, short-lived, low on the food
chain.

**Fish is one of the nine major US allergens**, and unlike molluscs it is fully
covered by labelling law — FDA requires the **species** to be declared, so a
package will tell you it is anchovy. See the medical gate above before a first
exposure.

**Composition is pending verification.** The USDA database was unavailable when
this record was researched, so there is no iron, calcium or sodium figure here.
Dried anchovy is conventionally described as a calcium food precisely because
you eat the skeleton, and that is plausible, but we could not check it and are
not going to print an unverified number.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**The bone conflict is the headline.** CDC says remove all bones from fish
before cooking. A dried anchovy is the bones. Grinding to a powder is the only
preparation that satisfies the rule, and it is our reconciliation, not CDC's.
Whole 멸치 is not a finger food here at any age.

**Sodium is the second hazard and it is a shopping problem, not a cooking
problem.** Buy unsalted and verify on the label. You cannot rinse or dilute salt
back out of a dried fish.

**Mercury is not a hazard here** — Best Choices, and on the *even lower*
sub-list.

**Fish allergy** is managed by the medical gate above, then by ordinary early
introduction. Watch for about two hours after a first exposure; IgE reactions
happen within minutes to two hours. The familiar "wait three to five days
between new foods" rule adds nothing diagnostically.

**No guideline body addresses 멸치 as an infant food.** What exists is
category-level: fish as a major allergen, anchovy's mercury rating, and CDC's
bone rule. The grinding, the head-and-viscera removal and the seasoning-not-a-
piece framing are inherited category rules plus our inference, and are labelled
that way above.

foods.name: Duck leg

ageBands.servingNote: Braised skinless until it shreds, then minced and loosened with the defatted cooking liquid.
ageBands.prepMd:
Skin and bone come off **before** cooking, per CDC. With duck that is also the
practical move: the skin carries most of the fat, and a duck leg cooked with its
skin on renders enough fat to make the meat greasy for a baby.

Braise the skinned leg in water or unsalted stock until the meat leaves the bone
without effort — usually an hour and a half to two hours. Let the cooking liquid
settle, spoon the fat off the top, then mince the meat fine and moisten it with
the defatted liquid.

Cook duck pieces to 165 °F (USDA FSIS), the same as any other poultry. A braise
passes that long before the meat is soft enough to serve.

Shredded. Braised duck leg falls into long soft strands that suit a pincer grasp
well. Stirred through [[oatmeal]], rice, or a mashed vegetable it is less greasy
on the hands than duck served alone.

However the family eats it, still deboned, still soft, still cut small — and
still not any of the cured or glazed preparations below. That rules out most of
the ways duck actually appears on a table, which is the honest situation rather
than an oversight.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin, fat, and bones before cooking, then finely chop or shred. Never chunks, and never a piece with a bone in it.

foods.backgroundMd:
Duck leg is the surprise of the poultry group. Braised skinless duck meat carries
2.33 mg of iron per 100 g and roasted duck with skin 2.08 mg, against
[[chicken-thigh]]'s 1.13 mg — roughly 1.8 to 2.1 times the iron for a bird most
people think of as a special occasion. It is heme iron, the readily absorbed
form, which puts duck leg in the same league as [[beef]] rather than in
chicken's.

**We publish no zinc figure for duck leg.** USDA's records for both the braised
and the roasted leg simply do not carry one. There is a zinc value on USDA's
all-parts duck record, but that is a different food — a composite of the whole
carcass, not the leg — and borrowing it would be inventing a number for this
page. If you want duck for zinc, [[lamb]] and [[turkey-dark-meat]] have verified
figures and duck does not.

Sodium in plain braised duck meat is 108 mg per 100 g, which is ordinary for
fresh meat. Everything in the Safety section below is about preparations where
that stops being true.

Duck is not one of the nine major US allergens.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Colour is not a doneness test, and duck is the food where that bites.** USDA
FSIS says plainly that duck cooked to 165 °F **may still be pink in the centre**.
Duck is also the bird most often served deliberately rare, so both errors are
live here: a cook who trusts pinkness will keep cooking meat that is already
safe, and a cook who has been told duck is "meant to be pink" may serve a baby
meat that never got there. Use a thermometer. FDA is explicit that children
should only eat poultry cooked to a safe internal temperature, so rare duck
breast — and any duck served pink on purpose — is out for a baby regardless of
how it looks.

**Confit is excluded.** Duck confit is salt-cured before it is cooked in fat.
That is the point of the technique, and it puts confit in the same category as
other cured meats under CDC's advice against high-sodium foods for children
under two. We publish no sodium figure for it: none was verified against a
primary source while this record was written.

**Peking duck and Chinese roast duck are excluded**, for added sugar as well as
sodium — the glaze and the marinade are both. CDC advises against added sugars
under two years as well as high sodium. Again, no figure is published here
because none was verified.

**Bones and chunks.** Duck legs are small and their bones splinter more readily
than chicken's. Debone before cooking, check the shredded meat by hand, and keep
the meat finely chopped or shredded rather than cubed — chunks of meat stay on
CDC's hazard list past the first birthday.

foods.name: Egg

ageBands.servingNote: Softly scrambled and well cooked — moist curds, no runny patches.
ageBands.prepMd:
Scramble in a little unsalted butter or oil over low heat and keep going until
there is no wet or glossy egg left — AAP names scrambled egg among suitable
finger foods, and soft moist curds are easy to gum. Hard-boiled works too; mash
the yolk and white together with a little breast milk, formula, or water, since
a dry hard-boiled white is rubbery on its own.

Serve the whole egg rather than the yolk alone — AAP's portion is about 1/3 of
a well-cooked egg, not a third of a yolk, and a yolk-only serving is a smaller
exposure than the one that was studied.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing — that is a
logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you are watching and your clinic
is open. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours. That two-hour window
is also why the familiar "wait three to five days before the next new food" rule
adds nothing diagnostically; it just slows down variety.

Same well-cooked forms in pincer-sized pieces: a thin omelette cut into small
squares, chopped hard-boiled egg, egg stirred into [[oatmeal]]. Keep it in the
rotation at least weekly rather than treating the first serving as done.

However the family eats eggs, with one exception that does not expire at twelve
months: still cooked through. Runny yolks, soft-set custards, homemade
mayonnaise, raw batter, and mousse are all uncooked-egg foods.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/3 of a well-cooked egg — scrambled or hard-boiled and mashed — per AAP's stated portion for keeping egg in a baby's diet.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to egg — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the baby could safely eat.

choking.requiredModification: Serve well cooked and soft — scrambled, or hard-boiled and mashed with a little liquid.

foods.backgroundMd:
Egg is the second-best-evidenced allergen introduction after peanut, and the
evidence carries an unusual condition attached: **the cooking is part of the
intervention.** A 2018 review and meta-analysis found moderate-certainty
evidence that introducing egg between four and six months reduces egg allergy,
with "much better efficacy with using cooked as opposed to raw egg." AAP's
wording is the same direction: well-cooked eggs have been studied and shown to
reduce the risk of egg allergy when fed to infants regularly.

So there is no tension between the allergy advice and the food-safety advice
here — well-cooked egg is both the safe form and the effective one.

Two things from AAP are worth carrying: **about 1/3 of a well-cooked egg** as
the portion, and **at least weekly** as the cadence. Introduction is not the
finish line for allergens; a single taste followed by months of nothing is not
what the trials tested.

Egg is also on CDC's list of heme iron foods, at 1.19 mg per 100 g. That is the
classification, given here as CDC gives it.

Related: [[salmon]] is the other major allergen in this batch and follows the
same medical gate.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cook it fully.** FDA and CDC advise against raw or undercooked egg for
everyone, and children under five are singled out: they are about three times
more likely to be hospitalized with *Salmonella*. Cook eggs until the white and yolk
are firm; egg-containing dishes such as casseroles and custards go to 160 °F
(USDA FSIS).

**The bodies disagree, and you should know it.** NHS permits raw or lightly
cooked hen's eggs for babies *if* the eggs carry the British Lion stamp, a
UK-specific *Salmonella*-control scheme with no US equivalent. FDA and CDC make
no such carve-out. This app follows FDA and CDC: in the US there is no stamp
that makes a runny egg a safe infant food. If you are reading UK guidance
alongside this, that is where the difference comes from — not a disagreement
about babies, but a difference in national egg supply controls.

Choking risk from well-cooked egg is low. A whole hard-boiled egg, or a large
piece of firm white, is a different matter — mash or cut it.

foods.name: Fortified infant cereal (non-rice)

ageBands.servingNote: Mixed with breast milk, formula, or water — never cow's milk before 12 months — until it is smooth and drops off a loaded spoon.
ageBands.prepMd:
Put a spoonful of dry cereal in a bowl and mix with breast milk, formula, or
water until it is smooth and just thick enough to stay on a loaded spoon. Start
thinner than you think and thicken it over the following weeks — moving food
from the front of the mouth to the back is a skill, and the thickening is how it
gets practised.

Hand over the loaded spoon, or hold it and let the baby take it off. Most of the
first fortnight lands on the tray and the chin. That is the job at this age.

**The dry-weight figures above are for the powder, not the bowl.** What actually
reaches your baby depends on how thickly you mix it. The comparison between
cereals still holds.

Thicker and lumpier, and increasingly self-fed. This is the age the cereal earns
its keep as a carrier: mashed [[black-beans]], flaked [[salmon]], puréed
[[spinach]] or fruit all stir in and go down easily, which gets the iron and the
vitamin C into one bowl.

Iron requirements are at their highest across this band, so if fortified cereal
is going to be in the diet at all, this is when it counts.

Still useful, still the easiest iron in the house, and by now one component of a
varied diet rather than the centre of it. If you have moved on to whole grains
cooked at home, keep CDC's kernel rule in view — cook and then finely grind or
mash whole-grain kernels — and keep an iron food somewhere in the day.

choking.requiredModification: Mix to a smooth porridge. If you move to whole grains cooked at home, CDC's rule applies to those: cook the kernels and then finely grind or mash them.

foods.backgroundMd:
**This is the single largest nutritional lever in the whole canon, and it is one
of the very few places where a guideline body names specific foods.** CDC's
wording is to "offer a variety of fortified infant cereals such as oat, barley,
and multi-grain instead of only rice cereal," and FDA names the same three in
its arsenic guidance. Most infant-feeding advice is deliberately generic; this
is not.

**The numbers, per 100 g dry.** Fortified infant **oat** carries **64.1 mg of
iron** and 12.7 mg of zinc. Fortified infant **barley**: 48.2 mg of iron, 3.13
mg of zinc. Fortified infant **multigrain**: 30.0 mg of iron, 10.7 mg of zinc.
For comparison, plain unfortified oats are 4.25 mg of iron dry — and **0.90 mg
once cooked in water.**

Two things fall out of those figures.

**Fortified oat carries about seventy-one times the iron of the porridge you
cook from a canister of oats.** Both get called "oatmeal" in a kitchen. They are
not the same food nutritionally, and if the homemade pot quietly replaces the
box, almost all of the iron leaves the diet without anything looking different.

**Fortified oat also carries more than double fortified multigrain** — 64.1
against 30.0. If iron is the goal, single-grain fortified oat is the strongest
non-rice option in USDA's data.

**Non-rice, specifically.** Rice cereal is fortified too, but rice concentrates
inorganic arsenic and CDC's concern is a rice-only diet: "only feeding your
child infant rice cereal can increase their risk of arsenic exposure." See
[[short-grain-rice]] for the detail. Rotating oat, barley and multigrain costs
nothing and removes the question.

**"Fortified" is not one thing — read the panel.** One organic rice cereal in
USDA's data is labelled *fortified only with iron*: 47.5 mg of iron and **1.84
mg of zinc**, roughly a sixfold zinc shortfall against the other fortified
cereals in the table. Zinc matters at this age for the same reason iron does.
The word on the front of the box does not tell you which nutrients are in it;
the panel on the back does.

Added iron is non-heme and absorbs inefficiently, so serve a vitamin-C food in
the same meal — [[mango]], [[broccoli]], [[potato]] — and keep dairy out of that
particular bowl, since calcium inhibits non-heme absorption. See [[oatmeal]] and
[[barley]] for the single-grain records.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Mix with breast milk, formula, or water. Not cow's milk before 12 months.**

Smooth cereal is a low-risk texture; that is most of why it exists. The hazard
appears when you switch to home-cooked whole grains, where **cooked whole grain
kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list** and the instruction is to cook and
then finely grind or mash them.

**On allergens:** oat and barley are not among the nine major US allergens.
Multigrain cereals often contain wheat, which **is** one of the nine — so if
wheat matters in your household, the ingredient list is what settles it, not the
word "multigrain."

foods.name: Gim (김, unseasoned laver)

ageBands.servingNote: Unseasoned, unsalted, un-oiled only. Crumbled over food rather than handed over as a sheet.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy plain roasted or plain dried sheets. Check the ingredients: it should say
laver or seaweed, and nothing else. No salt, no oil, no sesame.

**Crumble it over food** rather than handing over a sheet — over rice, over
[[oatmeal]], over mashed vegetables. A pinch is a serving at this age.

Two reasons for crumbling rather than handing over. The practical one: a dry
sheet of 김 goes limp and sticks the instant it touches anything wet, including
a wet hand. The cautious one: a dry sheet can adhere to the roof of the mouth.
**No guideline body names that as a hazard** — it is ordinary caution, not an
issued rule, and it is the reason this food is rated low-risk rather than
modify-required.

Do not use 김 as the vehicle for rice or as a wrapper at this age.

Still crumbled, still plain, still small amounts. A pincer grasp makes flakes
easy to pick up off a tray directly, which some babies enjoy more than having it
mixed in.

Frequency, not portion, is the thing to keep an eye on now — it is an easy food
to reach for daily because it is convenient and babies like it.

A toddler can manage torn pieces of a plain sheet, and 김 with rice is a normal
thing to eat. The constraints that stay are the two this page is about: **plain,
and not every day.**

Seasoned 김 is what most households actually have in the cupboard. It carries
salt, oil, and often sesame. If you serve it, treat it as a salted snack food
rather than a vegetable, and check the label for sesame if that allergen matters
in your family.

choking.requiredModification: Crumble it over food rather than giving a dry sheet. A dry sheet can stick to the roof of the mouth — no guideline body names this, so treat it as ordinary caution rather than an issued rule.
