foods.backgroundMd:
김 is one of the easiest foods in the Korean repertoire to hand a baby, and one
of the easiest to over-serve without noticing. Both facts come from the same
place: iodine.

**Buy it unseasoned, unsalted and un-oiled.** That is the only form this record
covers, and it rules out most of what is sold. Seasoned 김 — the glossy salted
snack sheets, the little travel packs — is a different food.

🚩 **And there is an allergen hiding in the seasoned kind: sesame.** Commercial
seasoned 김 is very often finished with sesame oil, sesame seeds, or both, and
**sesame has been one of the nine major US allergens since January 2023.** Plain
laver contains no major allergen at all; the seasoning is where one appears.
This makes 김 a label-reading item rather than a safe-by-default one — check the
ingredient list, not the front of the package.

**Now the iodine, which is the real subject of this page.** Dried nori carries
**2,316.7 µg of iodine per 100 g**, with a measured range of **1,640 to 2,850**
(USDA's iodine database, Release 4). NIH's Office of Dietary Supplements puts a
household portion on it: **2 tablespoons of flakes, about 5 g, supply 116 µg —
77% of the Daily Value.**

The Daily Value is an adult label reference. Against a baby's own number the
picture is sharper: the adequate intake for a 7-to-12-month-old is **130 µg a
day**, so ⚠️ **5 g of 김 flakes is roughly 89% of an infant's entire daily
reference intake.** That last figure is **arithmetic we did** — 116 divided by
130 — not a number any body published. Two tablespoons of flakes is not much
food.

🚨 **And here is the part that has no comfortable answer: there is no upper
intake level for iodine in infants.** NIH ODS lists the UL for both 0–6 months
and 7–12 months as **"Not possible to establish"** — the Food and Nutrition
Board judged the evidence insufficient to set one. The footnote reads that
formula and food should be the only sources of iodine for infants.

**That is an absence of a limit, not permission, and it is not a reversal of
anything.** Nobody withdrew a ceiling; one was never established. So the
question "how much 김 is too much?" genuinely has **no guideline answer**, and
this record will not manufacture one — you will find no maximum-per-week figure
here, because inventing one would be worse than admitting the gap.

What can be said honestly:

- A small amount is already a large fraction of the daily reference intake.
- It is **not a food to give freely or every day**, the way you might with
  [[broccoli]] or [[oatmeal]].
- Even the same product varies. The USDA range spans ±25% around the mean, and
  across commercial seaweeds generally ODS reports concentrations from **16 µg/g
  to 2,984 µg/g** — a 186-fold spread. **You cannot infer the dose from the
  package**, and that, rather than any number, is the actionable fact.
- Too much iodine causes some of the same problems as too little — goiter,
  elevated TSH, hypothyroidism.

If a baby is eating 김 most days, that is worth raising with your pediatrician.
That suggestion is **ours**; no guideline body says it.

For the seaweed where this gets genuinely extreme, see [[miyeok]] — and the note
there about 다시마, which is in a different league again.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Iodine is the governing issue, and it has no numeric ceiling to give you.** No
UL exists for infants — "not possible to establish" — so there is no
guideline-issued maximum, and this record declines to invent one. Practically:
small amounts, not daily, and raise it with your pediatrician if 김 has become
an everyday food. The last part is our inference.

**Content is unpredictable per package.** A 186-fold range across commercial
seaweeds, and ±25% within dried nori alone. No amount of label-reading tells you
the dose.

🚩 **Sesame in seasoned 김.** Plain laver has no major allergen; the seasoned
product frequently contains sesame seeds or sesame oil, and sesame is one of the
nine. Read the ingredient list.

**Sodium in seasoned 김.** Salted snack sheets are salty by design. Sodium
adequate intake is 110 mg a day from birth to six months and 370 mg from seven
to twelve months (NASEM 2019) — note that these are adequacy targets, not
ceilings, since no UL or EAR for sodium exists at any age.

**Choking risk is low.** The dry-sheet-sticking-to-the-palate caution above is
ordinary practice, not a recognised mechanism named by any body.

**No guideline body addresses 김 as an infant food.** The iodine figures, the
absence of an infant UL and sesame's allergen status are all issued or measured.
The serving advice — crumble it, keep it small, do not make it daily — is our
inference from those facts.

foods.name: Green peas

ageBands.servingNote: Peas roll. Smashed onto a loaded spoon or into a thicker purée, they stay put long enough to reach a mouth.
ageBands.prepMd:
Simmer or steam until a pea flattens when you press it. Then smash them —
against the side of a bowl with a fork, or stirred into a thicker purée such as
[[butternut-squash]] so they have something to hold onto.

Loose peas at this age mostly end up on the floor. That is not a safety problem,
it is a physics one: a whole-hand grasp cannot pick up a sphere. Loading a spoon
and handing it over, or spreading smashed peas on a strip of toast, gets more
into the baby.

The pincer grasp — AAP puts it at most often between 9 and 10 months — is
exactly the tool a pea is shaped for, and picking them up one at a time is good
practice. Many parents keep squashing each pea between finger and thumb first.

Be clear about what that habit is. **No AAP or CDC document names green peas as
a choking hazard.** AAP's rule concerns round *firm* food — "do not feed
children younger than 4 round, firm food unless it is chopped completely" — and
a properly cooked pea is soft, not firm. Smashing is a conservative
extrapolation from that rule rather than an instruction anyone issued. It costs
nothing, so it is a reasonable thing to do; it is not a thing you have failed to
do if you skip it.

Whole, cooked, however the rest of the table is eating them. Mushy peas, peas
stirred through rice, peas in a soup.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a pea crushes under light pressure. Smashing each one is a conservative habit, not a rule any guideline body issues — see below.

foods.backgroundMd:
Both CDC and NHS name peas among early vegetables, and they are one of the few
foods on this list that pair themselves: 1.54 mg of iron and 14.2 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g cooked, in the same spoonful. Vitamin C improves absorption of plant
(non-heme) iron eaten in the same meal, so the pea does the pairing work that
[[spinach]] or [[tofu]] need a second food for.

Frozen peas are fine and often better than fresh — they are picked and frozen
quickly, and they cook in minutes. Raw peas hold more vitamin C (40 mg per 100 g
against 14.2 cooked) but are firm, so cooking is the trade you make.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The real failure mode is undercooking. A pea straight from the freezer, or one
blanched for thirty seconds, stays firm — that is when AAP's round-and-firm rule
genuinely applies. Cook until they give.

Dried whole peas and split peas are a different food and need cooking to a soft
mash; CDC lists whole beans as a choking hazard, and a hard dried pulse belongs
in that group.

foods.name: Ground walnut

ageBands.servingNote: Finely ground to a powder or paste and stirred into a moist food. No piece, ever, at any age in this app's range.
ageBands.prepMd:
Grind walnuts in a spice grinder, a small food processor, or a mortar, and keep
going past the point where it looks done. You want a powder, or a paste — walnut
is oily enough that a fine grind will start clumping into a butter, which is
fine. **If you can see distinct pieces, it is not ground yet.** Pass it through
your fingers: no grit you can feel as an individual fragment.

Stir a quarter teaspoon through something moist — [[oatmeal]], [[yogurt]],
mashed [[banana]], a puree. The moisture matters for a second reason besides
taste: dry nut powder on a tray is inhalable, and a baby who breathes in over a
spoonful of dust has a different problem from a choking one.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing, and watch for
about two hours. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours.

ageBands.servingNote: Still finely ground. The pincer grasp arriving does not make a nut piece safe.
ageBands.prepMd:
Still finely ground. The pincer grasp arriving is the reason parents start
offering small pieces of other foods around now, and it is exactly the wrong
instinct here — the pincer grasp lets a baby pick up a nut fragment, it does not
give them the molars or the coordination to deal with one.

Grind a batch and keep it in the freezer; it goes rancid fast at room
temperature. Stir it through porridge, mashed vegetables, a thick soup.

ageBands.servingNote: Still finely ground. Whole nuts are off the table until at least four, and NIAID says five.
ageBands.prepMd:
Still finely ground, folded into whatever the table is eating — baked into
things, stirred through sauces, blended into a dip. A twelve-month-old is not
closer to handling a walnut half than a six-month-old is.

Watch for walnut arriving as pieces in adult food at this age: banchan, salads,
brownies, baklava, muesli, walnut-topped breads. That is where the accidental
first piece usually comes from, not from a bowl of nuts.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of walnuts ground to a fine powder or paste and stirred through a moist food your baby already eats. No body publishes a first-serving amount, a weekly target or an introduction order for tree nuts — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before the first exposure to tree nuts — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no tree-nut testing protocol, no tree-nut dose and no tree-nut weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food.

choking.note: Whole nuts are a high-risk choking hazard. NIAID says they should not be given under 5 years; AAP's general framing is "until 4 years of age or older". Both positions are live and NIAID's is the cautious default.
choking.requiredModification: FINELY GROUND ONLY, stirred into a moist food. Not chopped, not "chopped fine", not crushed into bits — CDC's hazard entry is "whole or CHOPPED nuts and seeds", so chopping is inside the hazard, not a way out of it. NHS issues the only sanctioned form: serve them finely ground.

foods.backgroundMd:
Walnut is the third distinct tree-nut sensitization in this canon, after
[[almond-butter]] and [[cashew-butter]]. Tolerating one tree nut says nothing
about another; walnut's reported clustering is with hazelnut, not with almond or
cashew.

**Read this before anything else: "chopped fine" is not a safe form.** CDC's
choking-hazard entry is "**whole or chopped** nuts and seeds." Chopping is
*inside* the hazard entry. It is not a mitigation, not a compromise, and not a
smaller version of a hazard — it is the hazard, listed by name, alongside the
whole nut. This matters because "finely chopped" sounds careful. It sounds like
the responsible thing a parent does with a nut. It is not, and a chopped walnut
fragment is a hard, irregular, airway-sized piece with the density to lodge.

**The only sanctioned form is finely ground.** That is NHS's instruction —
serve them finely ground — and it is the single positive form-instruction any
body issues for nuts. Ground means powder or paste: the walnut has stopped being
pieces. Then stir it into something moist so it cannot be inhaled as loose dust.

**Every age band in this record is the same form**, which is unusual in this
canon and deliberate. No band gets a piece of walnut. Nine months does not earn
one, and neither does eighteen. The bands differ in what you stir it into, not
in how coarse it can be.

This is one of the few foods here that is genuinely useful nutritionally in the
same breath: ground walnut is a real non-heme iron contributor at **2.91 mg per
100 g**, and the USDA id behind that figure is for whole English walnuts, which
is the exact food — ground walnut is walnut, ground. Pair it with a vitamin-C
food in the same meal, since non-heme iron absorbs poorly on its own:
[[mango]], [[broccoli]], [[butternut-squash]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**This is the highest-risk food in this batch, and the risk is entirely about
form.**

**Chopped is a hazard, not a mitigation.** Saying it again because it is the one
thing people get wrong: CDC lists "whole or **chopped** nuts and seeds." A
recipe that says "finely chopped walnuts" has not made the food safe for a baby.
Grind it.

**Whole nuts have a hard age floor, and the bodies disagree on where it is.**
NIAID: whole nuts should not be given to children **less than 5 years** of age.
AAP's general framing is "until **4 years** of age or older." Both positions are
current. **NIAID's five-year floor is the more cautious default and is the one
this record encodes**, which is why the restriction on this record reads 60
months. This record surfaces the disagreement rather than picking one and
pretending it is unanimous — if your pediatrician works to the four-year line,
that is a defensible position with AAP behind it.

**Ground is not restricted.** The 60-month floor is about whole and chopped
nuts. Finely ground walnut stirred into a moist food is appropriate from six
months, and that is the whole point of this record existing.

**Nut butters are a separate hazard entry with a separate rule.** If you make
walnut butter by grinding far enough, treat it like [[almond-butter]]: smooth,
thinned until it pours, never a spoonful, never a thick glob.

foods.name: Kabocha squash

ageBands.prepMd:
Steam or roast until completely soft, then cut into finger-length wedges about
two fingers thick. Remove the skin for a beginner — kabocha skin stays chewy
even when the flesh is soft, and chewy is the harder texture.
Soft cubes around thumbnail size once the pincer grasp arrives.

Serve it the way the rest of the table eats it — cubed in a soup, mashed as a
side, or roasted in wedges. Skin can stay on now if it's roasted soft.

choking.requiredModification: Steam or roast until a fork meets no resistance; skin removed for beginners.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics
American Academy of Pediatrics

foods.backgroundMd:
Dense, sweet winter squash — 단호박 in Korean, where it's a common early
weaning food, often steamed and mashed thin. Behaves almost identically to
[[sweet-potato]] once cooked, so it's a natural second food if the first went
well: same shapes, same softness test, different flavour.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The raw squash is very hard and needs real force to cut — that firmness is
exactly the hazard, so the softness test matters more here than with a
softer-fleshed vegetable. Press a cooked piece between thumb and forefinger
before serving; if it holds its shape under pressure, cook it longer.

foods.name: Korean pear

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked slices, or grated raw. Waiting for it to ripen does not soften it — this is not a European pear.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Grated.** This is the easier route and the one that suits the fruit. Peel it,
then grate on the coarse side of a box grater. The shreds are short, wet, and
soft enough to gum. Serve on a loaded spoon or stirred into yogurt or porridge.

**Cooked.** Peel, core, slice, and simmer with a splash of water until a slice
collapses under a fork. It takes noticeably longer than an apple — a dense
Korean pear can want fifteen to twenty minutes — so test rather than time it.
Serve as finger-length slices held in the fist with an end sticking out.

The pincer grasp, most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP, means cooked cubes
about the size of your thumbnail can be picked up one at a time. They still have
to be cooked soft. Being able to lift a raw cube is not the same as being able
to chew one.

Grated raw stays the low-effort option, and now that the pincer grip exists a
small pile of shreds is something the baby can manage alone.

Cooked soft or grated raw, still peeled. Raw chunks and raw batons are the part
that does not change at twelve months — AAP's line for raw fruit chunks is four
years.

If the household is eating bae at the end of a meal, grate the toddler's portion
off the same fruit rather than handing over a slice.

choking.note: No guideline body names Korean or Asian pear specifically. It sits inside AAP's "raw fruit chunks" entry, which AAP keeps off the menu until 4 years of age or older, and inside CDC's hard-raw-fruit line. That is category-level coverage, and this record says so rather than implying a food-specific ruling exists.
choking.requiredModification: Treat it as raw apple. Cook until it mashes easily with a fork, or grate it raw. Peel it either way. Ripening will not make raw chunks safe.

foods.backgroundMd:
**No guideline body names Korean or Asian pear.** AAP, CDC, NHS and Health
Canada all cover it only at the category level — hard raw fruit — so everything
below is that category rule applied to this fruit, not a ruling anyone issued
about *Pyrus pyrifolia*. That distinction is worth stating plainly, because the
category rule it lands in is a strict one.

**Do not carry over the logic from [[pear]].** A European pear is safe raw once
it ripens because ripening softens it. A Korean pear does not do that. It stays
crisp and dense at full ripeness — that crunch is the point of the fruit — which
puts it squarely inside AAP's "raw fruit chunks, such as apple pieces" entry
rather than inside NHS's permission for soft ripe fruit. So it inherits the
[[apple]] rules: cook until fork-mashable, or grate raw, peel either way.

**Iron is zero.** Not low — zero, verified in USDA's entry, alongside 3.8 mg of
vitamin C per 100 g. This is a hydration and flavour food. It is very juicy,
mildly sweet, and pleasant on sore gums when grated; it contributes nothing to
the 11 mg of iron a day a 7–12 month old needs, and it is not strong enough on
vitamin C to serve as the partner for an iron meal. Use it for enjoyment and
variety, and get iron from [[tofu]], [[barley]] cereal, or [[green-peas]].

**Two Korean-kitchen forms that are not appropriate for a baby.** Grated bae is
the standard tenderiser in bulgogi and galbi marinades, mixed with soy sauce and
sugar — that combination is high sodium and added sugar, both off the menu under
24 months. And bae juice, or baesuk simmered with honey, runs into three
separate rules: no juice before 12 months, no added sugars before 24, no honey
before 12. Serve the fruit plain.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The specific trap here is that it looks like a pear and is sold as a pear, so it
invites the pear reasoning: wait until it is ripe, then serve it raw. That
reasoning is wrong for this fruit. Ripeness does not soften it, and a ripe
Korean pear cut into cubes is the same hazard as raw apple cubes — hard, smooth,
and breaking into airway-sized pieces under a bite.

Peel it at every age in this range. The skin is tougher than a European pear's
and does not break down under gums.

Serve it plain: no marinade, no juice, no honey.

foods.name: Lamb

ageBands.servingNote: Braised until it shreds under a fork, then minced fine and loosened with its own cooking liquid.
ageBands.prepMd:
Take a shoulder cut, trim the fat, and remove any bone **before** cooking rather
than picking it out afterwards — that is CDC's instruction and it is much easier
in a raw piece than a hot cooked one. Braise it low and slow, in water or
unsalted stock, until it pulls apart with no resistance at all.

Then mince it finer than you would for yourself and stir in enough of the
cooking liquid that it clumps on a spoon. Dry mince scatters across a tray and
a six-month-old cannot gather it; wet mince holds together and gets eaten.

On temperature: USDA FSIS sets 145 °F plus a three-minute rest as the minimum
for lamb chops and roasts, and 160 °F for ground lamb. Those are floors, not
targets. A braise goes far past either, which is what you want here — FDA is
explicit that children should only eat meat cooked to a safe internal
temperature, so a pink or rare centre is not an option for a baby even though it
is legal for an adult.

Shredded rather than minced. Once the pincer grasp arrives, long soft strands
are easier to pick up than fine crumbs, and lamb that has been braised properly
falls into exactly that shape. Mixed through [[oatmeal]] or a mashed vegetable it
travels better than lamb on its own.

However the family eats it, with two things unchanged: still soft enough to mash,
and still not in chunks. Grilled lamb chops and kebab cubes are the wrong form —
firm cubes of meat stay a hazard well past the first birthday.

choking.requiredModification: Ground, finely minced, or shredded to collapse — never chunks. Remove fat and bones before cooking, and cook until it mashes with light pressure.

foods.backgroundMd:
Lamb is here for zinc as much as iron. Braised shoulder carries 2.39 mg of iron
and 6.08 mg of zinc per 100 g, and broiled shoulder 2.12 mg iron with 5.01 mg
zinc — the highest zinc values of any non-liver food in this set, and comfortably
above [[beef]]'s. Roasted leg is a little lower on both (1.98 mg iron, 4.66 mg
zinc), so if you are choosing a cut for a baby, shoulder wins twice: more of both
minerals, and it is the cut that braises into shreds.

The iron is heme iron, the form CDC says is more easily absorbed than the
non-heme iron in plants and fortified cereals. It does not need a vitamin-C food
alongside it — heme absorption is not vitamin-C dependent. Serve lamb with
whatever vegetable you like, for taste rather than chemistry.

Zinc matters at this age for the same reason iron does: WHO's 2023 complementary
feeding guideline asks for animal-source foods daily from six months, and the
Canadian Paediatric Society asks for iron-rich foods twice a day from about six
months. Lamb does both jobs in one ingredient.

Lamb is not one of the nine major US allergens.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Chunks.** AAP keeps chunks of meat on its list of foods to avoid until age
four, and "tough or large chunks of meat" is a named entry on CDC's
choking-hazard list. Ground, finely minced, or shredded-to-collapse is the safe
form. A cube of lamb is not, at any age in this range.

**Bones.** Lamb shoulder and leg are usually sold bone-in. Bone out before
cooking — both CDC and NHS put bones on the remove-first list — then run the
cooked meat between your fingers before serving, because shoulder in particular
sheds small fragments during a long braise.

**Doneness.** FSIS's 145 °F plus rest is a food-safety minimum for a whole cut,
not a texture instruction. For a baby the texture is the harder test: if the
meat holds together when you pull at it, it is not ready, regardless of what the
thermometer says. Cook it further.

foods.name: Lentils

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked until they collapse into a puree — red and split lentils get there on their own.
ageBands.prepMd:
Rinse, then simmer in unsalted water or broth until they lose their shape
entirely. Red and split lentils fall apart on their own in about twenty minutes;
brown, green, and Puy lentils hold together much longer and need either more
time or a mash at the end.

Serve as a thick puree off a loaded spoon, or spread on a strip of toast. No
salt — high-sodium foods are advised against under two years.

Thicker and lumpier is fine now, and lentils are a good carrier for iron-rich
company: stir in finely chopped [[chicken-thigh]] or mix with [[oatmeal]]. Mash
any lentils that are still visibly whole.

However the family eats them — dal, soup, stirred through rice. Softness is
still the test.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until the lentils break down, and mash any that still hold a round shape.

sources.body: NHS Start for Life — what to feed your baby around 6 months
Canadian Paediatric Society
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — iron
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards

foods.backgroundMd:
**The highest non-heme iron of any whole food in this batch — 3.33 mg per 100 g
cooked**, plus 9.02 g of protein, from something that costs almost nothing and
cooks in half an hour without soaking. Both NHS and the Canadian Paediatric
Society name lentils for this age.

Non-heme iron is absorbed less readily than the heme iron in [[beef]] or
[[salmon]], and CDC's answer is to serve it with a vitamin-C food. Lentils bring
only 1.5 mg of vitamin C themselves, so pair them — [[broccoli]] is one CDC
names by name. A dal with a green vegetable stirred through it is doing real
nutritional work, not just filling a bowl.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Here is an honest ambiguity rather than a resolved rule. **Lentils are not
individually named on CDC's choking-hazard list, but "whole beans" is**, and
lentils are pulses. Nobody has published a ruling on whether a cooked lentil
falls inside that entry.

What is clear is the physical difference: a cooked black bean stays a smooth
round object, while a cooked red or split lentil has usually already
disintegrated. This record treats lentils as needing modification — cook them
down, mash what is left round — which costs nothing and stays on the right side
of an entry that may or may not include them. Whole firm lentils, the kind that
survive a salad, are the form to avoid.

No salt, for the same reason as everywhere else in the first two years. Lentils
are not one of the nine major US allergens.

foods.name: Lotus root

ageBands.servingNote: Finely grated or puréed into another food. Not a finger food, and not a slice — lotus root stays crisp no matter how long it is cooked.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Finely grated or puréed into another food.** Peel it, grate it on the fine side
of a box grater, and cook it into a porridge, a soup, or a pancake batter, where
it disappears into the texture of whatever it is in. That is the form that works,
and it is the same form as under 12 months — the age band does not change the
root.

**What not to do:** slices, half-moons, batons or chunks, no matter how long they
have been braised. A braised slice of 연근 that an adult reads as "soft" is still
crisp against a toddler's gums and molars, and it is round and firm, which is the
shape both AAP and CDC warn about.

Skip 연근조림 for this age even in small pieces. The soy sauce and sugar are
separate problems from the texture, and both are on CDC's under-24-month list.

If what you want is the vitamin C, [[broccoli]], [[potato]], [[mango]] or
[[plantain]] deliver it in a form that mashes.

choking.note: This ruling is derived, not issued. No guideline body names lotus root. It comes from applying CDC's rule — cook food until it is soft enough to easily mash with a fork — to a root that structurally cannot get there. A human reviewer should ratify it before this record is treated as settled.
choking.requiredModification: Finely grate or purée it into another food. Never a round slice, a baton, or any piece a child bites from — boiling, braising and stewing do not make lotus root soft enough to mash with a fork.

sources.body: CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods ("cook food until it is soft enough to easily mash with a fork"; cut cylindrical foods into short thin strips rather than rounds)
CDC — Choking Hazards (hard raw vegetables; round firm shapes)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (added sugars under 24 months; sodium)
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention (round firm foods; no piece larger than one-half inch)

foods.backgroundMd:
**The frustrating thing about lotus root is that the nutrition is good and the
texture disqualifies it.** Cooked, it carries **27.4 mg of vitamin C per 100 g —
the highest of any food in this part of the canon** — plus 0.90 mg of iron and
useful fibre. On paper it looks like an excellent vitamin-C partner for an iron
meal.

It does not pass the one texture rule that matters. CDC's instruction is to
"cook food until it is soft enough to easily mash with a fork." **Lotus root
cannot be cooked to that point in a home kitchen.** Its crispness is structural
rather than a matter of doneness: the rhizome is full of air channels
(aerenchyma), and its cell walls are lignified and cross-linked with calcium, so
they hold together through boiling, braising and long stewing. That is not a
defect — it is exactly why the root is prized in Korean, Chinese and Japanese
cooking. 연근 is served *because* it stays crunchy.

Compare it with the other roots in this batch. **[[potato]], [[taro]] and
[[cassava]] all pass the fork-mash test after ordinary cooking. Lotus root does
not, at any household cooking time.** Two of those three carry real toxicology
warnings and are still easier to serve safely than this one, because their
hazard can be cooked or peeled away and lotus root's cannot.

Its culinary form makes it worse rather than better: the standard cut is a hard
round slice, and a firm round is the shape AAP singles out. And 연근조림, the
most common household preparation, braises it in soy sauce and sugar — added
sugars and sodium, both of which CDC puts off the menu under 24 months.

**So the ruling here is: lotus root is not appropriate as a finger food before
12 months, in any size or shape, and this record's `firstOkMonths` of 12 is for
lotus root as its own food.** Before then, the only defensible use is finely
grated or puréed into something else, where it contributes very little.

**This is an editorial judgement, not a guideline.** No guideline body names
lotus root at all. What is issued is CDC's fork-mash rule; applying it to this
root is a derivation, and it is labelled as one throughout. If you disagree, you
are disagreeing with our reading rather than with CDC. A human reviewer should
ratify this before it is treated as settled.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Lotus root is not a finger food.** That is the whole safety note, and it is the
one thing worth remembering from this record.

It fails CDC's fork-mash rule structurally, not because of undercooking, so
"cook it longer" is not the fix — there is no cooking time at which a crisp
rhizome becomes mashable. Its standard cut is a firm round, which is the shape
AAP explicitly warns about for children under four, and its air channels mean a
slice holds together as a ring rather than collapsing.

**This assessment is derived from a general CDC rule, not issued by any body
about this food, and is badged accordingly.** It is the most restrictive call in
this batch and the least externally supported one, which is precisely why it is
labelled as an opinion rather than dressed up as guidance. A human should
review it.

foods.name: Lump crabmeat

ageBands.servingNote: Picked over by hand under good light, then flaked fine and moistened so it holds together.
ageBands.prepMd:
Use cooked, refrigerated lump crabmeat, or meat you picked yourself from a crab
you cooked. Tip it into a shallow white bowl or plate, spread it out, and go
through it with your fingertips under a bright light — the whole tub, not a
spot check. You are feeling for anything firmer than the meat: a translucent
sliver, a curved chip, a papery membrane. It is slow, and it is the job.

Then flake it fine and stir it into something moist — mashed [[avocado]],
[[sweet-potato]], a thick puree — so it holds together instead of scattering
into dry threads.

Serve it fully cooked. NHS's rule for shellfish is never raw or lightly cooked.

Larger flakes the pincer grasp can gather, still picked over the same way, still
mixed through something that binds it. Nothing about the shell check relaxes
with age; a nine-month-old is not better at spitting out a shell chip than a
seven-month-old.

Crab folded into whatever the family eats — a rice bowl, a soft cake, a soup.
Still picked over. Still fully cooked. Still no imitation crab.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of fully cooked crabmeat, picked clean of shell and flaked into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for crustacean shellfish, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to crustacean shellfish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol, dose, or weekly target for shellfish, and peanut's numbers should not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Pick the meat over by hand, under good light, every single time — pasteurized lump crab routinely carries shell and cartilage shards. Serve it fully cooked, never raw or lightly cooked, and never as imitation crab.

foods.backgroundMd:
Crab closes the same allergen slot as [[shrimp]] — **crustacean shellfish**, one
of the nine major US allergens — and it is worth knowing that either one does
that job, so you do not need both.

**The shell fragment is the hazard, not the meat.** This is the whole reason
crab gets its own record. Crabmeat itself is soft, flaky and about as low-risk a
texture as exists. But pasteurized lump crab, the tub sold in the refrigerated
case, routinely carries shell and cartilage shards that survived picking at the
plant. They are thin, pale, sharp-edged and near-invisible against white meat.
The preparation step that matters is not cutting. It is picking over.

**This record publishes no iron figure and no USDA id.** A verified composition
entry for lump crabmeat could not be established while this was written, and the
honest options were to leave it blank or to borrow [[shrimp]]'s numbers and call
them crab's. It is left blank. Do not read that as "crab has no iron" — read it
as "nobody here has checked." Crab is a protein food in this canon; if you need
an iron food, use [[sardines]], [[beef]] or [[lentils]], which have figures
behind them.

Sodium is the other gap. Crab is typically packed with salt and the actual
figure is unverified, so rinse it, do not add more, and do not treat it as a
low-sodium protein.

**On "shellfish" as a category:** FDA splits it. Crustacean — crab, shrimp,
lobster, crawfish — is a major allergen and must be declared on labels.
**Molluscs — oyster, clam, mussel, scallop — are not**, and carry no mandatory
declaration, even though a mollusc allergy is real and can be severe. Everyday
usage merges the two. Regulation does not.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Pick it over by hand, under good light, every time.** Not once per tub, every
serving. Shell and cartilage shards are the entire risk profile of this food,
and no amount of cooking softens them. Crab is not a named entry on any official
choking list — this instruction is an application of CDC's general principle of
removing bones before the food reaches a child, and it is labelled as such.

**Never imitation crab.** Surimi sticks are not a substitute here and swapping
them in is actively counterproductive on three counts: they are fish paste plus
starch, so they add **wheat** in most formulations, they carry added salt, and
they **do not close the crustacean slot** — a baby who tolerates imitation crab
has been introduced to fish and wheat, not to crab. If you are serving crab to
cover the allergen, the label has to say crab.

**Never raw or lightly cooked**, per NHS.

**Do not read a tolerated crab as a tolerated scallop.** Crustacean and mollusc
are separate allergens, and tolerating one says nothing about the other.

foods.name: Mango

ageBands.servingNote: Ripe mango is slippery. Leaving a strip of peel at the gripping end helps — but the peel is not the part to eat.
ageBands.prepMd:
Pick a mango that gives under gentle pressure and smells sweet at the stem end.
Peel it, cut the two cheeks off either side of the flat stone, then cut
finger-length strips.

Ripe mango is genuinely slippery, which is the main practical problem at this
age. Two things that help: leave a band of peel at one end as a handle while
keeping the eating end bare, or roll the strip in a little infant cereal or
ground oats for grip. Neither is a safety measure — they are grip aids.

An underripe mango is firm. Do not serve that raw in strips: cook it soft or
grate it, exactly as with raw [[apple]].

With the pincer grasp — most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP — soft mango
cubes about the size of your thumbnail work well, with a couple of larger strips
alongside so biting stays in practice.

Mashed mango is also a good carrier for something less popular: stirred into
plain [[yogurt]], or over [[barley]] cereal.

However the rest of the table is eating it, peeled and stoned. Cubes, strips,
blended into a lassi with plain yogurt and no added sugar.

choking.requiredModification: Peel it and remove the stone. Use a ripe mango — an underripe one is firm and needs cooking or grating like raw apple.

foods.backgroundMd:
A ripe mango is about as easy as first foods get: soft, sweet, and mashable
without cooking. Neither AAP nor CDC names mango individually — NHS covers it at
the category level as a soft ripe fruit — so its place here is category-level
coverage rather than a food-specific ruling.

**Vitamin C varies by cultivar by roughly fivefold**, so this record gives a
range rather than a number: USDA's verified entries run from **25.5 mg per 100 g
for Tommy Atkins to 168 mg for Ataulfo**, with the generic entry at 36.4 mg. Any
of those makes mango a genuinely useful vitamin-C partner for a plant-iron meal
— [[tofu]], [[green-peas]], [[barley]] cereal — since vitamin C improves
absorption of non-heme iron eaten alongside it. Mango's own iron is a trace
0.16 mg per 100 g, and the two Foundation cultivar samples measured zero.

Peel it and take the stone out. NHS's instruction is to always remove hard pips
or stones, and a mango stone is large, fibrous, and exactly the wrong shape.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The stone is the hazard, and it is the only one that comes with an actual
guideline instruction: remove hard pips and stones. Do not hand over a gnawed
stone as a teether — it is the wrong size and shape, and the fibres come away.

**Skin contact, not food allergy.** Mango peel, leaves and stem contain
urushiol-family compounds — the same chemical family as poison ivy — and
peer-reviewed dermatology literature documents type-IV *contact* dermatitis on
the lips and face in people already sensitised to poison ivy or oak. Two things
about that. First, it is not a food allergy and not an IgE reaction; it is a
delayed rash from touching the peel. Second, prior sensitisation is very
unlikely in an infant who has never met poison ivy. This is peer-reviewed
literature, **not** a pediatric guideline, and no body issues advice about it.

The practical consequence is small and you were going to do it anyway: serve
peeled flesh, and keep the peel off the tray.

foods.name: Manila clam

ageBands.servingNote: Chopped fine and moistened. Clam meat is small and firm — it needs loosening to be gatherable, not just cutting.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Purge first.** Put the clams in cool salted water for an hour or so somewhere
dark and let them spit out their sand, then lift them out rather than pouring
them out — the grit is now at the bottom of the bowl and you do not want to pour
it back over them. Rinse.

**Discard any clam whose shell is already open before cooking.** That is CDC's
rule, and it is stricter than FDA's, which is why it is the one here.

**Cook by boiling until the shells open, then keep boiling another 3 to 5
minutes.** Steaming works too, 4 to 9 minutes. **Throw away any that do not open
fully.**

Then the taking-apart, which matters more than the cooking:

- **Feel through every clam for shell chips.** Clam shells are brittle and
  fragments end up in the meat.
- **Cut off the tough siphon tip** — the dark rubbery neck. It does not soften.
- **Chop the rest fine and moisten** it with a spoonful of the cooking broth so
  it clumps instead of scattering across the tray.
- **Nothing larger than half an inch** — AAP's rule and the only dimensional
  rule any US guideline body issues.

Use the broth sparingly and unsalted. Clam liquor is naturally salty before
anyone adds anything.

Same purge, same cooking, same shell check. Pieces up to half an inch suit the
pincer grasp that most babies develop around nine to ten months. Clams mixed
into soft rice or [[oatmeal]] are easier to gather than loose pieces, and the
broth carries the flavour into the rest of the bowl.

However the household eats them, with the baby's share lifted out **before** the
soup is seasoned. This is the practical constraint on 바지락 for a toddler:
칼국수 broth, 된장 and the salt that goes into most clam dishes carry far more
sodium than a small child's day should, and you cannot dilute your way out of
it once it is in the pot.

Never the shells to play with. The broken edges are sharp.

choking.requiredModification: Purge the grit, shuck completely, feel through the meat for shell chips, remove the tough siphon tip, and cut to no larger than half an inch.

foods.backgroundMd:
바지락 turns up in more Korean home cooking than almost any other shellfish — in
칼국수, in soups, in 된장찌개 — so for a lot of families the question is not
whether to serve it but how to get a baby's portion out of a pot that was made
for adults.

**The defining prep problem is grit, not nutrition.** A clam that has not been
purged carries sand, and sand in a shellfish stew is unpleasant for an adult and
genuinely off-putting to a baby who is still deciding whether they like this
food at all. Purging in salted water is the standard fix. It is **ordinary
practice** — no guideline body addresses it, and it is a palatability step
rather than a safety one.

**The iron figure you were expecting is not here, on purpose.** Clams are
conventionally listed among the densest iron foods there are. We could not
verify that: the USDA database was unavailable when this record was researched,
and NIH's iron fact sheet does not list clams at all. This is exactly the case
where a well-known number is most tempting to supply from memory and most
important not to. What we will state is the classification — shellfish flesh
carries **heme** iron, the more readily absorbed form — and that the quantity is
pending verification. If you need a verified iron figure today, [[oyster]] and
[[beef]] have one.

**Iodine, with a caveat attached to the number.** USDA's iodine database gives
**66.5 µg per 100 g** — but that entry is for **canned, mixed-species clams**,
not fresh Manila clams. It is a proxy, and it is labelled as one here because
species and preparation both move iodine content around. It is enough to say
clams are a moderate iodine food: well above [[scallop]], well below the
seaweeds, and not a reason to avoid them.

**On allergy, the same split that catches everyone with molluscs.** Clams are
molluscs, and molluscs are **not** among the nine US major allergens — that list
names **crustacean** shellfish (crab, lobster, shrimp), not clam, oyster, mussel
or scallop. FDA's January 2025 final guidance sets out how it handles allergens
outside the nine. So: mollusc allergy is real, but **a US label need not warn
about it**, and "Contains: shellfish" refers to crustacean. Read the ingredient
list rather than the allergen line. And a shrimp reaction does not by itself
predict a clam reaction.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Raw or barely-opened clams are out at every age.** FDA names children among
the groups who should avoid raw or undercooked shellfish. "Just opened" is not
cooked — CDC's 3-to-5-minutes-past-opening is the standard to hit.

**Shell chips and the siphon tip** are the two things to remove by hand. The
meat itself is soft once cooked; those two are not.

**Mercury is not a concern.** FDA and EPA place clams in **Best Choices**, and
on the sub-list of choices that are *even lower* in mercury.

**Sodium is the constraint families actually run into**, because clams are
almost always cooked into something salted. Pull the baby's portion before
seasoning — a sound and widely given instruction, but one that traces to no
numbered rule, so treat it as practice rather than a guideline.

**No guideline body addresses Manila clam as an infant food.** The cooking
rules, the mercury rating and the half-inch limit are issued. The purge, the
siphon trim, the shell check and the chopping are category rules plus ordinary
practice, applied here by us.

foods.name: Millet

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked soft and mashed or ground — millet grains stay distinct and round even when well cooked.
ageBands.prepMd:
Cook with plenty of water until the grains have swollen and gone soft, then mash
or grind them and loosen with breast milk, formula, or the cooking liquid.
Millet gets creamy easily, which makes it a forgiving first porridge.

**Cooked millet grains are whole grain kernels**, and CDC's instruction for those
is to cook and then finely grind or mash. Millet is not named in that list, but
"and other grains" is. The grains are small enough that people skip this step —
the rule is written about kernels rather than about diameter, so do not.

Softer-cooked millet mashed into other foods, or millet porridge with mashed
vegetables and a protein stirred through. Loose dry grains scatter and get
scooped by the handful; keeping it wet keeps it manageable.

Mixed into the family's rice, in porridge, or in soups, kept soft. Millet in a
rice cooker with [[short-grain-rice]] is the normal household form and is fine
here, as long as the grains are soft and mashed through for anything still
distinctly firm.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until soft, then finely grind or mash. CDC's whole-grain-kernel rule covers it: millet grains stay small, round and separate after cooking, which is exactly the texture the rule is about.

CDC — Choking Hazards

foods.backgroundMd:
Millet cooks quickly, is mild, and is a normal part of mixed-grain rice in
Korean households — 기장밥 and 조밥 are the everyday forms. It is worth having in
the rotation for variety and texture.

**It is not an iron food, and this is the thing to be clear about.** Cooked
millet carries **0.63 mg of iron per 100 g — the lowest of any grain in this
part of the canon.** Cooked [[quinoa]] is more than twice that, [[teff]] more
than three times, and [[fortified-infant-cereal]] is in a different category
entirely at around a hundred times.

That does not make millet a bad food. It makes it a food that should sit
*alongside* the iron rather than in place of it. The realistic failure mode is
quiet: a homemade multigrain porridge feels more wholesome than a box of
fortified cereal, replaces it, and the iron in the day drops by most of it
without anything visibly changing. If millet is doing a lot of the work in your
baby's bowl, put the iron somewhere else in the day — [[beef]], [[lentils]], or
fortified cereal.

Millet's iron, like every plant iron here, is non-heme, so a vitamin-C food in
the same meal helps: [[potato]], [[broccoli]], [[mango]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cooked grain kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list** and the issued
instruction is to cook and then finely grind or mash them. Small size is not an
exemption in the way the rule is written.

The other risk with millet is nutritional rather than physical: **used as a main
grain, it displaces iron.** Treat it as texture and variety, not as a
contribution to the iron requirement.

foods.name: Miyeok (미역, sea mustard)

ageBands.servingNote: Rehydrated and chopped very short, or the soup broth alone with the seaweed strained out. Occasional, not daily.
ageBands.prepMd:
**The broth, with the seaweed strained out, is the gentler starting point.**
Soak dried 미역 until it swells — it expands a great deal, so use much less than
looks right — rinse it well, and simmer it into a plain unsalted soup with beef
or nothing at all. Strain the fronds out and offer a few spoons of the broth,
or use the broth to moisten rice or [[oatmeal]].

**If you are serving the seaweed itself, chop it very short.** Rehydrated 미역 is
long, slippery and slithery, and a strand does not break cleanly under a baby's
bite the way a soft vegetable does. Chop it far shorter than you think you need
to — well under half an inch, AAP's limit.

**No 간장, no salt, no 국간장.** 미역국 is normally seasoned with soy sauce or
salt; take the baby's portion before that happens.

**Occasional, not routine.** That is the frequency guidance, and it is
deliberately not a number, because no number exists to give you.

The same, with slightly more of the seaweed itself if the baby is managing it —
still chopped short, still unsalted, still occasional. A pincer grasp handles
short chopped fronds well; long strands remain a bad idea regardless of hand
skill, because the hazard is the strand, not the picking-up.

미역국 as the family eats it, lightly seasoned or unseasoned, with the fronds
chopped. Frequency is still the open question — a toddler now has a 200 µg
iodine upper limit to reason against, which is more than an infant had, but a
bowl of soup whose iodine content is unknowable within two orders of magnitude
is still not an everyday food.

Keep 다시마 stock out of the child's cup as a drink, whatever their age.

choking.requiredModification: Chop rehydrated fronds very short — they are long, slippery and slithery, and a strand does not break under a baby's bite. No guideline body addresses this; it is our caution, not an issued rule.

González et al. (2020), Biol Trace Elem Res — human exposure to iodine from edible seaweeds (European kombu 27.7 ± 5.4 mg/kg DW)

foods.backgroundMd:
미역국 is the soup a Korean mother eats after giving birth and the soup the
family eats on birthdays. It is going to be in the house, and a baby is going to
be offered some. This page is about what is actually known — which is less than
you would expect, and we are going to be straight about that rather than dress
it up.

🚨 **The primary literature on seaweed iodine disagrees with itself by up to two
orders of magnitude.** Not a small measurement discrepancy. Two peer-reviewed
studies, both credible, roughly 50 to 150 times apart:

- **Dawczynski and colleagues (2007)**, using ICP-MS on 34 dried algae products,
  found brown algae containing **as much as 1,316 ± 1,669 mg of iodine per kg of
  fresh matter**, with more than **4,000 mg/kg** in several *Laminaria* species.
- **González and colleagues (2020)**, using redox titration on 30 samples,
  reported **European kombu at 27.7 ± 5.4 mg/kg dry weight**, and calculated
  that 4 g a day would supply about 111 µg of iodine.

Different methods, different sample origins, different answers. **This record
reports both and does not average them, and does not pick one.** An average of
two numbers that far apart would be a fabricated third number with no source
behind it, and picking the low one would be optimism dressed as evidence.

⚠️ **Neither figure is actually about 미역.** Dawczynski's number is a group mean
across three genera of brown algae; there was **no 미역-specific figure we could
verify at all.** Attributing a brown-algae group mean to 미역 alone would be
invention, so we have not done it.

**Nobody has written the guidance you are looking for.** No guideline body we
checked — AAP, CDC, NHS, Health Canada, ESPGHAN, EFSA — **addresses 미역국 for
infants at all.** Not to permit it, not to restrict it, not to set a frequency.
That is a genuine gap in the literature and not something we are going to paper
over with a confident-sounding rule.

Here is what *is* established, and it is enough to act on:

- **There is no upper intake level for iodine in infants.** NIH ODS lists the UL
  for both 0–6 and 7–12 months as **"not possible to establish."** An absence of
  a limit, never a limit that was withdrawn — and not permission.
- The nearest real ceiling is the **200 µg UL at ages 1 to 3.** Applying it to an
  eleven-month-old is inference, not guideline.
- Adequate intake is **110 µg/day (0–6 months)** and **130 µg/day (7–12
  months)**.
- Iodine content across commercial seaweeds spans **16 µg/g to 2,984 µg/g** — a
  186-fold range. **You cannot read the dose off a package.**
- Too much iodine produces some of the same effects as too little: goiter,
  elevated TSH, hypothyroidism, and it is also associated with thyroiditis.

**Our inference, clearly labelled as ours:** occasional 미역국 with the seaweed
strained out is a very different exposure from a daily bowl with the seaweed
eaten, and a daily bowl is worth raising with your pediatrician. No body issues
that. It follows from the facts above, and we think it is the sensible reading,
but you should weigh it knowing where it came from.

### 다시마 (kombu) is the real outlier, and families use them interchangeably

This matters because 다시마 usually shares a shelf with 미역, both go into stock,
and it is natural to assume they behave alike. **They do not.**

⚠️ Working across two sources with different methods: Miyai's kombu contained
**35 mg of iodine in 15 g**, about **2,333 µg/g**, against roughly **23 µg/g**
for dried nori — **on the order of a hundredfold difference.** Treat that as an
order-of-magnitude statement rather than a precise ratio; the arithmetic is
ours, spanning two studies that did not use the same method.

And 다시마 is the only seaweed here with a **human trial** behind the concern.
**Miyai and colleagues (2008)** gave normal Japanese adults **15 and 30 g of
kombu daily** and saw serum **TSH rise significantly, exceeding normal limits in
some subjects.** Fifteen grams a day for 55 to 87 days kept TSH elevated; values
returned to baseline 7 to 40 days after stopping. That is ordinary culinary
quantities, in healthy adults, producing measurable thyroid suppression.

**Our inference again:** do not let a baby drink 다시마 stock routinely, strain
the kelp out, and do not reduce the stock — reducing concentrates the iodine
along with the flavour.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Iodine, and the honest position is that it is unquantifiable per package.**
The literature disagrees by up to two orders of magnitude, no 미역-specific
figure exists, and commercial seaweed spans a 186-fold range. Treat seaweed
iodine as **unknowable from the label** — that is the cautious default.

**There is no infant upper limit to check against.** "Not possible to establish"
for both infant bands. That is an absence of a limit, not a clearance, and this
record does not convert it into a permission or into an invented maximum. You
will find no maximum-per-week figure here for that reason.

**No guideline body addresses 미역국 for infants.** Every frequency and portion
statement on this page is our inference from the iodine facts, and is labelled
where it appears.

**다시마 is not interchangeable with 미역** — roughly a hundredfold more iodine by
the arithmetic above, and the only one of these seaweeds with a human trial
showing thyroid suppression at normal culinary amounts. Strain it, do not reduce
the stock, and do not serve it as a drink.

**Strands are a choking consideration.** Rehydrated fronds are long and
slippery. Chop them short. No body names this hazard for seaweed specifically —
it is our caution, applied from the general principle, not an issued rule.

**Sodium.** 미역국 is normally salted or seasoned with 국간장. Pull the baby's
portion before seasoning.

**Excess iodine looks like deficiency** — goiter, elevated TSH, hypothyroidism.
If a baby is eating seaweed regularly and you are unsure, that is a
pediatrician conversation, not a thing to resolve from a package label. See
[[gim]] for the same issue at a scale that is at least measurable.

foods.name: Mung bean sprouts (숙주)

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked all the way through — never raw, never blanched — with the root tails trimmed and chopped short.
ageBands.prepMd:
🚨 **Cook it all the way through. Raw is out, and so is lightly cooked.**

FDA's reasoning is specific to how sprouts are grown: seeds and beans sprouted
in warm, humid conditions, which are also ideal for bacteria — so a few
organisms present on the seed multiply to high levels during sprouting, **even
if you grow them yourself under clean conditions at home.** The named pathogens
are *Salmonella*, *Listeria* and *E. coli*. FDA's instruction is that people
more vulnerable to foodborne illness should avoid **"raw or lightly cooked
sprouts of any kind (including onion, alfalfa, clover, radish, and mung bean
sprouts)"** — and the vulnerable list opens with **children**.

**"Lightly cooked" being prohibited alongside raw is the part that catches
people.** 숙주나물 is traditionally made by dunking the sprouts in boiling water
for well under a minute to keep them crunchy. That is precisely the preparation
FDA rules out. **A blanch is not the mitigation.** Cook them until they are
genuinely soft — a few minutes of simmering or steaming, not a dip.

Then:

1. **Trim the root tails** — the fine threadlike ends. They stay tough and
   stringy however long you cook them. Pinching them off is standard practice
   for 숙주나물 anyway.
2. **Chop short — no longer than half an inch.** That is AAP's rule and the only
   dimensional rule any US guideline body issues. The hazard with a sprout is
   its *length*: a cooked stem is a long slippery fibrous string.
3. **Chop fine and moisten** at this age, stirred through rice, [[oatmeal]] or a
   puree so it clumps rather than scattering across the tray.

Unseasoned. 숙주나물 is normally dressed with salt, sesame oil and garlic — take
the baby's portion out before any of that. Note that sesame oil brings a major
allergen with it, which matters if that is one you are tracking.

Same cooking, same tails, same length limit. Chopped pieces suit the pincer
grasp that most babies develop around nine to ten months. Better hand skills are
not a reason to serve longer strands — the string is the hazard, and picking it
up was never the difficult part.

숙주 as the family eats it, still **cooked through** and still **cut short**.
FDA's rule is about susceptibility rather than age, so it does not lapse at the
first birthday — raw 숙주 on top of 쌀국수 or in a salad is still not the version
to serve.

Cooked into 잡채, soups or a stir-fry it is easy at this age. Watch the seasoning
rather than the sprout.

choking.requiredModification: Cooked thoroughly — raw and lightly cooked are both out. Trim the root tails and chop to no longer than half an inch; the stems are long fibrous strings.

foods.backgroundMd:
🚩 **숙주 is not soy, and it is not a major allergen.** Mung bean is a different
plant from soybean, and it appears nowhere on the list of nine major US food
allergens.

That is worth stating clearly and right at the top, because **[[soybean-sprouts]]
(콩나물) *is* soy — one of the nine** — and the two sprouts look nearly identical
in a bowl. This is the pairing most likely to cause a mistake in a Korean
kitchen. The difference is at the head end: 숙주 has a small pale head and a
short plump stem; 콩나물 has an unmistakable yellow soybean on top, bigger and
firmer, on a longer stem. If someone in the family is avoiding soy, that is the
distinction to learn, and it is the same comparison written from the other side
on the 콩나물 page.

**숙주 is also the one food in this batch that a US guideline body names
directly** — twice, in fact. Almost everything else here is a category rule we
have applied by inference. This one is not: FDA names mung bean sprouts
explicitly, both as an example of sprouts that may carry bacteria and again in
the list of sprouts that vulnerable people should avoid raw or lightly cooked.
That makes it the strongest food-specific citation on this whole set of pages.

**Composition figures are not in this record.** The USDA database was
unavailable when it was researched, so no iron or vitamin value is printed here.
The iron in a sprout is **non-heme** — a classification, not a measurement.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
🚨 **Raw and lightly cooked are both out — and this is FDA naming this exact
food.** Not an inference, not a category rule stretched to fit: mung bean
sprouts appear by name in FDA's sprout guidance, twice, and children head the
list of people who should avoid them raw or lightly cooked. Cook them properly.
Washing does not fix a sprout, because the bacteria grow throughout it rather
than sitting on the surface.

**Strings.** Long fibrous stems are the mechanical hazard. Trim the tails, chop
to under half an inch.

**Not a major allergen** — mung bean is not soy. But **do not confuse it with
콩나물**, which is. If you are tracking a soy introduction or avoiding soy
entirely, check which sprout is actually in the bag.

**Watch what it is dressed with.** The sprout is plain; 숙주나물 usually is not.
Sesame oil is a major allergen and salt is the usual seasoning.

**Beyond FDA's sprout rule, no body addresses 숙주 as an infant food.** The
cooking prohibition and the half-inch limit are issued. The tail trimming and
the chop length applied here are ordinary practice.

foods.name: Mussels

ageBands.servingNote: Chopped fine and loosened with a spoonful of the cooking liquid — dry chopped shellfish scatters and almost none of it gets eaten.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy them live and cook them the same day. Before cooking, tap any mussel whose
shell is open — CDC's instruction is to **discard shellfish that are already
open before cooking**, and that is the stricter of the two rules in circulation,
so it is the one this record publishes.

Cook by boiling until the shells open, then **keep boiling another 3 to 5
minutes**. Steaming works too, 4 to 9 minutes. **Throw away any that do not open
fully.** FDA stops at "the shells open during cooking — throw out ones that
don't open"; CDC asks for the extra minutes past that point. For a baby, take
the longer rule.

Then take the meat apart properly, which is where the actual work is:

- **Pull the beard.** The byssal threads are the tough fibrous tuft on the flat
  side. They do not soften with cooking and they are not something a baby can
  break down.
- **Feel for shell chips.** Shells crack during cooking and fragments end up in
  the meat. Run each mussel between your fingers before it goes on the tray.
- **Cut to no larger than half an inch** — AAP's dimension, and the only
  dimensional rule any US guideline body actually issues.

Chop the cleaned meat fine and stir in a spoonful of the cooking liquid or a
puree the baby already eats so it holds together in a fist.

Same cleaning, same cooking, slightly larger pieces. A pincer grasp arrives for
most babies around nine to ten months and makes half-inch pieces easy to pick up
where they used to be pushed around the tray. The beard, the shell check and the
half-inch limit do not change.

Mussels as the household eats them, still shucked, still bearded, still
checked by hand, still cut down. Serve them out of the pot before wine, stock
cubes or salt go in — a seasoned adult portion of shellfish broth carries far
more sodium than a toddler's day should.

Never the shell as a toy or a scoop. A cracked shell edge is sharp.

choking.requiredModification: Shuck completely, pull the beard out, run the meat through your fingers for shell chips, and cut to no larger than half an inch.

foods.backgroundMd:
Mussels are ordinary table food in a lot of households, and there is no reason a
six-month-old can't eat them once they are cooked properly and taken apart
carefully. What this record cannot give you is the nutrition number you were
probably expecting.

**The composition figures are not verified and are deliberately left out.**
Mussels are conventionally described as an iron-rich food, and that may well be
true, but the USDA database was unavailable when this record was researched and
NIH's iron fact sheet lists only oysters among the shellfish. Rather than print
a number we could not check, this record prints none. The iron in shellfish
flesh is the heme form, the kind CDC says is absorbed more readily than the
non-heme iron in plants — that is a classification, not a measurement, and it is
all we are willing to state. If you are serving mussels *for* the iron, [[beef]]
and [[oyster]] both carry figures we could verify.

**On allergy, mussels are not what most families assume.** Mussels are molluscs.
Molluscs are **not** among the nine major food allergens in US law — that list
is milk, egg, fish, **crustacean** shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans
and sesame, and FDA glosses crustacean as crab, lobster and shrimp. Oyster,
mussel, clam and scallop appear on none of it. In January 2025 FDA issued final
guidance setting out how it evaluates allergens *other* than the nine, which is
the category molluscs fall into.

Two practical consequences, and they cut in opposite directions. A mollusc
allergy is real and can be severe, but **a US label is not required to warn you
about it** — "Contains: shellfish" means crustacean. The label shortcut that
works for peanut or milk does not work here, so the ingredient list has to be
read. Conversely, a child who reacted to shrimp has not necessarily reacted to
mussels; they are different animals. This record does not print a
cross-reactivity percentage because no source we could verify gives one for
infants.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Mercury: we do not know, and that is the honest answer.** Mussels appear on
**no** FDA/EPA mercury list — not Best Choices, not Good Choices, not the "avoid"
list. That is an **absence of assessment, not a clearance.** The advice does not
say mussels are fine; it does not consider them at all. Treat them as one food
among several rather than a weekly fixture, and if you want an actual position,
ask your pediatrician rather than reading reassurance into a gap.

**Raw is out, at every age.** FDA names children among the groups who should
avoid raw or undercooked fish or shellfish. That applies to mussels served
barely opened as much as to raw oysters.

**The beard and the shell chips are the choking and injury story**, not the
meat itself, which is soft once cooked. Both are removal jobs, and both are easy
to skip when you are cooking a pot of mussels for adults and pulling a portion
out for the baby. Do the baby's portion separately and deliberately.

**No guideline body addresses mussels as an infant food.** Everything specific
above — the beard, the shell check, chopping fine — is a category rule for
shellfish safety and choking applied to this food by us, plus ordinary practice.
The cooking times and the half-inch limit are the parts that are actually
issued.

foods.name: Oatmeal (fortified infant oat cereal)

ageBands.servingNote: Mixed with breast milk, formula, or water until it is smooth and drops off the spoon.
ageBands.prepMd:
Follow the box, then follow CDC: mix the cereal with breast milk, formula, or
water until it is smooth. Start thin — closer to a pourable consistency than a
paste — and thicken it over the following weeks as your baby gets better at
moving food to the back of the mouth.

Load the spoon and hand it over, or let them take it off a loaded spoon you hold.
Either way most of the first weeks land on the tray and the chin. That is the
job at this age.

Thicker, and increasingly self-fed. This is also the point where oatmeal earns
its keep as a carrier: mashed [[black-beans]], flaked [[salmon]], or fruit stir
into it and go down easily.

However the family eats it. If you have moved to rolled or steel-cut oats cooked
from scratch, keep the smoothness rule in view — CDC's instruction is to cook and
then finely grind or mash whole-grain kernels, and steel-cut oats are kernels.

choking.requiredModification: Serve as a smooth porridge. Whole or steel-cut grain kernels must be cooked and then finely ground or mashed — whole cooked kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — iron
American Academy of Pediatrics
U.S. Food and Drug Administration — inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereal

foods.backgroundMd:
**The fortification is the entire point, and it is easy to lose by accident.**
Fortified infant oat cereal carries 64.1 mg of iron per 100 g dry. Plain oatmeal
cooked in water, unenriched, carries 0.90 mg. That is roughly a seventyfold gap
between two things a parent would reasonably both call "oatmeal".

So: **a pot of homemade porridge is not a nutritional substitute for fortified
infant cereal.** It is a fine food and a fine texture. It is not doing the iron
job, and if it quietly replaces the fortified box, the iron in the diet drops by
almost all of it. If you prefer cooking your own oats, keep an iron-rich food
somewhere else in the day — see [[beef]] or [[lentils]].

The iron in fortified cereal is added, non-heme iron, not the heme iron in meat.
CDC's advice to serve a vitamin-C food alongside non-heme iron applies here:
[[broccoli]] is one CDC names by name.

**Why oat rather than rice.** CDC's own wording is to "offer a variety of
fortified infant cereals such as oat, barley, and multi-grain instead of only
rice cereal," and AAP notes rice cereal does not have to be the first cereal.
The concern behind that is inorganic arsenic, which concentrates in rice: FDA
has set an
action level of 100 ppb for infant rice cereal and notes that infants' rice
intake relative to body weight is about three times an adult's. Oat sidesteps
that without giving anything up.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Smooth porridge is a low-risk texture. **Whole cooked grain kernels are not** —
they are a named entry on CDC's choking-hazard list, and CDC's instruction is to
cook and then finely grind or mash them. Instant and quick oats break down on
their own; steel-cut and whole groats do not, so blend or mash those.

Oats are not one of the nine major US allergens. Oat products are sometimes
processed on shared lines with wheat, but no infant-feeding guideline addresses
that question, so this record makes no claim about it in either direction — if
wheat matters in your household, read the label.

foods.name: Oyster (cooked)

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked through, chopped fine, moistened. A very small portion does the nutritional work here — this is not a food that needs volume.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy them from a source you trust, refrigerated, and cook them the day you buy
them. If they are in the shell, discard any that are already open **before**
cooking.

**Cooking in the shell:** boil until the shells open, then continue boiling
**another 3 to 5 minutes.** Or steam 4 to 9 minutes. Discard any that do not
open fully. FDA's shorter rule stops at "the shells open"; CDC asks for the
extra minutes, and that is the rule this record publishes.

**Shucked oysters** — the more likely form for cooking — have their own set:
boil for at least 3 minutes, or fry at 375 °F for at least 3 minutes, or broil
3 minutes, or bake at 450 °F for 10 minutes.

Then shuck (if not already), feel through the meat for shell chips, chop fine,
and moisten with a little of the cooking liquid so it gathers rather than
scatters. Keep the portion small — this is a food where a teaspoon is doing
serious nutritional work.

Serve it plain. Oyster sauces, jarred oysters in brine and anything
restaurant-seasoned carry sodium well beyond a baby's day.

The same cooking rules, in pieces up to half an inch that a pincer grasp can
manage. Stirred through [[oatmeal]], soft rice or mashed vegetables it goes down
more easily than on its own, and it carries a strong flavour that some babies
need a few tries to accept.

However the family eats them — **cooked**. The raw prohibition does not lift at
twelve months, or at any age in this app's range. Watch the seasoning rather
than the oyster: take the child's share out before soy sauce, gochujang or salt
goes in.

choking.requiredModification: Cooked through, never raw. Shucked, checked by hand for shell chips, and cut to no larger than half an inch.
