foods.backgroundMd:
### 🚨 Never raw. Not once, not a taste, not even a "treated" one.

This belongs at the top because raw oysters are a normal adult food and will be
in the house — on a platter at a party, in a box from the fish counter, at a
grandparent's table. **FDA names children among the at-risk groups who should
avoid "raw or undercooked fish or shellfish" and, specifically, "raw oysters,
even if they are treated after they have been harvested."** Post-harvest
treatment kills some pathogens; FDA says plainly it does not remove all of them.

CDC is blunter about why you cannot manage this by judgement:

- **"You cannot tell that an oyster is bad by looking at it."** There is no
  smell, no colour, no texture that sorts the safe one from the dangerous one.
- You can get sick from oysters in **any month of the year** — the "months with
  an R" rule is not a safety rule.
- **Hot sauce and lemon juice do not kill *Vibrio*.** Neither does alcohol.
- For *Vibrio vulnificus*, **about 1 in 5 people with the infection die**,
  sometimes within a day or two.

There is no age at which raw oyster becomes appropriate in this app's range, and
no preparation short of cooking that fixes it. Cooked properly, an oyster is an
excellent food for a baby. That is the whole distinction.

---

**Now the good part, because it is genuinely remarkable.** NIH's Office of
Dietary Supplements says it outright: **"Oysters contain more zinc per serving
than any other food."** Not "one of the best" — the most. Three ounces of cooked
Pacific oysters carry **28.2 mg of zinc**; three ounces of raw farmed eastern
oysters, 32 mg. The zinc RDA for a 7-to-12-month-old is **3 mg a day.** A portion
far smaller than an adult serving covers it several times over, which is exactly
why this food does not need volume to be worth serving.

Zinc matters at this age for the same reason iron does: it is one of the two
nutrients that make the old "food before one is just for fun" line false. Breast
milk alone stops covering both somewhere around six months.

Oyster is also a real iron food, and one of the few where we have a figure we
could verify: **3 oz of cooked oysters supply 8 mg of iron, 44% of the Daily
Value**, against an 11 mg/day RDA for a 7-to-12-month-old. It is **heme** iron —
the form CDC says is absorbed more readily than the non-heme iron in plants, and
which, unlike the iron in [[lentils]] or [[spinach]], does not depend on a
vitamin-C food alongside it.

This record deliberately does **not** print an iron-per-100-g figure. The
verified number is per three-ounce serving; converting it to a per-100-g value
would be our arithmetic rather than a measured value, and the USDA database was
unavailable when this was researched. The per-serving figure above is the one to
trust.

**Iodine, worth knowing about but not alarming here.** Cooked oysters carry
about 109 µg per 100 g in USDA's iodine database, with a measured range of 81 to
132. A 100 g portion would be a large fraction of the 130 µg daily adequate
intake for a 7-to-12-month-old — but a baby's actual portion is a fraction of
that, and oyster's iodine is nowhere near the scale of the seaweeds. If you want
the food where iodine genuinely governs the serving size, that is [[gim]] and
[[miyeok]], not this.

**On allergy: oysters are molluscs, and molluscs are not among the nine US major
allergens.** The nine are milk, egg, fish, **crustacean** shellfish, tree nuts,
peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame; FDA glosses crustacean as crab, lobster and
shrimp. FDA's January 2025 final guidance covers how it evaluates allergens
outside that list, which is where molluscs sit. The practical upshot: mollusc
allergy is real and can be severe, but **a US label need not declare it**, so
you have to read the ingredient list rather than trust a "Contains" line. And a
child who reacted to shrimp has not necessarily reacted to oyster.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Raw oyster is the hazard, and it is absolute.** See the callout above. The
short version: FDA says children should avoid raw oysters even when
post-harvest-treated; CDC says you cannot identify a bad one by looking, that
any month is a risk, that hot sauce and lemon do nothing, and that about one in
five people infected with *Vibrio vulnificus* die. Cook them.

**Shell chips** are the choking-and-injury risk once cooked. Feel through the
meat with your fingers before it goes on the tray.

**Size.** No piece larger than half an inch — AAP's rule, and the only
dimensional rule any US guideline body issues.

**Mercury is not a concern here.** FDA and EPA place oysters in **Best Choices**,
and within that on the sub-list of choices that are *even lower* in mercury.

**Portion, not frequency, is the lever.** No body publishes a serving size for
shellfish under twelve months, so this record gives none. What it can say is
that the zinc and iron content means a small portion is already substantial, and
that a food this nutrient-dense does not need to be served in adult quantities
to count.

**No guideline body addresses oyster as an infant food specifically.** The raw
prohibition, the cooking times, the mercury rating and the half-inch limit are
all issued. Chopping fine, checking for shell chips and keeping the portion
small are category rules and ordinary practice applied by us.

foods.name: Peanut

ageBands.servingNote: Thinned to the consistency of a runny yoghurt — never a spoonful or a thick glob.
ageBands.prepMd:
Stir about 1/4 teaspoon of smooth peanut butter into warm water, breast milk,
formula, or a puree the baby already eats, until it's thin enough to pour off
a spoon. Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you're not rushing —
that's a logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you're watching, and
your clinic is open.

Watch for about two hours. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours,
which is also why the familiar "wait 3–5 days before the next new food" rule
adds nothing diagnostically — it just slows down variety.

Same thinned form. Thickness, not quantity, is the hazard here: nut butter
stiff enough to hold its shape can obstruct an airway.

Still thinned or spread thinly — on a strip of toast, stirred into oatmeal or
yoghurt. The maintenance target doesn't change: keep it in the rotation at
least three times a week rather than letting weeks lapse.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of smooth peanut butter thinned with warm water, breast milk, or formula, stirred into a familiar puree.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an egg allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first peanut exposure — that group may need testing and a supervised introduction between 4 and 6 months (NIAID 2017 addendum, Tier 1). Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in infants without symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance.

choking.note: Whole peanuts are a high-risk choking hazard and are not appropriate before age 4.
choking.requiredModification: Never whole nuts and never a spoonful or thick glob of nut butter — thin it, or spread it very thinly.

sources.body: NIAID (Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy, 2017)
LEAP trial (NEJM 2015)
CSACI — "early introduction is not enough" position statement
American Academy of Pediatrics

foods.backgroundMd:
The single most consequential food on this list. The LEAP trial randomized
infants at high risk to eat peanut or avoid it, and early, sustained
introduction reduced peanut allergy by roughly 81%. That result is why the
old "delay allergens" advice was reversed.

The part that gets lost: **introduction is not the finish line.** LEAP's
protocol wasn't a taste, it was about 6 g of peanut protein a week across
three or more feedings, sustained for years. CSACI's position statement is
blunt that occasional exposure may be worse than none — a single taste
followed by months of nothing can raise the risk of sensitization rather than
lower it. So this food has a maintenance schedule, not a checkbox.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Two separate risks, often confused.

**Allergy** is managed by early, regular exposure — with the medical gate
above for babies with severe eczema or egg allergy.

**Choking** is managed by form. Whole peanuts and tree nuts are firm, round,
and airway-sized: AAP keeps them off the list until age 4. A spoonful of thick
peanut butter is on the same list. Thinned or spread very thinly, peanut is
fine from six months.

foods.name: Pear

ageBands.servingNote: Ripeness is the whole decision. Press the flesh near the stem with your thumb — if it gives, it can go raw and peeled.
ageBands.prepMd:
Check ripeness first. Press the flesh just below the stem with your thumb. If it
yields, it is ripe.

**Ripe:** peel it, quarter it, remove the core, and cut finger-length slices.
The whole-hand grasp means the baby holds the slice in a fist and bites the
protruding end. Ripe pear is slippery once peeled — leaving a small band of skin
at the gripping end gives some purchase, but the eating end should be peeled.

**Firm:** peel, core, and simmer or roast until a slice collapses under a fork,
then serve the same way. Grating raw works too and needs no pan.

With the pincer grasp — most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP — soft ripe pear
cut into thumbnail-sized cubes is easy to pick up, and peeled. Firm pear still
gets cooked or grated first; the pincer grip changes what the baby can lift, not
what they can chew.

However the rest of the table is eating it, provided it is ripe and peeled. Firm
pear still wants cooking or grating.

choking.requiredModification: Judge the ripeness first. A ripe pear that yields to gentle thumb pressure can be served raw, peeled. A firm pear is treated exactly like raw apple — cook it soft or grate it — and peeled either way.

NHS — Your baby's first solid foods
American Academy of Pediatrics — Choking Prevention
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 169118, raw; 746773, Bartlett)

foods.backgroundMd:
Pear is the food on this list where the label on the shelf tells you nothing and
your thumb tells you everything. **Ripeness decides the whole record.**

A ripe European pear — one that gives when you press near the stem — is soft
enough that NHS's permission for soft raw fruit applies directly. Low risk,
peeled, no cooking.

An underripe pear is a hard raw fruit, and everything in [[apple]] applies to it
unchanged: cook until fork-mashable, or grate it raw, peel either way. Pears are
usually sold hard because they travel and store better that way, so most pears
you bring home are in this second category for a few days.

Nutritionally it is a trace contributor — 0.18 mg of iron and 4.3 mg of vitamin
C per 100 g. Serve it because it is soft, sweet, and easy, not because it moves
any number.

One thing this record deliberately does not claim: pear is often described as a
remedy or a trigger for infant constipation because of its sorbitol content. **No
primary-source guideline addresses pear, sorbitol, and infant stool**, so there
is no claim here in either direction. If stooling is a worry, that is a question
for your pediatrician rather than a fruit choice.

See also [[korean-pear]], which looks like a pear and behaves like an apple.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The mistake to avoid is treating "pear" as a single food. A rock-hard pear cut
into cubes is the same hazard shape as raw apple, and the fact that it is a pear
does not change that.

Peel it at every age in this range. Pear skin is thin but does not break down
under gums, and NHS notes that removing skin makes food easier to swallow.

Whole pear halves and long unpeeled wedges thick enough to snap into a chunk are
not appropriate; slices and cubes are.

foods.name: Plantain

ageBands.servingNote: Ripe plantain, cooked until it mashes easily, in finger-length pieces. Green plantain is firm and is not a 6-8 month food.
ageBands.prepMd:
Choose a ripe plantain — yellow going to black. Peel it, cut into
finger-length pieces about as thick as two of your fingers, and steam, boil or
bake until a piece gives way completely under light pressure. Roasted ripe
plantain is soft, sweet and holds together in a fist, which is close to ideal at
this age.

At this age the whole-hand grasp means a long piece with an end sticking out is
easier to manage than a small one. Small pieces are harder now, not safer.

**Not fried.** Tostones and fried maduros are firm, oily and usually salted, and
frying a green plantain and pressing it makes it harder rather than softer.

Soft cubes about thumbnail size, with a couple of larger pieces alongside so
biting still gets practised. Mashed ripe plantain also works well as a base for
mashed beans or meat, which is the pairing that makes the vitamin C count.

However the household eats it, kept soft and unsalted. Green plantain dishes are
fine here as long as they are cooked right through and mash easily; fried and
salted forms are still worth taking the baby's portion out of first.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a piece mashes with light pressure between two fingers. Green plantain stays firm even after boiling and needs to be cooked further and mashed; ripe plantain gets there easily.

sources.body: CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (cook hard vegetables and fruits so you can easily mash them)
CDC — Iron (serve a vitamin-C food alongside non-heme iron)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (added sugars and sodium under 24 months)
NHS — Your baby's first solid foods (cut into narrow batons; soft cooked fruit and vegetables)
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 2710817 plantain, ripe — iron 0.32, vitamin C 20.1 mg/100 g)

foods.backgroundMd:
A plantain is a cooking banana: starchier, firmer, and not eaten raw the way
[[banana]] is. Cooked ripe, it goes soft and sweet and holds its shape in the
hand, which makes it an easy food to give a baby who is learning to grip.

**Its useful number is vitamin C, at 20.1 mg per 100 g**, not iron — 0.32 mg per
100 g is a trace. That makes plantain a pairing food: served alongside
[[lentils]], [[black-beans]], [[teff]] or [[fortified-infant-cereal]], the
vitamin C improves absorption of the non-heme iron in the same meal, which is
CDC's own advice. On its own it is a pleasant carbohydrate and nothing more.

**Ripeness changes the food.** Green plantain is dense and starchy and stays
firm through boiling; a fully ripe one — skin mostly black — cooks soft in
minutes and tastes sweet. The ripeness stages have culinary names and rules of
thumb attached to them, but **no guideline body stages plantain ripeness**, so
what follows is the general rule applied honestly: cook it until it mashes
easily, whatever colour you started from, and ripe gets you there with less
work.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cook it until it mashes easily.** This is CDC's rule for hard fruits and
vegetables, and green plantain is firmly inside it — an undercooked piece of
green plantain is a hard food, not a soft one.

**No added sugar, no salt.** Ripe plantain is already sweet, and the common
preparations — fried in butter with sugar, or salted — both run into CDC's
advice to avoid added sugars before 24 months and to limit sodium.

Plantain is not one of the nine major US allergens. Cross-reactivity between
banana or plantain latex proteins and latex allergy is discussed in the research
literature, but **no infant-feeding guideline addresses it**, so this record
makes no claim about it in either direction.

foods.name: Pollock

ageBands.servingNote: Untreated fillet only — flaked fine, checked by hand for bones, and moistened so the flakes hold together.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy a plain frozen or fresh fillet and check the ingredient list — see the
sodium note in Safety, which is the thing most likely to go wrong with this
particular fish.

Skin and bones come off **before** cooking: CDC's order, NHS says to remove bones
from fish, and the Canadian Paediatric Society says plainly not to feed a baby
fish with bones. Go over the raw fillet with your fingers even if it was sold
boneless.

Bake, poach, or steam until the flesh is opaque through and flakes under light
pressure. USDA FSIS gives 145 °F for fish and shellfish. Pollock overcooks
quickly and goes rubbery, so check it early.

Flake fine, search the flakes by hand once more, and moisten with the cooking
liquid or a puree so they hold together rather than powdering.

Larger flakes, self-fed, still hand-searched. Pollock's mildness makes it a good
carrier — stirred into [[oatmeal]], rice, or mashed vegetables it is easy to
gather and does not dominate the dish.

However the family eats it, still deboned, still cooked through, and still from
an untreated fillet. Breaded fish sticks and crab sticks are different products
and the salt is in the coating and the binder rather than the fish.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned pollock, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish below twelve months, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway does not read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove all bones and the skin before cooking, then flake the cooked fish and run it through your fingers to find any bone you missed.

foods.backgroundMd:
On mercury, pollock is about as safe as a fish gets in US guidance: FDA and EPA
put it in **Best Choices** *and* on the shorter sub-list of Best Choices that are
**even lower in mercury**. [[cod]] and canned light tuna are Best Choices without
being on that sub-list; pollock is on it, alongside [[rainbow-trout]] and
[[salmon]].

Its iron is the lowest of the five fish here — 0.29 mg per 100 g for Alaska
pollock, 0.59 mg for Atlantic — with 0.44 mg of zinc. So this is not an iron
food. What it is: an extremely mild white fish with a soft, forgiving flake, in
the safest mercury classification FDA issues, which makes it a sensible fish to
introduce early and a sensible one to repeat.

Fish is one of the nine major US allergens. AAP's position is that there is no
evidence delaying fish past four to six months prevents allergy, and FDA states
directly that fish can be introduced at about six months of age.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**The sodium trap is a purchasing decision, and it happens before any
seasoning.** Plain cooked Alaska pollock carries **166 mg of sodium per 100 g**.
Pollock treated with moisture-retention additives — sold as fillets that have
been soaked in a salt-and-phosphate solution to hold water through freezing —
carries **419 mg per 100 g**, and that is the fish as it comes, before you add a
single thing to the pan. Both figures are USDA-verified. CDC advises against
high-sodium foods for children under two.

Treated fillets look identical to untreated ones. The tell is the ingredient
list: a plain fillet's ingredients are "pollock". Anything naming sodium
tripolyphosphate, salt, or "solution" is the other kind. Read the back of the
bag.

**The traditional Korean pollock preparations are all excluded, and on salt
rather than on mercury.** 명태 is the same fish, but almost every way it is
preserved makes it a salt product:

- **북어 and 황태** — dried and freeze-dried pollock
- **코다리** — semi-dried
- **자반** — salted
- **명란** — salt-cured roe

These are the forms most likely to be in a Korean kitchen already, which is
exactly why they are worth naming. **We publish no sodium figure for any of them**
— no USDA record or primary-source figure was verified for these preparations
while this record was written, and a made-up number on a page about a baby's food
would be worse than none. The qualitative position is enough to act on: they are
salt-preserved, salt is advised against for babies, and none of them belongs in
this age range. Rehydrating or rinsing them is not a fix; the salt is throughout
the flesh, which is what preserved it.

**Surimi is a separate product.** Crab sticks, 맛살 and fish cake are made from
pollock but they are formed, salted, starch-bound foods rather than fish
fillets, and nothing on this page applies to them.

**Bones.** Deboned pollock flesh is soft and low-risk; the bones are the entire
hazard. Debone before cooking, then check the cooked flakes by hand. The tweezers
technique is common practice — the issued rule is that the bones come out, and
that they come out before cooking.

**No raw fish.** FDA is explicit that children should not eat raw fish,
including sushi and sashimi.

**How much per week — there is no infant answer.** FDA and EPA's advice is titled
for children **ages 1 to 11**, and its smallest figure is one ounce at age one.
**No US body publishes a per-week amount for a six-to-eleven-month-old**, so this
record does not invent one. Pollock's position on the "even lower in mercury"
sub-list means it is among the fish that classification was written to
encourage, not restrict — but "encouraged" is still not a number, and we are not
going to supply one.

**One wording point, because two rules look identical and are not.** FDA's fish
advice suggests watching your child for **several days before feeding fish a
second time**, while the same paragraph explicitly rejects delaying allergen
introduction. That sentence is about the gap between the **first and second
exposure to fish itself**. It is **not** the familiar "wait 3–5 days between new
foods" rule, which is about *unrelated* foods and is not evidence-based: IgE
reactions happen within minutes to two hours. Keep introducing other new foods on
your normal schedule. The tension between FDA's two sentences is real and we are
flagging it rather than resolving it.

foods.name: Pork shoulder

ageBands.servingNote: Slow-cooked until it shreds, then minced and loosened with unsalted cooking liquid — pork dries out faster than beef.
ageBands.prepMd:
Trim the fat cap and remove skin and bone **before** cooking — CDC is explicit
about that order, and it means nothing has to be picked out of the finished
meat. Braise or slow-roast the shoulder in water or unsalted stock until it
falls apart under a fork with no resistance.

Mince it fine, then stir in enough of the unsalted cooking liquid or a familiar
puree that it clumps rather than scatters. Pork dries out faster than beef as it
cools, so add more liquid than feels necessary and check it again just before
serving.

USDA FSIS sets 145 °F plus a three-minute rest as the minimum for fresh pork
roasts and chops, and 160 °F for ground pork. A long braise passes both by a
wide margin, which is the point: for a baby you are cooking for texture, and the
safe temperature arrives long before the meat is soft enough.

Shredded. Slow-cooked shoulder pulls into exactly the long soft strands a pincer
grasp handles well, and strands are easier to pick up than fine mince. Stirred
through mashed vegetables or [[oatmeal]] it stays moist longer than it does on a
bare tray.

However the rest of the table is eating it, as long as it is fresh pork, still
soft, and still cut small rather than cubed. Large chunks of meat do not drop off
CDC's hazard list at twelve months.

choking.requiredModification: Ground, finely minced, or shredded — never chunks. Remove fat, skin, and bones before cooking. Fresh pork only, never cured or processed pork.

foods.backgroundMd:
Pork shoulder is the weakest red meat in this set for iron: 1.32 mg per 100 g
roasted, or 1.50 mg trimmed to lean only. That is under half of [[beef]]'s
2.93 mg and well below [[lamb]]'s. It still carries 3.71 mg of zinc, which is
respectable, and the iron it does have is heme iron — the readily absorbed form
CDC contrasts with the non-heme iron in plants and fortified cereals.

So think of pork shoulder as a good food that is not your iron workhorse. If
your week's iron is coming from one animal food, beef or lamb does more of the
job. Pork earns its place on texture and price: shoulder is cheap, forgiving,
and slow-cooks into shreds more reliably than almost anything else, which makes
it easy to serve to a baby who is still learning to gather food.

Pork is not one of the nine major US allergens.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Fresh pork only.** This is the instruction that matters most here. Bacon, ham,
pancetta, prosciutto, chorizo, salami, sausage, spam, and 햄 are excluded for two
separate reasons, either of which would be enough on its own:

- **Sodium.** They are salt-cured or salt-seasoned products, and CDC advises
  against high-sodium foods for children under two. We publish no sodium figure
  for any of them — none was verified against a primary source while this record
  was written, and an unverified number on a page about a baby's food is worse
  than no number.
- **Choking.** AAP names meat sticks and sausages directly on its list of foods
  to avoid, and CDC's shape rule for cylindrical foods is to cut them into short
  thin strips rather than coins. A sausage is the exact hazard those rules
  describe.

"Cooked pork" on a label is not the same as fresh pork. If it was cured, smoked,
or brined before it reached you, it belongs to the paragraph above.

**Chunks.** Fresh pork still has to be ground, minced, or shredded. Cubes of
meat are a named choking-hazard entry, and pork cubes in particular tend to stay
springy rather than mashing.

**Doneness.** Use a thermometer for the food-safety floor and your fingers for
the texture. If a shred holds its shape when you pull at it, keep cooking.

foods.name: Potato

ageBands.servingNote: Peeled and boiled or baked until it mashes with light pressure. Discard any potato that is green or sprouted — do not trim it.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Peel it.** The glycoalkaloids that matter concentrate in the peel, and peel
does not break down under gums in any case.

Boil, steam or bake until a piece gives way completely under light pressure
between two fingers, then cut into finger-length wedges about as thick as two of
your fingers. At this age the whole-hand grasp means the piece is held in the
fist with an end sticking out, so the baby controls the bite. Small pieces are
harder now, not safer.

Mash is equally good, thinned with breast milk, formula, or the cooking water.
Skip butter and salt.

Soft cubes about thumbnail size once the pincer grasp arrives, with a few larger
pieces alongside so biting and tearing still get practised. Potato takes other
foods well — mashed [[black-beans]], flaked [[salmon]], puréed [[broccoli]].

However the household eats it, kept soft and unsalted. Fried potatoes are a
different food: hard-edged, oily and salted, and none of those helps here.
Gamjajeon, gamjatang and other salted dishes are the family's food, and a baby's
portion is better taken out before the salt goes in.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until a piece mashes easily between thumb and forefinger. Undercooked potato is firm enough to be a hazard, and a firm cube is the wrong shape for it.

foods.backgroundMd:
A plain boiled or baked potato is one of the most useful ordinary foods on this
list. It cooks to exactly the texture CDC asks for, it is cheap, and babies
generally like it.

**Its job is vitamin C, not iron.** Boiled potato carries 0.31 mg of iron per
100 g, which is negligible, and **13.0 mg of vitamin C**, which is not. Vitamin C
eaten in the same meal improves absorption of plant and fortified (non-heme)
iron, so potato earns its place beside the foods actually carrying iron —
[[lentils]], [[black-beans]], [[fortified-infant-cereal]], [[teff]]. A bowl of
mashed lentils with potato is doing real work; a bowl of potato alone is
carbohydrate.

The safety note below is the part worth reading properly. It is not about
choking — a cooked potato is soft — it is about glycoalkaloids, where the usual
household habit of cutting the green bit off is the wrong response.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Discard green or sprouted potatoes. Do not trim them and use the rest.** This
is the whole safety note, and it runs against normal kitchen practice.

Potato glycoalkaloids — solanine and its relatives — concentrate in the sprouts
and flowers at **200 to 500 mg per 100 g**, and in the peel of bitter varieties
at **150 to 220 mg per 100 g**, against under 10 mg per 100 g in a healthy
tuber. Levels build with light exposure, which is what greening is. They inhibit
cholinesterase and, at dose, cause haemorrhagic gut damage.

**Cooking does not fix it.** FAO is explicit: glycoalkaloids "are not destroyed
during normal cooking because the decomposition temperature of solanine is about
243 °C." Nothing that happens in a domestic kitchen reaches that.

**And taste is not a guard.** Bitterness only becomes detectable at around **20
mg per 100 g — roughly twice the level of a normal healthy tuber.** So a potato
carrying a meaningfully elevated dose can taste perfectly fine, and a baby who
cannot tell you it tastes odd is the worst possible taster for it.

Put together: peel every potato, store them dark, and throw out anything green,
sprouting or soft. A potato costs less than the alternative.

**No infant-specific safe threshold has been established** in anything this
record could verify, so no number is given here for what is acceptable in a
baby's portion. The rule is avoidance of the affected tuber, not a limit.

foods.name: Quinoa

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked soft, then mashed or ground and stirred into something wetter — a cooked kernel served whole is on CDC's choking-hazard list.
ageBands.prepMd:
Cook it with more water than the package says and longer than you would for
yourself, so the kernels are soft rather than springy. Then mash or grind them
and stir into something wet — puréed [[butternut-squash]], [[apple]], a
fortified cereal.

**The reason for the grinding step:** CDC lists whole cooked grain kernels as a
choking hazard and instructs you to cook and then finely grind or mash them.
Quinoa isn't named in that list, but "and other grains" is, and a cooked quinoa
kernel is a cooked whole grain kernel. **How finely** to grind is not something
any guideline body specifies, so use your own judgement: no distinct hard
kernels left, and it should smear rather than roll between two fingers.

Rinsing dry quinoa before cooking to wash off saponins is standard kitchen
practice and makes it taste less bitter. No guideline body issues it as a safety
step, and this record does not present it as one.

Same cooking, less processing — mashed rather than ground, and stirred through
other foods so it does not scatter. Quinoa mixed into mashed [[lentils]] or
[[black-beans]] is a genuinely iron-dense bowl at this age, and the pincer grasp
makes small soft lumps something a baby can actually pick up.

However the household eats it, cooked soft, in a bowl with other things rather
than dry and loose on a tray. Whole kernels are still kernels: keep them soft
and mash through anything that stayed firm.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until soft, then finely grind or mash. CDC's rule for whole-grain kernels is to cook and then grind or mash them; quinoa cooks into intact little kernels, so it is inside that rule as written.

foods.backgroundMd:
Quinoa is a reasonable everyday grain for a baby: 1.49 mg of iron per 100 g
cooked, plus protein and fibre, and it cooks in about fifteen minutes. Uncooked
it measures 4.57 mg per 100 g, but that is the dry weight — water is most of
what you serve, so the cooked number is the one that matters at the table.

**The iron is non-heme, and quinoa carries no vitamin C of its own** (USDA
records it at zero). CDC's advice for non-heme iron is to serve a vitamin-C food
in the same meal, so pair it: mashed [[broccoli]], [[mango]], or [[potato]]
alongside will do more for absorption than a larger helping of quinoa will.

It is not a replacement for [[fortified-infant-cereal]]. Fortified infant oat
cereal carries roughly forty times quinoa's cooked iron. Quinoa is a good
texture and a good habit; the fortified box is still the iron.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cooked whole grain kernels are a named choking hazard.** The modification is
CDC's: cook, then finely grind or mash. That instruction is issued; the degree
of grinding is not, so judge it by texture rather than by a rule.

If you serve quinoa in a mixed dish, AAP's one dimensional rule still applies to
everything else in the bowl — no piece larger than half an inch. That is the
only size rule any US guideline body issues, and everything else you read about
finger-lengths and thumbnails, this record included, is common practice.

foods.name: Rainbow trout

ageBands.servingNote: The boniest presentation in this set — flake fine, search by hand, then moisten so the flakes hold together.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Trout takes the most deboning work of any fish in this set**, mostly because of
how it is sold: usually whole or butterflied, with the frame and the fine bones
still in place, rather than as a clean fillet. Budget real time for this.

Take the skin off and lift out the bones from the raw flesh, running your
fingers along the whole fillet rather than only the spine line. This happens
**before** cooking — CDC's order, NHS says to remove bones from fish, and the
Canadian Paediatric Society says plainly not to feed a baby fish with bones. The
practical reason is that raw flesh holds together while you search it and hot
cooked flesh falls apart around the bone you are trying to find.

Bake, poach, or pan-cook until the flesh is opaque through and flakes cleanly.
USDA FSIS gives 145 °F for fish and shellfish.

Flake fine, search the flakes by hand once more, and moisten with cooking liquid
or a puree so they hold together instead of powdering.

Larger flakes, self-fed, still hand-searched. Trout is mild enough to serve
fairly plain at this age, and stirred through rice or a mashed vegetable it is
easier to gather than loose flakes on a tray.

However the family eats it, still deboned and still cooked through. Whole
pan-fried trout on the bone is the classic presentation and it is the one form
not to hand a toddler.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned rainbow trout, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish below twelve months, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway does not read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin and every bone before cooking — trout is usually sold whole or butterflied, so the bones are still in it. Then flake the cooked fish and search it by hand.

foods.backgroundMd:
Rainbow trout sits in FDA and EPA's **Best Choices** tier *and* on their shorter
sub-list of Best Choices that are **even lower in mercury** — the safest
classification FDA issues, shared here with [[pollock]] and [[salmon]] but not
with [[cod]] or canned light tuna.

Its iron is modest: 0.36 mg per 100 g farmed, 0.38 mg wild. That 0.02 mg
difference between farmed and wild is not worth choosing on — buy whichever is
fresher. Zinc is 0.54 mg. Like [[cod]], trout earns its place on allergen
introduction, on mercury standing, and on flavour rather than on minerals; if
iron is the goal, [[beef]] or liver does far more.

Fish is one of the nine major US allergens. AAP's position is that there is no
evidence delaying fish past four to six months prevents allergy, and FDA states
directly that fish can be introduced at about six months of age.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones, and more of them than usual.** Deboned trout flesh is soft and
low-risk; the bones are the whole hazard, and trout's presentation puts more of
them in front of you than any other fish here. Debone before cooking, search the
cooked flakes by hand. The tweezers technique is common practice — the issued
rule is only that bones come out, and that they come out before cooking.

**A caught-fish rule that is easy to over-apply.** FDA's advice singles trout out
in its guidance on **fish you or someone you know caught**: larger carp,
catfish, trout and perch are more likely to have local fish advisories, and where
no advisory exists, "children under the age of six should limit their consumption
of these fish to 1 to 2 ounces per week."

That is the only ounce figure in the whole advice whose wording reaches below age
one, so it gets quoted a lot — usually wrongly. **It is written for caught fish,
not for farmed retail trout**, and this record does not generalise it. If you
bought your trout at a shop, it is not the fish that sentence is about. If
someone caught it, check your state or provincial advisories first, because those
are issued per water body and FDA's national list does not replace them.

**No raw trout.** FDA is explicit that children should not eat raw fish,
including sushi and sashimi. Cold-smoked trout is not cooked either, and smoked
trout is salt-cured besides.

**Mercury does not cook out.** FDA states that mercury is found throughout the
tissue of a fish, so cleaning or cooking will not reduce it.

**How much per week — no infant answer, and two bodies disagree above twelve
months.** FDA and EPA's advice is titled for children **ages 1 to 11**; its
smallest figure is one ounce at age one, and **no US body publishes a per-week
amount for a six-to-eleven-month-old**. Above the first birthday:

- **FDA/EPA** tier on **methylmercury** alone, with no sex-specific child cap.
- **NHS** caps oily fish for children **by sex** — boys up to 4 portions a week,
  girls no more than 2 — on **dioxins and PCBs**, and names trout as an oily
  fish.

Neither reaches below twelve months. We are surfacing the disagreement rather
than picking a winner; NHS's construction is the more cautious of the two.

**One wording point, because two rules look identical and are not.** FDA's fish
advice suggests watching your child for **several days before feeding fish a
second time**, while the same paragraph explicitly rejects delaying allergen
introduction. That sentence is about the gap between the **first and second
exposure to fish itself**. It is **not** the familiar "wait 3–5 days between new
foods" rule, which is about *unrelated* foods and is not evidence-based: IgE
reactions happen within minutes to two hours. Keep introducing other new foods on
your normal schedule. The tension between FDA's two sentences is real and we are
flagging it rather than resolving it.

foods.name: Rye

ageBands.servingNote: Rye berries cooked very soft and then ground or mashed. Rye bread is not a food for this age — see the safety note on sodium.
ageBands.prepMd:
Whole rye berries need a long simmer — an hour or more, well past the chewy
texture an adult would stop at — and then grinding or mashing. **A cooked rye
berry is a whole grain kernel**, and CDC's instruction for those is to cook and
then finely grind or mash. Rye is not named in the list; "and other grains" is.

Ground cooked rye stirs into puréed vegetables or fortified cereal. Pair it with
a vitamin-C food, since the iron is non-heme: [[potato]], [[broccoli]].

Rye flour porridge is a simpler route to the same place, and cooked thin it
needs no grinding.

Softly cooked, mashed rye berries mixed through other foods, or rye porridge
thickened up. Rye is high in fibre and strongly flavoured — start small alongside
something familiar rather than as a bowl on its own.

Rye as part of family meals, kept soft and mashed where it stayed firm. **Rye
bread is still not appropriate here** — the sodium is the reason, and it does not
change at twelve months.

choking.requiredModification: Cook rye berries well past chewy, then finely grind or mash them. Whole cooked grain kernels are on CDC's hazard list, and a rye berry is a firm one.

foods.backgroundMd:
Rye grain carries 2.63 mg of iron per 100 g, which is respectable for a home-
cooked whole grain — better than [[quinoa]], better than [[teff]]. Cooked rye
berries, ground, are the form that belongs in an infant's bowl. The bread is a
different matter, and the safety note below is about it.

**Rye is a gluten grain. It is not wheat, and it is not one of the nine major US
allergens.** FDA's definition of gluten names "wheat, barley, and rye" together,
so a food containing rye cannot be labelled gluten-free. But rye carries no US
allergen-labelling requirement, and **a child with an IgE wheat allergy is not
automatically reactive to rye.**

Do not read that as permission, though, because the converse trips people up:
**most commercial rye bread contains wheat flour** — often more wheat than rye.
Rye is therefore **not a substitute for wheat in a wheat-allergic child**, both
because the product usually contains wheat anyway and because that decision
belongs with the clinician managing the allergy, not with a labelling
technicality. And rye is unsafe in celiac disease, full stop.

**On timing, there is nothing to wait for and nothing to optimise.** ESPGHAN's
2024 update — a reaffirming replacement of its 2016 position, not a retirement —
holds that gluten introduced at any time between completed 4 months and 12
months does not affect the cumulative incidence of celiac disease. It also says
this, which is worth quoting exactly rather than paraphrasing:

> "There is no specific guidance on the type of gluten-containing foods to be
> introduced at weaning."

**ESPGHAN is explicitly declining to rank the gluten grains.** Anyone who tells
you rye is a better or worse first gluten grain than wheat or [[barley]] is
giving you an opinion. So is anyone who ranks them the other way. There is no
guidance here, and this record is not going to invent one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Rye bread is a hard exclusion under 24 months, whatever its iron says.** USDA
measures rye bread at **603 mg of sodium per 100 g**. Its iron looks appealing at
2.83 mg per 100 g, and that is the trap: the sodium arrives in the same slice.
CDC's advice is to avoid added salt in this age group, and a food carrying six
hundred milligrams per hundred grams is not an infant food. Dense rye breads and
crispbreads are also firm, and crispbreads with whole kernels or seeds are
separately on CDC's hazard list.

**Cooked rye berries are whole grain kernels** — cook them very soft, then grind
or mash.

**Gluten, not wheat allergy — keep the two apart.** Rye belongs in a conversation
about celiac disease, where it is unsafe. It does not belong in a wheat-free
diet as a substitute, because most rye products contain wheat and because that
call is a clinician's.

foods.name: Salmon

ageBands.servingNote: Flaked fine and checked by hand for bones, then moistened so it does not crumble apart.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy it boneless if you can, and go over it with your fingers anyway. Remove the
skin and any bones **before** cooking, which is CDC's instruction and NHS's
("no bones") — pin bones are far easier to find in a raw fillet than in a hot
cooked one.

Bake, poach, or pan-cook until the flesh is opaque all the way through and
flakes apart under a fork. Flake it fine, run the flakes through your fingers
one more time, and moisten with a spoonful of the cooking liquid or a puree so
it holds together instead of powdering.

Deboned salmon flesh is soft and low-risk. The bones are the entire hazard.

Larger flakes, self-fed. Salmon stirred through [[oatmeal]] or mashed vegetables
is easier to gather than dry flakes on a tray.

However the family eats it, still deboned and still cooked through. No raw fish
at this age.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of well-cooked, fully deboned salmon, flaked fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. Note also that NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only; there is no equivalent testing protocol for fish, so peanut's testing pathway should not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Remove all bones and the skin before cooking, then flake the cooked fish and run it through your fingers to find any bone you missed.
