foods.backgroundMd:
Salmon does two jobs at once: it is heme iron at 1.03 mg per 100 g — the readily
absorbed kind, like [[beef]] and [[chicken-thigh]] — and it is the food most
families use to introduce fish, one of the nine major US allergens.

On the allergen side, AAP's position is that there is no evidence delaying fish
past four to six months prevents allergy. The old advice to hold allergens back
was reversed for peanut on trial evidence, and the delay advice for the other
allergens went with it. Fish is introduced like any other food, with the medical
gate above for the babies who need it.

On mercury: FDA and EPA place salmon in the **Best Choices** category, and
within that in the sub-list of fish that are *even lower* in mercury. Among
common fish it is close to the safest choice you can make.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones.** "Bones in meat or fish" is a named entry on CDC's choking-hazard
list. Debone before cooking, then check the cooked flakes by hand. Whole small
fish and bone-in steaks are not a form to serve here.

**Cooking.** Cook salmon through — opaque to the centre, flaking cleanly. No
raw, no smoked, no cured: none of those are cooked, and cured fish is
salt-preserved besides, where high-sodium foods are advised against under two
years. This record does not print a target internal temperature for fish: the
figure in general circulation could not be confirmed against USDA's own chart
while this was written, and we would rather give you the doneness test than a
number we cannot stand behind. Opaque through the middle, flaking cleanly under
a fork — that is what the temperature describes anyway.

**How much per week — there is no infant answer.** FDA and EPA's fish advice —
two servings a week from Best Choices, at a serving size of about one ounce for
a one-to-three year old — is written for **children ages 1 to 11**. It starts at
the first birthday. **No US body publishes a per-week amount for a six-to-eleven
month old**, so this record does not give one: any specific infant ounce figure
in circulation has been extrapolated by somebody, and we are not going to add
another. Serve salmon as one of several protein foods across the week, and if
you want an actual number for your own baby, ask your pediatrician.

For wild-caught fish from local waters, check your state or provincial
advisories — those are issued per water body and FDA's national list does not
replace them.

foods.name: Sardines

ageBands.servingNote: Mashed thoroughly so no intact bone segment remains, spine removed, then stirred into something moist.
ageBands.prepMd:
Open the can, drain it, and lift the fish out onto a plate. **Find the spine
first** — it runs the length of the fish, and it is the one bone that can stay
firm enough to matter. Lift it out with a fork or your fingers; it usually comes
away in one piece.

Then mash what is left, thoroughly, with a fork against the plate until it is a
uniform paste and **no intact segment of bone remains** — not softened, not
mostly broken, gone. Run your fingers through it afterwards. Anything you can
feel as a discrete piece comes out.

Stir the mash into something moist: [[oatmeal]], mashed [[sweet-potato]],
[[avocado]], a thick puree. Sardine is strong-tasting, so start with a small
amount stirred through a lot of something familiar rather than a spoonful on its
own.

Rinse the fish first if it is a salted pack.

Coarser mash, still spine-out, still checked by hand. Sardine mixed into a grain
or a vegetable mash is easier to gather than flakes loose on a tray, and it keeps
the taste in proportion.

This is a good age to pair it deliberately: heme iron does not need a vitamin-C
partner the way non-heme does, but the meal it is in usually could use one
anyway — [[broccoli]], [[mango]], [[green-peas]].

However the household eats them — mashed on [[wheat-toast]], through pasta, in a
rice bowl. Still mashed rather than served as a whole fish: a whole sardine, even
canned, is a bone-in fish, and CDC's bones entry does not stop applying because
the child had a birthday.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of canned sardine, spine removed and the rest mashed thoroughly, stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for fish, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to fish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY; there is no equivalent testing protocol, dose or weekly target for fish, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Find and remove the spine — it is the one bone that can stay firm — then mash the fish thoroughly so no intact bone segment remains, and check what is left with your fingers. CDC's rule is to remove ALL bones before cooking; canned sardines are sold bones-in and no body issues an exception, so serving them that way is a departure you are choosing, mashed down as far as it will go.

sources.body: CDC — choking hazards ("remove all fat, skin and bones from poultry, meat and fish before cooking"; bones in meat or fish)

Serving canned sardines bones-in is a DEPARTURE from that CDC rule. No US body issues an exception for pressure-softened canned bones — the practice is widespread and the calcium depends on it, but it is not sanctioned.
FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (sardine is a Best Choice; the serving advice is scoped to ages 1–11 and gives no amount below 12 months)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (no piece larger than one-half inch)
CDC — foods and drinks to avoid or limit (added salt)
USDA FoodData Central — canned sardines, fdcId 175139 (Fe 2.92, Ca 382, Na 307 mg/100 g). That entry is the SALTED pack; no verified id for a no-salt-added pack, so 307 mg is not the no-salt figure.

foods.backgroundMd:
Sardines carry **2.92 mg of iron per 100 g, and it is heme iron** — the readily
absorbed kind. That is the highest iron figure of any food in this batch and
close to three times [[salmon]]'s 1.03. They also carry **382 mg of calcium per
100 g**, which is unusual for a fish and comes almost entirely from the bones.

They add nothing to your allergen coverage that salmon does not — fish is one
slot, and either fish fills it. Sardines are here for the iron and the calcium.

**Now the conflict, because this food has a real one and you should decide about
it with your eyes open.**

CDC's instruction is to "remove all fat, skin and **bones** from poultry, meat
and fish **before cooking**." Canned sardines are sold **bones-in by design**:
the canning process pressure-cooks them until the skeleton is soft and crushable,
and **that softened skeleton is where the 382 mg of calcium comes from.** Remove
the bones and you have removed most of the reason to serve sardines rather than
any other small fish.

**No US body issues an exception for softened canned bones.** There is no
carve-out, no "except when pressure-cooked" clause, nothing. So serving sardines
bones-in is a **departure from a guideline**, done widely and with a good
rationale, and this record labels it as common practice rather than dressing it
up as sanctioned. The cautious version — remove the spine, mash the rest
thoroughly so nothing intact remains, check with your fingers — is what is
described below. The fully guideline-compliant version is to bone the fish and
lose the calcium. Both are defensible. Pick one deliberately.

**On mercury**, FDA and EPA place sardines in **Best Choices**, among the safest
fish available. But their advice is written for **ages 1 to 11** and its smallest
serving is one ounce for a one-to-three-year-old. **No US body publishes a
seafood amount below twelve months**, so this record gives you no infant weekly
figure; any number in circulation was extrapolated by somebody.

**On sodium, read the can.** The USDA entry behind this record shows **307 mg of
sodium per 100 g — and that is the salted pack.** A no-salt-added pack was not
verifiable, so do not read 307 mg as the figure for the tin you bought if it says
no salt added. Sodium is the **only** reason to specify pack type here: nutrition
is otherwise the same. Buy no-salt-added if you can find it, and rinse either
way.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bones are the hazard, and this is the one food in this canon where the rule
and the practice genuinely disagree.** "Bones in meat or fish" is a named entry
on CDC's choking-hazard list and CDC says to remove all bones before cooking.
The entire canned-sardine category depends on leaving them in. That is a real
conflict, not an oversight, and no body has resolved it.

What this record recommends: **remove the spine, mash everything else until
nothing is intact, check by hand.** What this record will not tell you: that
softened canned bones are approved for infants, because nobody has said so.

**Rinse a salted pack, and prefer no-salt-added.** 307 mg of sodium per 100 g is
the salted figure. CDC advises against added salt for babies, and this record
cannot give you an infant mg/day limit because **no verified figure was
available** — treat that silence as a reason for caution, not permission.

**Fish is one allergen slot.** If [[salmon]] has already gone in without trouble,
sardines are not a second introduction — they are a nutritional upgrade to a slot
you have already covered.

**No raw, no smoked, no cured.** Canned sardines are cooked in the can, which is
what makes them fine. Salt-cured and smoked small fish are neither cooked nor
low in sodium.

foods.name: Scallop

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked just to firm-and-opaque, then cut into short thin strips across the grain — never left as a round disc.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Remove the side muscle first** — the small tough tab on the side of the
adductor, sometimes called the foot. It peels off with your fingers. It is
chewier than the rest and does not soften. Removing it is ordinary practice, not
a rule anyone issues.

**Cook to the test, not to a timer.** Sear, poach or steam until the flesh is
**firm, pearly, and opaque** — FDA's words — and take it off the heat at that
moment. A scallop goes from tender to rubbery in well under a minute. If you are
cooking for adults at the same time and want a hard sear, cook the baby's one
separately and more gently; you cannot undo the toughening.

**Then cut it into short thin strips, across the round, rather than serving it
as a disc.** Keep every piece under half an inch.

⚠️ **A note on where that cutting rule comes from, because it is not issued for
this food.** CDC's instruction is to cut *cylindrical* foods into short thin
strips instead of rounds, and CDC wrote that rule about hot dogs. A scallop is a
squat cylinder of firm protein, so applying it here is a **defensible
extrapolation — an inference of ours, not a guideline instruction.** We think it
is the right call and we would rather you know it is an inference than assume
CDC issued it. The half-inch limit *is* issued: that one is AAP's.

Same cooking, same side-muscle removal, same doneness test. With a pincer grasp
the strips can be a little shorter and thicker. The failure mode at this age is
not the size, it is a scallop that was cooked while you were doing something
else and came off the pan tough — check it by pressing one between your fingers
before it goes on the tray. It should give.

However the household is eating them, still cooked no further than opaque, still
cut down rather than served whole. A whole seared scallop is a smooth firm round
about the size of an airway — it is not a form to hand over at this age, however
soft it is.

Take the child's portion out before butter, soy sauce or a pan sauce goes in.

choking.requiredModification: Remove the side muscle, stop cooking the moment it is firm, pearly and opaque, and cut into short thin strips no larger than half an inch — not into rounds.

sources.body: FDA — Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely (doneness test — "firm, pearly, and opaque")
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards (cylindrical foods into short thin strips, not rounds)
USDA/FDA/NIH — Database of Iodine in Common Foods, Release 4 (2024)
FDA — Food Allergies (the nine major food allergens; January 2025 final guidance on non-listed food allergens)
FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (scallop is a Best Choice)
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (the one-half-inch rule)

foods.backgroundMd:
Scallop is the one food on this list where **overcooking creates the hazard.**
That is backwards from almost everything else you have been told about feeding a
baby, where longer cooking means softer and safer — cook the carrot until it
mashes, cook the meat until it shreds. A scallop does the opposite. Properly
cooked it is soft and yields easily. Cooked past that point the proteins tighten
and it turns dense and rubbery, and a dense rubbery disc of protein is a much
harder thing for a baby to manage than a tender one.

So the instruction is not "cook it thoroughly", it is **cook it to the doneness
test and stop.** FDA gives the test in words for exactly this group of foods:
shrimp, scallops, crab and lobster are done when **"the flesh becomes firm,
pearly, and opaque."** That is the whole target. There is no benefit past it and
there is a real cost.

**Composition figures are not in this record.** The USDA database was
unavailable when it was researched, so there is no verified iron or protein
value to publish and none is printed. Shellfish flesh carries **heme** iron —
that is a classification, not a measurement.

**Iodine is genuinely not a concern here**, which is worth stating because it is
a concern for other foods in this batch. USDA's iodine database gives scallop
**7.4 µg per 100 g** — an order of magnitude below [[oyster]] and
[[manila-clam]], and several orders below [[gim]]. Scallop is not part of the
iodine conversation.

**On allergy: scallops are molluscs, and molluscs are not among the nine US
major allergens.** The nine name **crustacean** shellfish — crab, lobster,
shrimp — not scallop, oyster, clam or mussel. FDA's January 2025 final guidance
describes how it evaluates allergens outside the list. The consequence for a
family is that **a US label need not warn about molluscs**: "Contains: shellfish"
means crustacean, so the ingredient list has to be read. And a child who reacted
to shrimp has not necessarily reacted to scallop.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**The unusual one: overcooking is the hazard.** Stop at firm, pearly and opaque.
A tough scallop is harder for a baby to break down than a tender one, and no
amount of cutting fully compensates for the texture.

**Shape.** Not rounds. Short thin strips, nothing over half an inch. The strip
rule is our extrapolation from CDC's cylindrical-food instruction; the half-inch
limit is AAP's and is issued.

**The side muscle** is a small tough piece worth taking off.

**Raw is out**, as with every shellfish here — FDA names children among the
groups who should avoid raw or undercooked fish and shellfish. That includes
scallop crudo and 회.

**Mercury is not a concern.** FDA and EPA place scallops in **Best Choices**, on
the sub-list of choices that are *even lower* in mercury.

**Watch for "wet" scallops.** Scallops are often treated with a phosphate
solution that makes them hold water; they weigh more, they steam rather than
sear, and they are harder to cook to the right texture. Dry-packed scallops
behave more predictably. This is a cooking observation, not a safety finding,
and no guideline body addresses it.

**No guideline body addresses scallop as an infant food.** The doneness test,
the mercury rating and the half-inch limit are issued. The strip shape, the side
muscle and the stop-cooking-early emphasis are inference and ordinary practice,
labelled as such above.

foods.name: Semolina upma

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked smooth and thin, no salt, and tempered plainly or not at all — no whole mustard seed, no cashew pieces.
ageBands.prepMd:
Dry-roast the semolina in a pan for a few minutes until it smells nutty and
stops looking chalky — that step is what keeps it from going gluey. Then whisk
it into hot water, breast milk, or formula off the heat, and cook it out until
it is **smooth and thin**, thinner than you would serve an adult, which is CDC's
texture instruction for this age.

**No salt.** Upma is a savoury dish and salt is the default in every recipe you
will find; leave it out entirely for a baby. Lemon juice, a little grated
vegetable cooked in soft, or a pinch of ground spice carry the flavour instead.

**No tempering for a first wheat exposure.** If you want some of that character,
warm a little oil, add ground spices only — no whole seeds, no nuts — and stir
it through.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing, and watch for
about two hours.

Thicker, with soft cooked vegetables grated or mashed into it — [[carrot]],
[[green-peas]], [[butternut-squash]]. This is a good dish for the transition to
lumpier textures because the base carries the lumps rather than leaving them
loose on a tray.

If you want the tadka now, grind it: mustard seed ground to a powder is a spice
rather than a seed, and cashew ground fine is [[cashew-butter]] by another name.
Whole seeds and nut pieces stay out.

Fluffier upma with vegetables through it, still unsalted or barely salted, still
with the tempering ground or omitted. The whole-nut floor does not move at this
age — NIAID puts whole nuts at under 5 years and AAP at 4 years or older, and a
cashew half in a bowl of upma is a whole nut.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: A spoonful of plain semolina cooked smooth and thin with water, breast milk or formula, with no tempering and no salt. No body publishes a first-serving amount or a weekly target for wheat — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to wheat — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no wheat testing protocol, no wheat dose and no wheat weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food. If you are using upma as the FIRST wheat exposure, leave the tempering out altogether: a traditional tadka can add cashew, peanut and mustard, and a reaction to a dish carrying four allergens tells you nothing about which one caused it.

choking.requiredModification: The TEMPERING is the choking hazard, not the porridge. Whole mustard seeds and cashew halves both sit inside CDC's "whole or chopped nuts and seeds" entry. Temper plainly, grind the solids in, or omit the tadka entirely. Cook the semolina smooth and thin, and add no salt.

sources.body: FDA — Food Allergies (wheat, tree nuts and peanut are major food allergens; mustard is not one of the US nine)
CDC — choking hazards ("whole or chopped nuts and seeds") — the entry that covers mustard seed and cashew in a tempering
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (smooth, thin textures at first)
CDC — foods and drinks to avoid or limit (added salt)
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (nuts and seeds; no piece larger than one-half inch)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
FDA — Gluten-Free Labeling of Foods (wheat, rye and barley are the gluten grains; only wheat is one of the nine major allergens)

foods.backgroundMd:
Upma is a savoury semolina porridge, and semolina is wheat — so this is a way to
cover the **wheat** allergen inside a dish the household may already cook, rather
than through [[wheat-toast]] or [[wheat-pasta]].

**The porridge is easy. The tempering is where the problems are.** A traditional
tadka goes into hot oil at the start: mustard seed, curry leaf, urad or chana
dal, cashew, sometimes peanut. That short list contains **two more of the nine US
major allergens** — tree nut and peanut — plus mustard, which is a priority
allergen in the UK and EU but is **not** one of the US nine and carries no
US labelling requirement. For a baby's first exposure to wheat, that is three or
four allergens arriving in one bowl, and if something happens you will not know
which one did it.

**And it is the choking hazard too, not the porridge.** Whole mustard seeds pop
and stay whole. Cashews go in as halves and stay as halves. Both sit squarely
inside CDC's "whole or chopped nuts and seeds" entry. The semolina itself, cooked
smooth and thin, is one of the lowest-risk textures in this canon — all of the
risk in this dish is floating in it.

So: **temper plainly, grind the solids in, or leave the tadka out.** The dish is
still upma without it, and you can add it back for the rest of the family at the
table.

**This record publishes no iron figure and no USDA id, and the gap matters more
here than elsewhere.** Enriched and unenriched semolina differ enormously in
iron — enrichment is where most of the iron in a Western box of semolina comes
from — and no verified entry could be established for either while this was
written. That is not a rounding difference; it materially changes what the food
is for. Read the box: if it says enriched, there is meaningful added iron in
there, and this record simply cannot tell you how much. If you need an iron food
you can count, use [[barley]] cereal, [[lentils]] or [[beef]].
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**The tempering, not the porridge.** Whole mustard seeds and cashew halves are
inside CDC's "whole or chopped nuts and seeds" entry. Grind them or omit them.
Curry leaf is soft and not a choking concern, but it is also not something a
baby will chew — fish it out or chop it very fine.

**Three extra allergens can arrive unannounced.** Cashew (tree nut), peanut, and
mustard. Two are among the US nine; mustard is not, which means a US label is not
obliged to flag it even though a mustard allergy is real and is recognised as a
priority allergen in the UK and EU. If you are eating someone else's upma, ask
what went into the tadka.

**No salt.** CDC advises against added salt for babies, and this record cannot
give you an infant mg/day limit because **no verified figure was available** —
that silence is not permission.

**Semolina is wheat, not a separate grain.** If wheat is being avoided, upma is
out. And "gluten-free" is a different claim from "wheat-free" — see [[barley]].

foods.name: Toasted sesame oil

ageBands.servingNote: A few drops stirred through a finished dish for flavour. There is no verified infant quantity, so this is deliberately small.
ageBands.prepMd:
A few drops, stirred through food that is already cooked and already cool enough
to eat. Toasted sesame oil has a low smoke point and is a **finishing** oil, not
a cooking one — heat it and you lose the aroma that was the entire reason for
adding it, and it turns bitter.

**How much is genuinely unverified.** No body publishes a quantity of oil for an
infant, so this record does not print one. A few drops over a portion is a
sensible reading of "flavour, not a food," and it is the honest limit of what
can be said.

Good places for it: a spoonful of rice porridge, mashed [[green-peas]], steamed
[[broccoli]] blitzed soft, plain [[tofu]].

The same few drops, over more textured food. Sesame oil is what makes plain
steamed vegetables and mild proteins taste seasoned without salt, which is
useful at an age when the food is getting less interesting and salt is still off
the table.

However the household uses it — over rice, into a dipping sauce, through
namul-style vegetables, on noodles. Still a finishing oil, still added off the
heat.

sources.body: FDA — FASTER Act, sesame as the ninth major food allergen (signed 2021-04-23, effective 2023-01-01)
FDA — Food Allergies (sesame must be declared as a major food allergen)
CDC — choking hazards. Sesame oil is not a choking hazard; the seed and seed-butter forms are the ones listed, which is why they and not the oil carry the preparation rules.
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods

foods.backgroundMd:
Toasted sesame oil is in this canon as **flavour**, and only as flavour. A few
drops finish a bowl of rice, a plate of vegetables, a soup, a noodle dish — it
is one of the fastest ways to make plain infant food taste like the food the
rest of the family is eating, which matters more than it sounds like it should.

**It is not the way to introduce sesame, and this record carries no allergen
protocol for that reason.** The reasoning is worth stating rather than asserting:
allergen introduction depends on the baby eating enough of the **protein** to
matter, and oil is the fraction of the seed with the least protein in it.
Refined oils are generally low in allergenic protein. Unrefined and toasted oils
are variable — sometimes appreciable, sometimes not, and the label will not tell
you which jar you have. On top of that, **no guideline body anywhere sanctions
oil as an allergen-introduction vehicle.** There is no protocol, no dose, and no
statement that a baby who has had sesame oil has been introduced to sesame.

So: a baby who tolerates sesame oil has **not** had sesame introduced. Use
[[tahini]] or finely ground sesame seed for that job, and use the oil for
dinner. Treating the oil as the introduction is the failure mode this record
exists to prevent — it feels like the slot is closed when it is not.

The other half of that coin: a child with a **diagnosed sesame allergy** should
not be given sesame oil on the strength of "it's only oil." Sesame is a major
allergen and must be declared on US labels, and that declaration covers the oil.
The two statements are consistent — the oil is unreliable as a source of
allergen protein in both directions, which makes it useless for introduction and
unsafe for avoidance.

**No composition figures appear on this record.** A verified USDA entry for
toasted sesame oil could not be established while this was written, so there is
no id and no iron figure. It is a fat; treat it as one.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**No choking risk.** Oil is not a hazard form, and sesame oil appears on no
hazard list. It is the seed and the seed butter that carry preparation rules —
see [[tahini]].

**The real risk with this food is a false sense of coverage.** If your reason
for serving sesame is to introduce the allergen, oil does not do it, and no
guideline says it does. Do the introduction with tahini or finely ground seed,
and log that instead.

**Check labels if sesame is being avoided.** Sesame has had to be declared as a
major allergen in the US since 1 January 2023, so a current label will name it.
An older jar, or an imported one, may not.

foods.name: Short-grain rice

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked soft and wet — closer to juk than to a bowl of steamed rice — and mashed rather than served as loose grains.
ageBands.prepMd:
Cook it much wetter and longer than you would for the table — the porridge end
of the range, where the grains have broken down and it spoons rather than
scatters. Then mash it. Juk made with extra water, or rice cooked and blended
with the cooking liquid, is the right texture here.

Stir in something with vitamin C, since rice iron is non-heme and absorbs
better alongside it: mashed [[broccoli]], [[potato]], or fruit.

**Do not make rice cereal the only cereal.** CDC names oat, barley and
multigrain as the alternatives, and the reason is arsenic dose over time, not
any single meal. Rotating cereals costs you nothing.

Softly cooked rice, mashed, and mixed into other foods rather than served loose.
Short-grain rice sticks to itself, which is convenient for a baby learning to
pick things up and is also the thing to watch: break up any clump before it goes
on the tray. **No guideline body specifies a size for a rice clump**, so there
is no number to give you — squash it flat and it stops being a lump.

This is the age FDA's intake data peaks at. It is also the age iron matters
most, so if rice is displacing an iron food, that is the trade to look at.

Rice as the family eats it, kept soft. Sticky rice shaped into balls is a common
finger food and a reasonable one at this age, as long as the ball squashes
easily and is small enough to bite rather than swallow whole.

choking.requiredModification: Cook it soft and wet and mash it, and break up sticky clumps before serving. Cooked whole grain kernels are on CDC's hazard list, and short-grain rice also sticks to itself in lumps. No guideline body specifies a maximum clump size, so this record gives none.

sources.body: FDA — Final guidance, action level for inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereals (100 ppb; finalized 2020-08-05, live with no retirement notice as of 2026-08-06)
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (only feeding infant rice cereal can increase arsenic exposure; offer oat, barley, multigrain)
CDC — Choking Hazards (whole grain kernels of cooked barley, wheat, or other grains)

NHS — Drinks and cups for babies and young children ("Children under 5 years old should not have rice drinks as a substitute for breast milk, infant formula or cows' milk as they may contain too much arsenic")
CDC — Iron
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 168882 short-grain white rice, cooked, enriched; 168932 short-grain white rice, cooked, unenriched)

foods.backgroundMd:
Rice is the staple grain in a lot of households, this one included, and there is
no reason a baby cannot eat it. There are two things worth understanding before
you make it the default, and neither is a reason to panic.

**Arsenic, stated plainly.** Rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and
water than other grains. FDA set an action level of **100 ppb** of inorganic
arsenic for infant rice cereal — draft in 2016, **finalized in August 2020, and
still live** with no retirement or replacement notice as of today. FDA's
reasoning is about dose relative to body size: "Relative to body weight, rice
intake for infants… is about **three times greater than for adults**," and
"people consume the most rice (relative to their weight) at approximately
**8 months of age**."

Eight months sits inside the 9–11 band on this app and just past the 6–8 one.
**The peak exposure is not somewhere off in toddlerhood — it is right in the
middle of the window this record covers**, which is why the advice below is
about variety rather than avoidance.

CDC's wording is the practical version: "**Only feeding your child infant rice
cereal can increase their risk of arsenic exposure**," and it recommends
offering oat, barley and multigrain cereals as well. Note what that says and
what it does not: the concern is a rice-only diet, not rice.

**Enriched or not, and it is a sevenfold difference.** Cooked short-grain white
rice that has been enriched carries **1.46 mg of iron per 100 g**. The same rice
unenriched carries **0.20 mg**. Enrichment is a US labelling practice; **most
rice sold in Korean markets is unenriched**, and the bag will not necessarily
make that obvious. If rice is a daily food in your house, this is the single
biggest nutritional variable in it, and neither number comes close to
[[fortified-infant-cereal]] — check the panel rather than assuming.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Cooked whole grain kernels are a named CDC choking hazard**, and the issued
instruction is to cook and then finely grind or mash them. Rice grains are small,
but the rule is written about kernels rather than about size, and sticky rice
adds the clumping problem on top.

**The cooking trade-off — and both halves are real.** FDA says boiling rice
pasta-style in 6 to 10 parts water and draining it "can reduce **40 to 60
percent** of the inorganic arsenic." FDA also says in the same breath that doing
this "**also results in lowering the nutritional value… reduces the levels of
folate, iron, niacin and thiamine… by 50 to 70 percent**." Rinsing is not a
middle path: FDA says it "has a minimal effect on the arsenic" and "will wash
off iron, folate, thiamine and niacin."

So for a baby at risk of iron deficiency — which is most babies from about six
months — **these two pull in opposite directions, and FDA does not reconcile
them.** Neither will this record. What is left is the thing both agencies
actually recommend: rotate the grain. Serving oat or barley cereal on some days
lowers arsenic exposure without removing any iron at all.

**Rice drinks: the NHS prohibits them under five years old** — "Children under 5
years old should not have rice drinks as a substitute for breast milk, infant
formula or cows' milk as they may contain too much arsenic." That is the NHS's
position, and it is cited here as the NHS's. **No US body issues an equivalent
statement naming rice drinks**, so do not read this as a US rule; read it as the
more cautious of two positions, and a well-reasoned one.

foods.name: Shrimp

ageBands.servingNote: Shell and tail off before cooking, cooked all the way through, then minced fine and stirred into something moist so it does not scatter.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy it peeled or peel it yourself: shell, tail and the dark vein all come off
**before** cooking, not after. A tail fin left on a cooked shrimp is a firm,
sharp-edged piece of shell in a baby's mouth.

Poach, steam or pan-cook until the flesh is opaque all the way through and firm
— NHS's rule is that shellfish is never served raw or lightly cooked to a baby,
and that is a food-safety rule, not a texture preference. Cooked shrimp is
springy and slippery, which is a bad combination at this age, so mince it fine
and stir it into something that holds it: mashed [[avocado]], [[sweet-potato]],
[[oatmeal]], a thick puree.

Small pieces the pincer grasp can pick up, still cooked through, still with **no
piece larger than half an inch** — AAP's dimension is the only one any guideline
body issues, so it is the one this record uses. Shrimp firms up as it cooks; if a
piece feels rubbery to you, chop it smaller rather than trusting the gums.

Cooked shrimp cut down to bite size, in whatever the household is eating — fried
rice, a noodle dish, a stew. Still fully cooked. Still no shell, no tail.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of fully cooked shrimp, minced fine and stirred into a food your baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for crustacean shellfish, so treat this as a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to crustacean shellfish — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. Note that NIAID's addendum guidelines cover peanut only. There is no equivalent testing protocol, dose, or weekly target for shellfish, and peanut's numbers should not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Shell, tail and vein off before cooking. Cook it through — NHS's rule is that shellfish is never served raw or lightly cooked to a baby. Then mince fine, or cut so no piece is larger than half an inch.

NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children ("shellfish — do not serve raw or lightly cooked")
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (no piece larger than one-half inch)
CDC — choking hazards. Shrimp is not a named entry; the cutting rule here is an application of CDC's general shape rules, not a food-specific ruling.
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
FDA/EPA — Advice about Eating Fish (shrimp is a Best Choice; the serving advice is scoped to ages 1–11)
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods

foods.backgroundMd:
Shrimp is here for one reason: it closes the **crustacean shellfish** slot, one
of the nine major US allergens. It is not an iron food. At **0.51 mg of iron per
100 g** it contributes essentially nothing against a 7-to-12-month iron
requirement, and nothing in this record should be read as putting it in the same
job as [[beef]], [[sardines]] or [[salmon]]. What it does carry is protein —
**24 g per 100 g** — and zinc at 1.64 mg.

**The "shellfish" trap, stated plainly, because FDA and everyday language
disagree.** FDA's position is that crustacean shellfish is a major food allergen
and must be declared on a label, but **molluscan shellfish — oysters, clams,
mussels, scallops — is not**. Menus, relatives and most parenting advice treat
"shellfish" as one category. It is two. Shrimp, crab, lobster and crawfish close
the crustacean slot; no mollusc closes it. A mollusc allergy is real and can be
severe, it simply is not one of the nine and carries no mandatory declaration.

On mercury, FDA and EPA place shrimp in **Best Choices**, the lowest-mercury
group. But note what that advice does and does not say: it is written for
**children ages 1 to 11**, and its smallest serving size is one ounce for a one-
to three-year-old. **No US body publishes a seafood amount for a baby under
twelve months.** This record therefore gives you no weekly ounce figure, because
any figure in circulation has been extrapolated by somebody.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Never raw or lightly cooked.** That includes ceviche, "just pink" shrimp, and
anything from a raw bar. NHS names shellfish explicitly here.

**Shell and tail are the physical hazard, not the flesh.** Remove them before
cooking, when they are easy to see and pull.

**Shrimp is not on any official choking list by name.** The cutting instruction
in this record comes from applying CDC's general rules — cut cylindrical foods
into short thin strips, cook until it mashes easily — plus AAP's half-inch
maximum. That is category-level coverage, and this record says so rather than
implying a shrimp-specific ruling exists.

**Do not read a tolerated shrimp as a tolerated scallop.** Crustacean and
mollusc are separate allergens, and tolerating one says nothing about the other.

foods.name: Soybean sprouts (콩나물)

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked all the way through — never raw, never blanched — with the root tails trimmed and chopped short.
ageBands.prepMd:
🚨 **Cook it all the way through. Raw is out and so is lightly cooked.**

FDA's position on sprouts is unusually direct, and it is worth quoting the shape
of it. Sprouts are grown from seeds and beans in warm humid conditions — the
same conditions bacteria like — so a few organisms on the seed multiply to high
levels during sprouting, **even in a clean home setup**. FDA names *Salmonella*,
*Listeria* and *E. coli*. Its instruction is that people more vulnerable to
foodborne illness should avoid **"raw or lightly cooked sprouts of any kind"**,
and the list of vulnerable people opens with **children**.

Two things follow that families get wrong:

- **"Of any kind" covers 콩나물**, even though FDA's examples name onion,
  alfalfa, clover, radish and mung bean and never mention soybean. The rule is
  written to be general on purpose.
- **A blanch is not the mitigation.** "Lightly cooked" is prohibited alongside
  raw. The quick 30-second dunk that 콩나물무침 traditionally uses — the one that
  keeps the sprouts squeaky and crisp — is exactly the preparation FDA is ruling
  out. Cook them until they are properly soft.

Then handle the physical form:

1. **Trim the root tails.** The thin threadlike tail at the bottom is tough and
   stringy and does not soften with cooking. On 콩나물 many people also pull off
   the loose bean husks; that is a texture preference, not a safety step.
2. **Chop short — no longer than half an inch**, AAP's rule and the only
   dimensional rule any US guideline body issues. A cooked sprout stem is a long
   fibrous string, and length is the problem, not width.
3. **Chop fine and moisten** at this age — stirred through rice, [[oatmeal]] or
   a puree so it gathers rather than scattering.

Serve it unseasoned. 콩나물무침 and 콩나물국 are both salted; take the baby's
portion out before that.

Same cooking, same tail trimming, same length limit. A pincer grasp picks up
chopped sprout pieces easily. Do not read improving hand skills as a reason to
serve longer pieces — the string is the hazard and a better grasp does nothing
about it.

콩나물 as the household eats it, with two things unchanged: **thoroughly cooked**,
and **chopped short**. The raw-sprout rule does not expire at twelve months;
FDA's vulnerable list is about susceptibility, not about a birthday.

콩나물국밥 and 콩나물무침 are both realistic at this age with the salt reduced and
the sprouts cut down. Watch the 고춧가루 as much as the salt.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About a teaspoon of thoroughly cooked, tail-trimmed 콩나물 chopped fine and stirred into a food the baby already eats. No guideline body publishes a first-serving amount for soy, so treat this as a practical starting point rather than a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an existing food allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first soy exposure. That group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the child could have eaten safely.

choking.requiredModification: Cooked thoroughly — raw and lightly cooked are both out. Trim the root tails and chop to no longer than half an inch; the stems are long fibrous strings.

sources.body: FDA — Selecting and Serving Produce Safely (raw or lightly cooked sprouts of any kind; Salmonella, Listeria, E. coli)
FDA — Food Allergies (soybeans are a major food allergen)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (the one-half-inch rule)

foods.backgroundMd:
🚩 **콩나물 is soy. Soy is one of the nine major US allergens.**

That is the whole reason this food has its own page and its own medical gate,
and it is very easy to miss, because 콩나물 arrives at the table looking and
behaving like a vegetable — a side dish, a thing in the bottom of a soup bowl, a
crunchy handful in 비빔밥. Nothing about it announces "soybean."

**And it looks almost exactly like [[mung-bean-sprouts]] (숙주), which is not
soy and not a major allergen at all.** Side by side in a bowl the two are easy
to confuse. The tell is the head: 콩나물 has a distinct yellow soybean at the
top, noticeably larger and firmer. 숙주 has a small pale head and a shorter,
plumper stem. If you are tracking a soy introduction, or avoiding soy, that
difference is the thing to learn — see the 숙주 page for the same comparison
written from the other side.

If soy is what you are trying to introduce, [[tofu]] is a cleaner vehicle: more
soy protein per spoon, softer, and none of the string or cooking issues below.
콩나물 is worth knowing about mainly because it turns up in food the family is
already eating.

**Composition figures are not in this record.** The USDA database was
unavailable when it was researched, so there is no verified iron, zinc or
protein value and none is printed. The iron in a sprout is **non-heme** — a
classification, not a measurement. Non-heme iron absorbs better alongside a
vitamin-C food, so serving it with something like [[broccoli]] or
[[green-peas]] helps.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
🚩 **Soy — a major allergen wearing a vegetable's clothes.** This is the single
most important line on the page. See the medical gate above before the first
exposure, and watch for about two hours afterwards; IgE reactions occur within
minutes to two hours.

🚨 **Cooked thoroughly, always.** Raw and lightly cooked sprouts are both ruled
out for children by FDA. Sprouting conditions grow bacteria along with the
sprout, and washing does not fix it. A blanch does not count as cooking here.

**Strings.** Trim the tails, chop to under half an inch. Long fibrous stems are
the mechanical hazard.

**Do not confuse it with 숙주.** They look alike, one is a major allergen and
one is not.

**No guideline body addresses 콩나물 as an infant food.** FDA's sprout rule is
issued and covers it through "of any kind"; soy's allergen status and the
half-inch limit are issued. The tail trimming and the chop length applied to
this specific food are category rules plus ordinary practice.

foods.name: Spinach

ageBands.servingNote: The risk here is texture, not hardness — cook it and chop it fine so leaves cannot ball up into a wad.
ageBands.prepMd:
Wash it well — spinach carries grit, and grit is the most common actual problem
with it. Wilt it in a pan with a splash of water for two or three minutes until
it collapses, then squeeze out the liquid and **chop it finely**.

Then mix it into something with body: mashed [[butternut-squash]], [[barley]]
cereal, [[tofu]], mashed beans. A pile of loose cooked spinach is hard to pick
up and easy to gather into a wad; carried in a thicker food it goes down easily
and tastes less sharp.

Cook it fresh rather than reheating a batch. Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate
them, and serve them cold or not at all.

Same handling — cooked, squeezed, finely chopped, carried in something. The
pincer grasp does not help much with a leaf; what changes is that the baby can
now self-feed a thick spinach-and-grain mixture from a loaded spoon or as small
soft lumps.

A cooked spinach and egg or tofu scramble holds together well enough to pick up,
which is the first form of spinach most babies manage on their own.

However the household eats it, still cooked and chopped rather than served as
whole leaves. Stirred into rice or pasta, in a soup, in sigeumchi namul made
without salt or soy sauce, in a dal.

Raw spinach salad is a different proposition — thin whole leaves are the wad
problem in its purest form — and is better left until well past this range.

choking.requiredModification: Cook it, then chop it finely. A whole cooked leaf is thin and slippery and can gather into a wad — that, not firmness, is the hazard.

frequencyLimit.reason: EFSA advises that a risk cannot be excluded for infants eating more than one spinach meal in a day. One serving a day is well inside that. This is an EU precaution; CDC and the Dietary Guidelines impose no limit at all.

sources.body: NHS — Your baby's first solid foods (names spinach among first vegetables)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Encourage (cooked spinach, 6–12 months)

foods.backgroundMd:
Spinach has a better pedigree as a first food than its reputation suggests. NHS
names it among the vegetables to *start* weaning with — "vegetables that aren't
so sweet, such as broccoli, cauliflower and spinach" — and CDC's 6-to-12-month
list leads with cooked spinach. Two guideline bodies naming a single vegetable
by name is unusual.

The iron figure in this record, 1.26 mg per 100 g, is for **raw baby spinach**
(mature raw is 1.05). A USDA entry for cooked spinach could not be verified at
the time of writing, so none is quoted — cooking wilts spinach dramatically, so
the same weight of cooked spinach represents far more leaf than the same weight
raw, and the two numbers are not interchangeable.

**The oxalate story is wrong, and worth correcting.** You will be told that
spinach iron "doesn't count" because oxalate binds it. The absorption part is
true; the explanation is not.

Bonsmann and colleagues ran a randomized crossover trial using stable iron
isotopes, measuring incorporation into red cells at fourteen days. A kale meal
gave 10.7% iron absorption. The same kale meal with 1.26 g of potassium oxalate
added gave 11.5% — **P = 0.86, no difference at all.** The spinach meal ran
about 24% below kale, but not significantly. The authors' conclusion is that
potassium oxalate did not influence iron absorption in humans, and that oxalic
acid in fruits and vegetables is of minor relevance to iron nutrition. They
attribute spinach's disadvantage to **calcium and polyphenols** instead.

So: spinach is a modest non-heme iron food that is poorly absorbed, for reasons
that are real but are not oxalate. Oxalate's established relevance is calcium
binding and kidney stones, not infant iron status.

The practical advice does not change much, and it is the same advice as for
every plant iron source: pair it with a vitamin-C food ([[mango]],
[[green-peas]], [[butternut-squash]]) and do not pair it with dairy — the
calcium in [[yogurt]] works against you in the same meal.

**Nitrates: the US and the EU genuinely disagree.** Both positions are given
here because both are defensible and they lead to slightly different habits.

**The US position is permissive — and has quietly gone quiet.** AAP's 2005
clinical report on infant methemoglobinemia identified **well water** as the
real high-risk vector, found "little or no risk" from commercially prepared US
infant foods, and noted that reports of nitrate poisoning from **home-prepared**
vegetable foods continued to occur. **AAP retired that report in June 2025 and
has not replaced it**, so the US no longer has a current statement on dietary
nitrate in infancy at all. What remains is that CDC and the Dietary Guidelines
impose no nitrate restriction whatsoever, CDC actively recommends cooked spinach
for 6-to-12-month-olds, and NHS recommends it as a first vegetable.

The retirement is worth knowing precisely because of what it is *not*: there is
no new US finding that nitrate is more dangerous than previously thought. A
retired statement is an absence of guidance, not a reversal of it.

**The EU position is more cautious.** EFSA's CONTAM Panel set a nitrate ADI of
3.7 mg per kg of body weight per day and concluded that current nitrate levels
in vegetables are "not of health concern for most children" — but added that a
risk of methaemoglobinaemia cannot be excluded for 1-to-3-year-olds eating high
amounts, and that for infants a risk "cannot be excluded" for those eating more
than one spinach meal in a day. EFSA also recommends that children with
bacterial gastrointestinal infections not be given spinach, because infection
increases the conversion of nitrate to nitrite. Germany's BfR adds that cooked
spinach should not be reheated.

**What to actually do.** The US is not wrong that spinach is a good first food —
it plainly is, and two guideline bodies recommend it by name. But the EU's three
precautions cost nothing and the US does not contradict any of them, so this
record treats them as the default:

- No more than one spinach meal in a day.
- Do not reheat cooked spinach — cook it fresh, or serve leftovers cold.
- Skip it while a child has a gastrointestinal infection.

If your water comes from a private well, that is the part worth acting on: test
it for nitrate, and use tested water for anything you make up for an infant.
That was the strongest point in AAP's retired report, and nothing has come along
to weaken it.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Texture, not hardness.** Spinach is soft, so it is easy to assume it needs no
modification. The hazard is that thin cooked leaves stick together and to the
mouth, and a mouthful of whole leaves can gather into a slippery wad. Chopping
finely and mixing into a carrier food solves it.

**The three EU precautions** above are the practical nitrate advice: one spinach
meal a day at most, never reheated, skipped during a gastrointestinal infection.

**Home-made purée storage.** AAP's report singles out home-prepared vegetable
foods as the place where infant nitrate poisoning still occurs. Cool it fast,
refrigerate it promptly, and do not keep it for days — the same handling that
[[butternut-squash]] and other home-made vegetable purées need.

**Well water.** If your household is on a private well, have it tested for
nitrate. That is the vector AAP considers genuinely high-risk, and it has
nothing to do with which vegetables you serve.

foods.name: Sweet potato

ageBands.servingNote: Expect more on the face and tray than in the mouth. That is the job at this age.
ageBands.prepMd:
Roast or steam until a fork slides in with no resistance, then cut into
finger-length wedges about as thick as two of your fingers. Leave the skin on
for a beginner — it gives something to grip, and the flesh is what gets eaten.

At this age the palmar grasp means the whole piece is held in the fist with an
end sticking out, so the baby controls the bite. Pieces cut small are actually
*harder* now, not safer: they can't be picked up, and they end up scooped by
the handful.

Once the pincer grasp appears — usually around nine months — switch to soft
cubes roughly the size of your thumbnail. Keep offering a few larger pieces
alongside, since biting and tearing are their own skills worth practising.

Whatever the rest of the table is having — cubed, mashed, or in wedges. Keep
offering some pieces big enough to bite from rather than only pincer-sized
ones; biting and tearing are still skills in progress.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until it smashes easily between thumb and forefinger.

sources.body: American Academy of Pediatrics
American Academy of Pediatrics

foods.backgroundMd:
A soft, sweet root vegetable that holds its shape when roasted, which makes it
one of the easier first foods to hand over whole. Rich in beta-carotene, and
its vitamin C helps the body absorb non-heme iron from the same meal — worth
pairing with beans, lentils, or fortified cereal.

Related: [[kabocha]] behaves almost identically once cooked.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Cooked sweet potato is low risk once it mashes with light pressure between two
fingers. Undercooked pieces are firm enough to be a hazard, so test a piece
before serving rather than trusting the timer.

Raw sweet potato is a hard raw vegetable and is not appropriate at any age in
this range.

foods.name: Tahini

ageBands.servingNote: Stir the jar back together first, then thin the stirred paste until it pours off a spoon. Never a spoonful, never a thick glob.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Stir the jar first, properly.** Tahini separates hard: a layer of oil on top
and a dense, near-solid paste underneath, and if you skim off the top you are
serving thin oil while the concentrated paste waits for the next spoon. Take it
down to the bottom of the jar with a sturdy spoon or a butter knife and bring it
back to one uniform consistency. A jar stored upside down for a day makes this
easier.

**Then thin it further.** The stirred paste is still thick, and the oil layer is
not thinning — it is part of the food that got separated from itself. Add warm
water, breast milk, formula, or a familiar puree a little at a time, and stir
until **it no longer holds its shape and pours off the spoon.**

**There is no issued dilution ratio.** The specific one in circulation for nut
and seed butters is issued by nobody. AAP's rule is qualitative — spread thinly.
CDC names the hazard and gives no fix. The one numeric preparation anywhere in US
guidance belongs to NIAID's peanut-allergy-prevention protocol: **written for
peanut**, a dosing instruction rather than a choking rule, and it does not
transfer to sesame. A borrowed number would be the wrong ratio applied to the
wrong food. Thin until it pours.

Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you are not rushing, and watch for
about two hours.

Same thinned form, stirred through [[yogurt]], [[oatmeal]], mashed
[[sweet-potato]], or a bean mash. **Thickness, not quantity, is the hazard.**

Hummus is a reasonable route at this age if it is smooth and unsalted, but read
it as a chickpea food that contains tahini rather than as a sesame serving —
the amount of sesame in a spoonful of hummus is small and variable, and if you
are deliberately introducing the allergen, tahini itself is the honest vehicle.

Thinned into sauces and dressings, stirred through vegetables, spread very
thinly on [[wheat-toast]]. Still never off a spoon, still never a thick layer.

Whole sesame seeds appear on a lot of things at this age — bread crusts, bagels,
banchan, dressings. Whole seeds are inside CDC's "whole or chopped nuts and
**seeds**" entry, and NHS's instruction for the seed form is to serve them
finely ground. A scatter of seeds baked into a crust is a different case from a
spoonful of loose seeds; the loose seeds are the ones to grind or skip.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of well-stirred tahini thinned with warm water, breast milk or formula until it pours off a spoon, stirred into a food your baby already eats. No body publishes a first-serving amount or a weekly target for sesame — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before the first exposure to sesame — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no sesame testing protocol, no sesame dose and no sesame weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food.

choking.requiredModification: Stir the separated jar back together, then thin the paste further until it no longer holds its shape. CDC's hazard entry is "chunks or spoonful of nut and SEED butters" — tahini is inside that entry, not adjacent to it. The oil floating on top is not a substitute for thinning.

sources.body: FDA — FASTER Act, sesame as the ninth major food allergen (signed 2021-04-23, effective 2023-01-01)
CDC — choking hazards ("chunks or spoonful of nut and seed butters"; "whole or chopped nuts and seeds")
American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention ("thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters — be sure to spread thinly instead")
NHS — foods to avoid giving babies and young children ("serve seeds finely ground")
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens

USDA FoodData Central — whole sesame seeds 170150 (Fe 14.6, Ca 975); roasted whole 170151 (Fe 14.8, Ca 989); hulled kernels 170152 (Fe 7.78, Ca 131). PROXIES for the seed, not values for tahini; no verified id for tahini itself.

foods.backgroundMd:
Tahini is the best vehicle in this canon for **sesame**, the ninth major US
allergen: it is the highest-protein-density, lowest-choking-risk form the seed
comes in, and it mixes into food a baby already eats without changing the
texture much.

Sesame became a major allergen late. The FASTER Act was signed on **23 April
2021** and took effect **1 January 2023**, so any jar bought before 2023, and a
great deal of parenting advice written before then, predates mandatory sesame
declaration. If you are reading an older label or an older article, it was
written under different rules.

**This record publishes no iron figure and no USDA id, and the reason is
interesting rather than merely cautious.** Sesame seeds are one of the most
iron- and calcium-dense foods in this canon — whole seeds run about 14.6 mg iron
and 975 mg calcium per 100 g, roasted whole about 14.8 and 989. But
**decortication changes them enormously**: hulled kernels drop to 7.78 mg iron
and **131 mg calcium**, a loss of roughly 47% of the iron and **about 87% of the
calcium**. Most commercial tahini is made from hulled kernels, so tahini tracks
the kernel row rather than the whole-seed row — which means the "sesame is a
calcium powerhouse" line you may have read is describing a food most jars are
not. **The tahini value itself is unverified**, so no number appears on this
record. If you want the whole-seed profile, that is whole sesame seed, finely
ground, not tahini.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Tahini is on the hazard list, not near it.** CDC's entry reads "chunks or
spoonful of nut and **seed** butters." The word "seed" is doing real work there:
parents often read the nut-butter warnings as not applying to tahini, and they
do apply, by name.

**The separation is a safety issue, not a texture one.** Unstirred tahini at the
bottom of a jar is stiffer than peanut butter. Stir, then thin.

**Never off a spoon, never a thick glob**, for the same physical reason as the
nut butters: a paste stiff enough to hold its shape can obstruct an airway.

**Sesame oil does not do this job.** If you are trying to introduce sesame, use
tahini or finely ground sesame seed — see [[sesame-oil]] for why an oil is not
an introduction vehicle.

**A note on the form gap.** NHS issues "serve seeds finely ground." The US has
no equivalent form instruction for sesame despite sesame now being a major
allergen. That gap is real, and this record leans on the NHS wording because
nothing domestic fills it.

foods.name: Taro

ageBands.servingNote: Peeled, thoroughly cooked, mashed. Never raw, never undercooked, and never wild taro in any form.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Peel it completely**, ideally under running water or with gloves — raw taro sap
irritates skin, which is the same mechanism you are avoiding in the mouth.

Boil or steam until a piece collapses under light pressure with no firmness left
anywhere, then mash it and loosen with breast milk, formula, or the cooking
liquid. Taro mash is naturally smooth and a little glutinous, which suits this
age.

**Cook without salt.** USDA's cooked-without-salt entry is 15 mg of sodium per
100 g; the salted entry is **251 mg — about seventeen times more.** That
difference is entirely a cooking decision.

Still peeled, still thoroughly cooked, still mashed — this is one of the few
foods where the texture instruction does not relax with age, because the reason
for it is not grasp or chewing. Mash it into other foods if you want variety:
[[potato]], [[lentils]], a fortified cereal.

Taro as the household cooks it, as long as it is cooked right through and soft.
Torantang and other taro soups are normal family food; take the baby's portion
out before salt or seasoning goes in, and check that every piece is soft — a
piece that is still firm in the middle is undercooked, and undercooked is the
problem.

choking.requiredModification: Peel completely, cook right through until it mashes with light pressure, and serve mashed. Cooking is required here for a reason beyond texture — see the safety note.

sources.body: Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety — Food Safety Bulletin: the acrid taste of raw edible taro is substantially reduced after cooking because cooking destroys the enzymes, but calcium oxalate crystals are insoluble in water and heat resistant, so washing and cooking cannot reliably remove them; cooking cannot remove the poisoning effect of wild taro
Hong Kong Centre for Food Safety — Food Poisoning from Consumption of Wild Taro (raphides shoot out of plant cells when chewed; they cannot be destroyed by washing or cooking)
CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (cook hard vegetables until they mash easily)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (sodium)
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 168486 taro, cooked without salt — sodium 15 mg/100 g; 170543 cooked with salt — sodium 251 mg/100 g)

foods.backgroundMd:
Toran, satoimo, dasheen — a starchy corm that cooks to a smooth, slightly sticky
mash and is a familiar autumn food in Korean and Japanese kitchens. Cooked, it
carries 0.72 mg of iron per 100 g, which is a small contribution; it is here as
a carbohydrate and a cultural food rather than a nutritional one.

**Taro has a specific hazard that is not choking and is not an allergy, and the
usual explanation of it is subtly wrong.** Taro tissue contains calcium oxalate
**raphides** — microscopic needle-shaped crystals. When the plant cells are
damaged by chewing, the needles are propelled out and stab the tongue, gums and
throat. The result is immediate burning, stinging and swelling in the mouth.

The part people get wrong: **cooking destroys the enzymes** that make the sting
worse — which is why cooked taro loses the acrid, prickly taste of raw taro —
**but the raphides themselves are insoluble in water and heat resistant.**
Washing and cooking do not remove the needles. Hong Kong's Centre for Food
Safety states both halves of that plainly.

So thorough cooking is necessary and is what makes edible taro comfortable to
eat. It is not a process that removes the crystals, and that is exactly why the
rules below have no exceptions in them.

This record publishes **no oxalate figure for retail taro.** The number usually
quoted, about 780 mg per 100 g, is FAO's figure for some species of cocoyam, not
a measurement of the taro on a supermarket shelf, and repeating it here would be
inventing a value.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Never wild taro, under any preparation.** Wild taro and ornamental aroids look
similar to the edible corm and to its leaves. Hong Kong's food safety authority
is explicit that "cooking cannot remove the poisoning effect of wild taro and it
should not be consumed." Poisoning cases there mainly involve wild taro, or
produce suspected of being mixed or wrapped with wild taro leaves. Buy taro as
food, from a food shop.

**Peeled, thoroughly cooked, mashed. That is the whole preparation, and there is
no shortcut inside it.** Raw or undercooked taro is not a texture problem, it is
a raphide exposure.

**If your baby complains of the mouth or throat after taro, treat it as a
raphide exposure, not as fussiness.** Burning, refusal, drooling, pawing at the
mouth or a hoarse cry shortly after eating are what oxalate raphide irritation
looks like, and the reaction is local rather than allergic. Stop the food, offer
something cold to drink, and get medical advice if there is any swelling,
breathing difficulty, or distress that does not settle — mouth and upper-airway
symptoms in a baby are worth a call, not a wait.

foods.name: Teff

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked into a soft porridge and mashed — teff grains are tiny, but they are still cooked whole kernels.
ageBands.prepMd:
Teff cooks into a soft porridge in about fifteen minutes with plenty of water —
it is small enough to go creamy on its own. Cook it past that point rather than
short of it, then mash any remaining texture out and thin with breast milk,
formula or water.

**The grains are tiny, and that is not an exemption.** CDC's rule is to cook and
then finely grind or mash whole grain kernels; teff isn't named, "and other
grains" is, and cooked teff is a cooked whole kernel. In practice a well-cooked
teff porridge already meets this — you are checking, not doing extra work.

Thicker porridge, and teff's mild molasses flavour carries other foods well —
mashed [[lentils]], [[black-beans]], puréed fruit. This is a good age to lean on
it, since iron requirements are highest and the grain is doing real work.

However the household eats it, kept soft. If injera is on the table, read the
safety note below first — it is a different question from teff.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until soft and mash or grind. Teff grains are very small but they are whole grain kernels, and CDC's rule is written about kernels rather than about size.

sources.body: CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods (cook and finely grind or mash whole-grain kernels)
CDC — Choking Hazards
CDC — Iron
FDA — Food Allergies (wheat is one of the nine major food allergens; teff is not)
CDC — Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit (sodium)
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 168918 teff, cooked; 169747 teff, uncooked). USDA has no record for injera.

foods.backgroundMd:
**Teff is the standout iron grain in this canon.** Cooked, it carries **2.05 mg
of iron per 100 g** — more than three times cooked [[quinoa]] and more than ten
times cooked [[millet]]. Uncooked it measures 7.63 mg per 100 g. For a whole
grain cooked at home, nothing else here comes close.

Two honest caveats sit next to that number.

**First, the iron may not all come from the grain.** Teff seeds are minute and
are traditionally threshed on the ground, and part of teff's measured iron is
attributed in the literature to soil contamination rather than to the plant
itself. **How much has not been quantified in anything this record could verify**,
so this record does not claim teff's iron is fully intrinsic — and does not
claim it isn't. What is measured is what USDA measured.

**Second, it is still non-heme iron**, so it absorbs far less efficiently than
the iron in [[beef]]. Serve a vitamin-C food in the same meal — [[potato]],
[[broccoli]], [[mango]] — which is CDC's own advice for non-heme sources.

Even at 2.05 mg, teff is not a substitute for [[fortified-infant-cereal]], which
is roughly thirty times higher per 100 g dry. It is, though, the best of the
home-cooked grains here by a wide margin.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Injera is where the allergen risk is, and it is easy to miss.** Commercial
injera is frequently made from teff **blended with wheat**, and sometimes barley
or sorghum. **Wheat is one of the nine major US allergens**, so an injera made
this way is a wheat exposure — one that is invisible to anyone who has learned
"teff is gluten-free" and stopped there. Teff on its own contains no gluten.
Injera made from it may. **Read the label or ask, and do not treat injera as
gluten-free by default.**

**This record publishes no nutrition figures for injera at all.** USDA has no
record for it — zero entries — so any iron, calcium or protein number you see
attached to injera, including from us, would be made up. The teff figures above
are for the cooked grain.

Injera is usually eaten with berbere-spiced stews, which are salty and hot.
CDC's advice on sodium applies, and a spiced stew is not the way to introduce
either the bread or the grain. Serve it plain.

**Cooked grain kernels are on CDC's choking-hazard list**, and the instruction is
to cook then finely grind or mash. Teff porridge satisfies this by its nature;
teff cooked drier and served in grains does not.

foods.name: Tofu

ageBands.servingNote: Firm tofu holds a baton shape. Press it under a weight for ten minutes first and it holds together far better in a fist.
ageBands.prepMd:
Buy firm or extra-firm. Drain it, wrap it in a clean towel, and press it under
something heavy for ten minutes — it firms up and stops falling apart in a fist.

Cut finger-length batons about as thick as two of your fingers. The whole-hand
grasp means the baton is held in a fist with an end sticking out and the baby
sets their own bite size. Plain and cold is fine; pan-frying briefly gives a
slightly firmer surface that holds together better, with no oil needed beyond a
film.

Tofu is slippery. Rolling a baton in ground oats, infant cereal, or a little
ground sesame gives grip — that is a handling aid, not a safety measure.

Mashed tofu also mixes into anything: purées, [[barley]] cereal, mashed
vegetables.

Serve it plain. Soy sauce is very high in sodium and is not appropriate before
24 months.

With the pincer grasp — most often from 9 to 10 months per AAP — cubes about the
size of your thumbnail are easy to pick up, and tofu holds a cube shape better
than most soft foods. Keep a couple of larger batons alongside so biting and
tearing stay in practice.

Crumbled firm tofu scrambled in a pan takes on other flavours well and is an
easy way to carry a vegetable the baby is less sure about.

However the household eats it — in soup, stir-fried, crumbled through
vegetables, in a soft stew. Silken tofu comes into its own here as a texture
rather than an iron source.

Watch the seasoning rather than the tofu: soy sauce, doenjang and most stir-fry
sauces carry more sodium than a toddler portion should, so take the child's
share out before the sauce goes in.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1 teaspoon of plain mashed firm tofu — on its own, or stirred into a food the baby already eats.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an existing food allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first soy exposure. That group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in infants without symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the child could have eaten safely.

choking.requiredModification: None beyond cutting it to a size the baby can hold. Tofu compresses under pressure rather than blocking, and it appears on no choking-hazard list.

CDC — When, What, and How to Introduce Solid Foods
American Academy of Pediatrics — Starting Solid Foods
NHS — Your baby's first solid foods
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Iron
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 172476 regular calcium-sulfate; 172475 firm; 174291 nigari; 172461 silken; 172450 koyadofu)

foods.backgroundMd:
Tofu has the strongest first-food credentials of anything in this batch: Health
Canada, CDC, AAP and NHS all name it, and Health Canada lists it among iron-rich
*first* foods — the category it treats as the priority at six months. It is
soft, compressible, appears on no choking-hazard list, and needs almost no
preparation.

**The iron depends entirely on how the tofu was set, and the spread is about
fivefold.** Tofu is made by curdling soy milk with a coagulant, and the
coagulant ends up in the food. Per 100 g, USDA's verified entries run: regular
tofu set with calcium sulfate, **5.36 mg** iron and 350 mg calcium; firm
calcium-sulfate tofu, 2.66 mg iron and 683 mg calcium; hard tofu set with nigari
(magnesium chloride), 2.75 mg and 345 mg; silken firm tofu, 1.03 mg and 32 mg;
and dried-frozen koyadofu, 9.73 mg and 364 mg.

Silken tofu carries a fifth to a tenth of the iron of calcium-set regular tofu.
If you are buying tofu *for* the iron — and at 5.36 mg per 100 g against an
11 mg daily target for a 7–12 month old, it is one of the few plant foods that
genuinely moves that number — read the ingredients panel for calcium sulfate.
The figure in this record is that form.

**The honest complication:** the same calcium that makes calcium-sulfate tofu
iron-rich also inhibits absorption of plant (non-heme) iron. You cannot resolve
that from the label, and no guideline body addresses it. What you can do is the
thing that helps regardless — serve a vitamin-C food in the same meal, since
vitamin C improves non-heme absorption. [[mango]], [[green-peas]] or
[[butternut-squash]] all work. Do not use [[yogurt]] as that partner: dairy
calcium works against you here.

**On soy and hormones.** Claims about phytoestrogens in infant diets are not
supported by any AAP, CDC or Health Canada prohibition, and all four of those
bodies name tofu as a food to give babies. This record does not repeat them as
guidance.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
There is very little to flag, which is unusual on this list. Tofu is soft,
compresses under pressure, and sits on no AAP or CDC hazard list. Cut it to a
size the baby can hold and it needs nothing else.

Two ordinary handling points. Keep opened tofu refrigerated and covered in
water, and use it within a few days — it is a fresh, high-protein food and it
spoils. And check that what you bought is plain: flavoured, smoked and marinated
tofu is usually salted heavily.

foods.name: Turkey (dark meat)

ageBands.servingNote: Finely chopped and moistened with unsalted broth or pan juices — dark meat holds moisture, but not once it is chopped and cooling.
ageBands.prepMd:
Skin, fat, and bones come off **before** cooking — CDC's order, and it keeps
bone fragments out of the finished meat entirely. Braise, poach, or roast the
thigh or leg until it pulls apart with a fork.

Cook all poultry to 165 °F (USDA FSIS), which explicitly covers legs and thighs.
Then chop the meat finely and stir in enough unsalted broth or pan juice that it
holds together on a spoon instead of scattering.

Run the chopped meat between your fingers before it goes on the tray. Turkey leg
in particular carries hard tendons that a fork will not catch and a baby cannot
chew.

Shredded rather than chopped. Long soft strands suit a pincer grasp better than
crumbs, and dark meat shreds cleanly once it is cooked through. Stirred into
[[oatmeal]] or mashed vegetables it stays moist longer than it does alone.

However the family eats it, still soft, still cut small, still deboned. Sliced
deli turkey is a different product and does not belong here — it is cured or
brined and carries the sodium that comes with that.

choking.requiredModification: Remove skin, fat, and bones before cooking, then finely chop or shred. Never chunks, and never a piece with a bone in it.
