Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — iron
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — choking hazards
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — foods and drinks to avoid or limit (sodium under 24 months)
USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service — safe minimum internal temperatures, all poultry including legs and thighs (updated 2025-04-14)
Canadian Paediatric Society — feeding your baby in the first year
WHO — guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children 6–23 months (2023)
USDA FoodData Central (fdcId 171091, turkey dark meat roasted; 172388, chicken thigh roasted; 174508 and 174510, turkey with added solution)

foods.backgroundMd:
Dark turkey meat is the quiet upgrade on [[chicken-thigh]]. Roasted, it carries
1.43 mg of iron and 3.51 mg of zinc per 100 g against chicken thigh's 1.13 mg
iron and 1.92 mg zinc — about 27% more iron and roughly 83% more zinc, for a
food that cooks the same way and tastes almost the same to a baby. The zinc gap
is the more interesting one.

**These figures are for dark meat only.** Thigh, leg, and drumstick meat — not
breast. Turkey breast is a different food nutritionally, and carrying these
numbers across to it would overstate what a breast portion delivers. If you buy
a whole bird, the dark meat is the part this record is about.

The iron is heme iron, the readily absorbed form. As with [[beef]] and lamb, it
does not need a vitamin-C food beside it.

One honesty note on form. AAP names "well-cooked, finely chopped chicken" as a
finger food — unusually specific for a guideline body, which mostly describes
textures rather than dishes. No body says the same sentence about turkey.
Extending chicken's phrasing to turkey is our inference and common practice, not
an issued instruction; it is a reasonable one, because the two behave
identically in a pan, but you should know which is which.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Buy an unenhanced bird.** This is the purchasing instruction that actually
changes the numbers. Turkey sold "with added solution", "enhanced", "self-
basting", or brine-injected is water, salt and phosphate injected into the meat,
and USDA's own records for those products show roughly 25% *less* iron per 100 g
than plain roasted dark meat, plus the added sodium — while CDC advises against
high-sodium foods under two years. You lose on both counts at once. Read the
label on the package: the added-solution declaration is required to be there,
usually in small print near the weight.

**Tendons and bones.** Turkey legs carry more and tougher tendons than chicken.
Debone before cooking, then check the chopped or shredded meat by hand. Bones in
meat are on CDC's hazard list and do not become safe by being small.

**Chunks.** "Tough or large chunks of meat" stays on the hazard list past the
first birthday. Finely chopped or shredded is the form, at every age in this
range.

**Doneness.** 165 °F, measured, not judged by colour. Turkey thigh meat stays
slightly rosy near the bone even when fully cooked, so colour will mislead you
in both directions here.

foods.name: Wheat pasta

ageBands.servingNote: Cooked well past al dente until it mashes under a fork. Short shapes or wide flat pieces — not long strands.
ageBands.prepMd:
**Cook it well past al dente.** Whatever the box says, add several minutes, and
test by squashing a piece between two fingers — it should give completely. CDC's
standard for infant food is that it mashes easily, and pasta cooked to an
adult's bite does not: it stays springy and slick, which is the worst pair of
properties to hand a baby with no molars.

**Short shapes beat long strands.** A single elbow, a wide flat piece, a large
shell — something the whole hand can hold and the gums can crush. If you only
have spaghetti, cut it short after cooking. CDC's shape rule is to cut
cylindrical foods into short thin strips rather than rounds, and a long strand
of pasta is the one form that invites a baby to take in more than they can
manage.

**No salt in the cooking water.** This is the step people skip because it feels
like it belongs to the pot rather than the baby. Salted water is how a
6 mg-per-100 g food stops being one.

Toss the cooked pasta with a little of its water, or a plain sauce, so it does
not stick to itself in a clump.

Smaller shapes for the pincer grasp, still cooked soft, still no piece larger
than half an inch. Pasta with a mashed vegetable or a soft protein stirred
through is easier to gather than bare pieces that slide around the tray.

Still no salt in the water, and be careful with jarred sauces at this age — they
are usually where the sodium arrives once the pasta itself has stopped
contributing any.

However the household eats it, cooked softer than the adults would choose, and
cut down. Long strands can come in around now with supervision, cut into short
lengths.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: A spoonful of plain wheat pasta cooked soft and mashed, or one or two soft pieces to hold. No body publishes a first-serving amount or a weekly target for wheat — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to wheat — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no wheat testing protocol, no wheat dose and no wheat weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food. Check the ingredients before a first wheat exposure: many pastas also contain EGG, which is a second major allergen, and a first taste of two allergens at once tells you nothing about which one caused a reaction.

choking.requiredModification: Cook it well past al dente, until a piece mashes between your fingers or under a fork — CDC's rule is to cook until it mashes easily. Use short shapes rather than long strands, or cut strands short; CDC's shape rule is to cut cylindrical foods into short thin strips, not rounds.

CDC — foods and drinks to avoid or limit (added salt)
FDA — Gluten-Free Labeling of Foods (wheat, rye and barley are the gluten grains; only wheat is one of the nine major allergens)
American Academy of Pediatrics — introducing common food allergens

foods.backgroundMd:
Pasta is the **low-sodium** way to cover wheat. Cooked whole-grain pasta runs
about **6 mg of sodium per 100 g**; wheat toast runs 473 mg untoasted and 601
toasted. If you are covering the wheat allergen and the sodium in
[[wheat-toast]] bothers you — it should — this is the same allergen at a
hundredth of the salt. Iron is 1.65 mg per 100 g, non-heme, so pair it with a
vitamin-C food in the same meal: [[broccoli]], [[green-peas]], a tomato sauce.

**Check the label before the first exposure, because pasta frequently contains
egg.** Fresh pasta almost always does, "egg noodles" say so, and plenty of dried
pastas include it without making a point of it. **Egg is a second major
allergen**, and if it arrives unannounced inside a first wheat exposure you have
introduced two allergens simultaneously and learned nothing useful from either.
It is on the label — US law requires egg to be declared — so it takes ten
seconds to check. See [[egg]] for how to introduce it deliberately.

**On iron, a gap worth knowing about.** The figure on this record is for
whole-grain pasta. **Enriched** pasta — most standard white pasta in the US — is
meaningfully higher in iron because iron is added back, but no verified USDA
entry for it was available while this was written, so no enriched figure appears
here. Do not read 1.65 mg as the ceiling for all pasta; read it as the one number
that could be stood behind.

Wheat is one of the nine major allergens. Barley and rye contain gluten but are
not major allergens, and "gluten-free" is not the same claim as "wheat-free" —
[[barley]] covers that distinction, and the separate question of celiac disease,
in full.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Pasta is not a named entry on any official choking list.** The instructions
here are applications of CDC's general rules — cook until it mashes easily, cut
cylindrical foods into short thin strips — plus AAP's half-inch maximum. That is
category-level coverage and this record says so rather than implying a
pasta-specific ruling exists.

**Undercooked pasta is the actual hazard.** Al dente is a texture designed for
teeth. A firm, curved, slippery piece is exactly the profile that lodges.

**Egg is the allergen that arrives by surprise.** Read the ingredients, not the
shape of the noodle.

**Salt is the thing you control.** No salt in the water, and check the sauce.

foods.name: Wheat toast strips

ageBands.servingNote: Toasted until dry through, cut into narrow strips no more than half an inch wide, one strip at a time.
ageBands.prepMd:
Toast a slice **until it is dry the whole way through**, not just browned on the
outside. Press the middle with a finger: if it gives like fresh bread, it is not
there yet. The point is to remove the property that makes bread awkward — soft
crumb compresses into a dense, gummy wad against the palate, and a baby cannot
easily clear that.

Cut it into narrow strips, along the slice, **no more than about half an inch
wide** — AAP's half-inch rule is the only dimension any guideline body issues,
and here it applies to the width of the strip. Length is what lets a
six-month-old hold it with a whole-hand grasp and gnaw the protruding end. Crusts
on or off is your call; the crust is the part most likely to come off in a lump,
so trim it if it is thick.

One strip at a time on the tray. A handful of strips gets crammed.

Nothing on it, or a very thin scrape of something — see [[almond-butter]] or
[[tahini]] for how thinly, since a thick layer of any butter is separately a
hazard.

Smaller pieces for the pincer grasp, still dry-toasted, still no bigger than
half an inch in any direction. This is also the age where soggy toast becomes a
problem in a new way: toast dipped in soup or milk and left to sit reverts to
the balled-up texture toasting was meant to fix. Serve it dipped and eaten, not
dipped and abandoned.

However the family eats it, within the sodium caveat above. Sandwiches cut into
strips, toast with a thin spread, toast crumbs through other food. Keep watching
the loaf's label rather than the shape of the toast — by this age the shape has
stopped being the interesting part and the salt has not.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: A narrow strip of plain wheat toast, or a spoonful of toast crumbs softened in a familiar puree. No body publishes a first-serving amount or a weekly target for wheat — this is a practical starting point, not a dose.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema and/or an existing food allergy, talk to your pediatrician before the first exposure to wheat — that group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in an infant with no symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance. NIAID's addendum guidelines cover PEANUT ONLY. There is no wheat testing protocol, no wheat dose and no wheat weekly target in US guidance, and peanut's numbers must not be read across to this food. If celiac disease runs in your family, that is a separate question from allergy and belongs with your pediatrician too.

choking.requiredModification: Toast it until it is dry the whole way through, not just coloured on the surface. Soft fresh bread balls up into a dense wad in the mouth. Cut narrow strips — AAP's half-inch maximum applies to the width — and never serve a doughy centre or a torn handful.

American Academy of Pediatrics — choking prevention (no piece larger than one-half inch)
NHS — baby's first solid foods (narrow batons; finger foods cut to a size the baby can hold)

foods.backgroundMd:
Toast is the most convenient way most families cover **wheat**, one of the nine
major US allergens, and it doubles as an early self-feeding food. Both of those
are true. The thing nobody mentions is the sodium.

**Wheat bread carries 473 mg of sodium per 100 g. Toasted, the same bread carries
601 mg.** Toasting does not add salt — it drives off water, which concentrates
everything left behind by roughly 27%, sodium included. A number like 601 mg per
100 g in a food routinely handed to six-month-olds as a first finger food
deserves a second look, and this record is giving it one. Buy the lowest-sodium
loaf you can find, or a no-salt-added one, and do not treat toast as a neutral
background food you can serve at every meal. If you want a low-sodium wheat
vehicle, that is [[wheat-pasta]], at 6 mg per 100 g.

**Be careful about what the numbers describe.** Both USDA entries behind this
record are for "**Bread, wheat**" — not whole-wheat. A verified entry for a
genuinely whole-wheat loaf could not be established while this was written, so
this record is labelled wheat, not whole-wheat, and you should not read its
figures onto a whole-grain loaf. The iron, 4.09 mg per 100 g, is **largely from
enrichment rather than from the grain**, which is why this record's iron is
tagged fortified.

**Wheat, gluten and celiac are three different things**, and they get muddled
constantly. Wheat is one of the nine major allergens and must be declared on a
label. Barley and rye contain gluten but are **not** major allergens — see
[[barley]], which covers that distinction and the celiac timing question in full.
"Gluten-free" and "wheat-free" are not the same claim. And celiac disease is not
an IgE allergy: it is not governed by allergen-introduction timing, and it is not
what this record's medical gate is about.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
**Bread is on no official choking list, and "toast it first" is issued by
nobody.** That is worth saying out loud. Toasting is sound, widespread practice
and this record recommends it, but it is common practice and not guidance, so it
is tiered that way. What *is* issued: AAP's half-inch maximum, NHS's narrow
batons, and CDC's principle of cutting cylindrical foods into short thin strips
rather than rounds. The strip shape here comes from those.

**Soft fresh bread is the form to avoid**, especially white sandwich bread torn
into pieces. It compresses instead of breaking up.

**Sodium is the ongoing risk, not the acute one.** 601 mg per 100 g toasted. CDC
advises against added salt for babies, and this record cannot give you a mg/day
infant limit because **no verified figure was available** — do not read that
silence as permission. Choose the lowest-sodium loaf available and vary the
grain: [[oatmeal]] and [[barley]] carry no salt at all.

**Wheat toast with a nut or seed butter is two hazard entries at once.** The
toast is fine; the thick glob is not. Spread it very thinly.

foods.name: Plain whole-milk yogurt

ageBands.servingNote: Load the spoon and hand it over handle-first. A dipped strip of toast or cooked vegetable works as an edible spoon.
ageBands.prepMd:
Plain, pasteurized, whole-fat. Start with about a teaspoon, on its own or
stirred into something familiar.

Loading a spoon and handing it over handle-first is the practical move at this
age — a whole-hand grasp can hold a spoon long before it can fill one. A strip
of cooked [[butternut-squash]] or a finger of toast dipped in yogurt works as an
edible spoon and gives more grip.

Watch for about two hours after the first exposure. IgE reactions happen within
minutes to two hours, which is also why the familiar "wait 3–5 days before the
next new food" habit adds nothing diagnostically — it just slows down variety.

Greek yogurt is thicker and less likely to run off a spoon, which some babies
prefer and most trays do.

Same food, more independence. This is a good age to let the baby hold the spoon
themselves and accept the mess; self-feeding a wet food is a skill with a
learning curve and no shortcut.

Stir in mashed fruit yourself rather than buying it pre-mixed — flavoured
yogurts marketed to babies carry added sugar, which is off the menu under 24
months.

However the household eats it. Plain yogurt with fruit stirred in, as a dip, in
a smoothie, spooned over grains.

Keep it whole-fat. Babies should get roughly half their calories from fat, and
AAP does not recommend restricting fat before age two.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1 teaspoon of plain, pasteurized, whole-milk yogurt — on its own, or stirred into a food the baby already eats.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an existing food allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first milk exposure. That group may need a supervised introduction. Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in infants without symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance of a food the child could have eaten safely.

foods.backgroundMd:
Yogurt is not a food that squeaks past the cow's-milk rule. Before twelve months
it is the **preferred** form of cow's milk protein, and four bodies say so
independently: AAP calls plain, whole-fat or whole Greek yogurt "a good first
form of cow's milk protein" and puts dairy foods at around six months; CDC says
yogurt without added sugars can be introduced before twelve months; NHS puts it
from around six months; Health Canada from six to nine.

**Why the drink is prohibited and the food is not.** The rule against cow's milk
before twelve months is about *large-volume unmodified* milk. CDC names three
concrete problems with it: risk of intestinal bleeding, more protein and mineral
load than an immature kidney handles easily, and the wrong nutrient profile for
an infant. AAP adds that cow's-milk protein can irritate the lining of the
stomach and intestine, and frames the rule around **quantity**. The fourth
problem is displacement — a bottle of milk crowds out breast milk or formula and
the iron-rich food a baby needs at this age.

Yogurt escapes every one of those. It is eaten in food-sized portions rather
than drunk by the bottle — AAP's own 8-to-12-month sample menu puts it at 2 to 4
oz — so it does not displace the primary milk. And fermentation partially breaks
down both casein and lactose before the baby ever meets them. It is also the
usual vehicle for introducing the milk allergen early, which is why it is
recommended rather than merely tolerated.

**A real disagreement between national bodies, reported not resolved.** Health
Canada permits pasteurized homogenized cow milk as the *main* milk source from
**9 to 12 months** for an infant no longer breastfed. CDC and AAP say twelve
months, not before. This record does not pick a winner. Nothing about that
disagreement touches yogurt, which all four bodies allow from around six months.

**Iron is essentially zero** — 0.05 mg per 100 g — and this matters more than it
sounds. Dairy calcium *inhibits* absorption of plant (non-heme) iron. So do not
use yogurt as the "something alongside" for an iron meal: pair [[tofu]],
[[barley]] cereal, [[green-peas]] or [[spinach]] with a vitamin-C food like
[[mango]] instead, and serve the yogurt at a different sitting.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Three hard rules, all of them about the pot you buy rather than how you serve it.

**Plain only.** AAP is explicit about avoiding the added sugar commonly found in
yogurt marketed to babies. No added sugars under 24 months.

**Pasteurized only.** This applies to the yogurt and to any milk used to make
it.

**Whole-fat, not low-fat.** Reduced-fat dairy is an adult recommendation applied
to the wrong body.

Yogurt itself is not a choking risk — it is already a safe consistency. The
thing to check is what has been mixed *into* it: whole grapes, whole berries,
chunks of dried fruit and granola clusters in an adult pot are all on the hazard
lists in their own right.

Yogurt is not a substitute for breast milk or formula. It is a food that sits
alongside them, not a drink that replaces them.
